papers.title: Extending Healthspan Through Lifestyle: Nutrition, Physical Activity, Sleep, and Other Modifiable Behaviors-A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Population aging has increased interest in extending healthspan, defined here as the period of life characterized by preserved physical and cognitive function, independence, and well-being. This narrative review examines major modifiable determinants of healthspan and critically evaluates how established lifestyle strategies compare with newer approaches promoted within the longevity field. A structured, topic-driven search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science focused primarily on publications from January 2015 to August 2026, with earlier studies included when relevant. To provide a mechanistic and translational frame, the major interventions were mapped to the hallmarks of aging and stratified by level of evidence, distinguishing human clinical outcome data from biomarker, mechanistic, and animal findings. The most consistent human evidence supports high-quality dietary patterns, regular physical activity, and healthy sleep as central components of healthy aging. Stress management, social connection, avoidance of harmful exposures, and the physical and socioeconomic environment are also relevant to healthy aging and influence the context in which these behaviors occur. Observations from long-lived real-world populations, such as the blue zones, are consistent with this evidence. The gut microbiome represents an important interface between lifestyle and host physiology, although changes in microbial composition should not be assumed to translate into improved healthspan. Evidence for dietary supplements is strongest when use addresses deficiency, inadequate intake, or a defined clinical indication. Intermittent fasting and time-restricted eating can improve selected weight and cardiometabolic outcomes, but evidence that they extend healthspan remains limited. Similar uncertainty applies to several emerging longevity practices, where biomarker changes or short-term physiological responses often precede evidence of meaningful clinical benefit. Greater personalization may refine lifestyle and nutritional interventions, but its added value over well-designed standard care requires further study. Healthy aging is therefore best supported by sustained, evidence-based lifestyle behaviors, while newer strategies should be judged by their ability to improve long-term function, disease burden, and independence rather than by biological plausibility alone.

papers.title: Associations Between Chronic Diarrhea and Geriatric Syndromes, Dietary Habits, and Health Outcomes Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults.
papers.abstract: Background: The present study examined the associations between chronic diarrhea and geriatric syndromes, dietary habits, and health outcomes among community-dwelling older adults. Methods: This cross-sectional study included data from the 2005-2006, 2007-2008, and 2009-2010 NHANES cycles. The primary analytical sample comprised 3498 adults aged ≥65 years with available information on chronic diarrhea. Chronic diarrhea was operationalized according to participants usual stool consistency using the Bristol Stool Form Scale (types 6-7). Outcomes included disability, multimorbidity, polypharmacy, frailty, risk of sarcopenia, malnutrition, sleep disorders, dietary patterns, self-rated diet quality, hospital admission, and mental health service use. Logistic and linear regression models were used to examine associations, with adjusted models including age and sex. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was applied to control the false discovery rate (FDR). Results: Chronic diarrhea was identified in 328 participants (9.4%). After adjustment for age and sex, chronic diarrhea was associated with higher odds of disability in basic (OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.15-2.48) and instrumental activities of daily living (OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.37-2.31), polypharmacy (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.13-1.78), and frailty (OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.26-4.02). Participants with chronic diarrhea were also less likely to report good dietary quality (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.42-0.72). These five associations remained statistically significant after FDR correction (q < 0.05). Although chronic diarrhea was initially associated with sleep disorders (OR 1.89, 95% CI 1.08-3.30), this association did not remain significant after FDR correction (q = 0.121). No significant associations were observed with multimorbidity, sarcopenia-related measures, malnutrition, protein or fiber intake, dietary-pattern scores, hospital admission, or mental health service use. Conclusions: These findings suggest that usual loose or watery stools may identify older adults with greater functional and clinical vulnerability. However, the results should be interpreted cautiously, and longitudinal studies incorporating the NHANES sampling design and more comprehensive confounder adjustment are needed.

papers.title: Creatine Beyond Muscle: Pleiotropic Effects with and Without Exercise-A Critical Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Creatine is an established ergogenic aid, but its benefits beyond its effects in muscles remain uncertain. This critical narrative review examines cognitive, neurological, psychiatric, metabolic, vascular, skeletal, inflammatory, and rehabilitation outcomes. Targeted searches and citation tracing included publications available on 30 October 2026. We distinguished effects without prescribed exercise, incremental benefits within a common programme, interaction, intervention packages, and mediation. Small studies under sleep loss or hypoxia reported selected cognitive signals; findings in rested adults were inconsistent and benefits in the neurodegenerative conditions examined remained unestablished. Psychiatric findings remained heterogeneous and did not establish clinically important average efficacy. A potentially clinically important glycated haemoglobin reduction in one small exercise-add-on trial in type 2 diabetes remains unreplicated and at a high risk of bias. Vascular findings concerned short-term surrogates; bone-density outcomes were largely null, chronic anti-inflammatory efficacy unestablished, and rehabilitation findings inconsistent. Creatine modestly increased lean mass during resistance training, but downstream clinical mediation was unproven. Sparse evidence on randomised creatine-by-exercise interaction and mediation limits causal attribution without invalidating incremental effects estimated in suitable two-arm trials. Heterogeneous regimens preclude a generalisable dose recommendation. Clinical interpretation should remain indication-specific, prioritising the replication of relevant effects and testing interactions or mediations when those are the research questions.

papers.title: Development and Evaluation of a Cap-Mounted Tripolar Concentric Ring Electrode System with a Central Gel-Delivery Opening for tEEG and EEG Recording.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) commonly uses conventional disc electrodes with conductive gel or paste to record electrical activity from the scalp. However, conventional disc electrodes have limited spatial selectivity because they detect electrical activity spreading from different brain regions. Tripolar concentric ring electrodes (TCREs) have been developed to improve spatial selectivity by estimating the scalp surface Laplacian. Nevertheless, establishing electrical contact at hair-bearing scalp locations remains challenging. To address this challenge, we developed a modified gold-plated copper TCRE with a 2 mm central opening for conductive gel delivery and a custom 3D-printed cap-mounted holder. After electrode placement, conductive gel is delivered through the opening to establish electrical contact between the metallic contacts and the scalp beneath the hair. The system was evaluated in ten healthy adults using eyes-open/eyes-closed resting-state EEG and pattern-reversal checkerboard visual stimulation. For the experimental recordings, two modified TCREs were positioned at the occipital scalp locations O1 and O2, where conductive gel was delivered through their central openings to establish electrical contact with the scalp. A third TCRE was positioned at Pz and coupled using conductive paste, while a separate conventional disc electrode was placed 1 cm superior to Pz. Recordings from these electrode configurations were analyzed to evaluate resting-state alpha activity, visual evoked potentials (VEPs), and signal quality. Each TCRE provided tripolar EEG (tEEG) and EEG Emulator (eEEG) signals. The modified TCREs recorded identifiable VEP components, with negative and positive peaks near 105 and 141 ms, respectively, along with stimulus-related spectral activity. The eEEG VEP waveforms at O1 and O2 showed strong correlations with Pz eEEG (median r=0.897 and 0.938, respectively). Alpha-band power also increased significantly during eye closure in both gel-coupled tEEG channels (Holm-adjusted p=0.0195). Impedance measurements, signal-quality analyses, and circuit modeling provided additional characterization of the system. These findings support the feasibility of acquiring tEEG and eEEG signals using the modified TCRE system at hair-bearing scalp locations.

papers.title: GamSleepNet: A Lightweight Automatic Sleep Staging Framework Based on Gabor Feature Extraction and Mamba Sequence Modeling for Single-Channel EEG.
papers.abstract: Automatic sleep staging is a key technology for the precise diagnosis and treatment of sleep disorders and for long-term home sleep monitoring. Due to its convenience of use, single-channel electroencephalogram (EEG) has become a research focus in home sleep monitoring. However, existing algorithms still face several practical bottlenecks. For example, models with a large number of parameters are prone to overfitting on small labeled datasets; the hardware heterogeneity of customized portable sensors makes datasets not directly shareable; large-scale labeled samples are hard to obtain in real scenarios; there is low recognition accuracy for difficult-to-distinguish sleep stages such as N1 and REM; and there is a lack of suitable research methods for evaluating the required scale of training data for lightweight deployment scenarios. In this paper we propose GamSleepNet, a low-parameter-count automatic sleep staging framework for single-channel EEG. The framework combines a feature extraction module (FEB), which integrates improved Gabor kernels with a learnable filter branch, with a standard Mamba selective state-space model (SSM) used for temporal modeling. A teacher-student feature alignment loss (FAL) and a two-stage training strategy are introduced to enhance the discriminative ability for difficult sleep stages. In addition, following the established paradigm of varying the training dataset's size and observing the performance curve, we make four adaptations tailored to sleep staging, thereby determining the appropriate training data volume for GamSleepNet and providing a methodological reference for determining the training data scale required for deploying other models. Under the limited-labeled-subject setting of the Sleep-EDF dataset, the model has 30.86 k parameters and achieves an overall accuracy of 87.86% and a macro F1 score of 82.62%-the highest values among the compared models-and improves the recognition of difficult REM and N1 samples. The model still maintains stable staging performance under low signal-to-noise ratio and label-scarce scenarios.

papers.title: Motor Imagery Decoding with Common Spatial Filters and Compact CNNs: A Controlled Study of Hybrid CSP-FBCSP.
papers.abstract: Motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable communication through brain activity, but reliable decoding of electroencephalography (EEG) remains challenging due to low signal quality, inter-subject variability, and limited training data. This study investigates a lightweight hybrid framework combining Common Spatial Pattern (CSP), Filter Bank CSP (FBCSP), and their feature-level fusion with an exceptionally compact EEGNet classifier. Using a subject-specific, session-to-session evaluation protocol, we assess four classification tasks across BCI Competition IV-2a (9 subjects) and Lee2019_MI (54 subjects). The hybrid CSP-FBCSP framework achieves higher mean classification accuracy than a raw-EEG EEGNet baseline across all four tasks, with improvements of 3.0-11.2 percentage points, statistically significant in three tasks under uncorrected Wilcoxon tests. However, fusion significantly outperforms individual CSP or FBCSP front-ends in only two of eight paired comparisons. A matched-input-size ablation further shows that fusion achieves the highest mean accuracy on the two binary BCI IV-2a tasks, but not on the four-class task or Lee2019_MI. Feature-redundancy analysis provides additional insight into the overlap between spatial representations. These findings demonstrate the potential of classical spatial-spectral feature extraction for compact EEG classification while revealing that the additional benefit of feature fusion is task-dependent.

papers.title: Development and Characterization of a Multi-Directional Light Dosimeter for Environmental Light Qualification: The Light Tracker.
papers.abstract: Light is essential for several biological functions: it enables vision, regulates circadian rhythms, and influences neuroendocrine activity. However, both the quality and the quantity of light strongly determine its effects on the human body. Accurate characterization of light exposure in free-living conditions is therefore required to distinguish natural illumination from artificial sources. A common practice is to use 1000 lux as a threshold to differentiate outdoor from indoor conditions, and by extension natural versus artificial light. However, this categorization is unreliable, as it is highly sensitive to measurement conditions such as sensor orientation and shadowing. To overcome these limitations, we developed a multi-directional light dosimeter designed for seamless daily life use while capturing spatial variations in light and enabling robust environmental qualification. The Light Tracker is equipped with multiple spectral sensors positioned across different orientations to quantify directional dependence and identify the orientation that best represents a wearer's light environment. The device is USB-powered for ease of use in any context and is controlled through a dedicated mobile application. Characterization and calibration procedures employed controlled broadband sources, neutral-density filtering, and outdoor reference measurements to ensure the reliability of the collected data. Initial measurements demonstrate a strong angular dependence of absolute illuminance but higher stability of spectral ratios. They also highlight the robustness of the upward-facing side. Overall, the Light Tracker provides an effective tool for multi-dimensional light characterization, enabling real-world environmental classification and wearable photometric monitoring.

papers.title: Physiology-Guided Spiking Neural Networks for EEG Motor-Imagery Recognition.
papers.abstract: Motor-imagery electroencephalography (EEG) decoding depends on rhythm-specific modulation, cue-locked temporal evolution, and structured electrode topology, yet many decoders treat EEG as a generic multichannel time series. (1) Background: A physiological prior that stays in preprocessing cannot constrain what the decoder represents, and spiking networks let such a prior act on the event code itself. (2) Methods: We introduce PG-SNN, which embeds EEG priors in the event code, spatial operator, temporal dynamics, and readout. A causal eventizer converts EEG into sparse, sign-preserving spikes using rhythm-sensitive, temporal-change, and montage-contrast operators; an electrode-prior graph restricts message passing to local montage adjacency and homologous inter-hemispheric coupling; and a multi-timescale adaptive spiking backbone represents rapid event transitions and slower mu/beta modulation. (3) Results: On BCI Competition IV-2a the model reaches 84.72% accuracy (kappa = 0.796), 2.56 and 5.64 percentage points above the strongest matched ANN and SNN baselines; on the EEGMMIDB four-class subject-independent protocol, it reaches 71.28% (kappa = 0.617), 3.86 points above the strongest matched ANN baseline, and a fifteen-variant ablation attributes the largest single effect to the event code. (4) Conclusions: Embedding sensorimotor physiology into event generation, spatial propagation, and spike dynamics is a practical route to compact motor-imagery decoders, within the limits of the two benchmarks and the single shared protocol.

papers.title: Operational Definitions of Transition Onset Shape EEG Biomarker Timing in Drowsiness: A Single-Channel Method Comparison.
papers.abstract: Early-warning claims for electroencephalography (EEG)-based drowsiness detection rest on lead times, yet a lead time depends on how onset is operationally defined and is rarely tested against a null. We developed a benchmarking framework and applied it to seven onset estimators and 32 features from single-channel frontal EEG (17 participants, observer-verified drowsiness reports), with external replication in the DROZY dataset (13 sessions with an eligible vigilance-lapse anchor, of 20 retained). Estimator choice shifted onsets by minutes and changed detection coverage from 45% to 100% (Kendall's W = 0.53; external W = 0.71; absolute-agreement intraclass correlation 0.05). In simulation, two-standard-deviation baseline rules flagged onsets in 77-88% of no-change trajectories; null-calibrated thresholds (about 4.6 standard deviations) restored a nominal 5% rate. No estimator showed a statistically detectable excess of onsets in the final 150 s before the anchor relative to spectrum-preserving surrogates, a consensus detector fired before pseudo-anchors as often as before the true anchor, and adding EEG to elapsed session time gave no detectable improvement (area-under-the-curve difference 0.01, 95% confidence interval -0.11 to 0.13). Higuchi fractal dimension and line length correlated weakly with measured electrooculography (|r| ≤ 0.15). We propose interpretability criteria, evidence levels and a reporting checklist for early-onset claims.

papers.title: EEG Theta Power as an Indicator of Cognitive Workload in Student Pilots.
papers.abstract: Aviation operates within a highly cognitively demanding environment, where assessing pilot workload is essential for preventing errors and accidents associated with excessive or insufficient cognitive demand. This study presents a neurophysiological experiment designed to assess pilot brain activity using electroencephalography (EEG) in a high-fidelity Pilatus PC-21 flight simulator. The study focuses on the theta frequency band (4-8 Hz), given its association with mental effort and cognitive engagement. EEG signals were recorded from eight scalp locations in ten pilots during baseline conditions and three flight simulation modules with different levels of task difficulty. Subjective workload was assessed using the NASA-TLX questionnaire, completed after each simulation phase. The results showed higher theta power during the most cognitively demanding flight phase, particularly across frontal, temporal, and occipital regions. NASA-TLX results similarly indicated increased mental demand, effort, and frustration in the scenario associated with the highest cognitive workload. However, correlation analysis revealed a weak and inconsistent relationship between subjective workload ratings and EEG-derived theta measures across participants, with no clear or statistically significant overall association at the group level. These preliminary results indicate that scalp-recorded theta activity is sensitive to changes in task difficulty during flight simulation. However, given the exploratory nature of the study, the absence of flight-performance metrics, and the lack of strong correlation with subjective ratings, theta-band modulation should be interpreted as an index of task demand rather than a fully consolidated operational workload estimator.

papers.title: Sensorimotor EEG Responses and Parietal Symmetry Objectively Reflect Ankle Kinesthesia and Position Sense in Healthy Middle-Aged and Older Adults.
papers.abstract: Objective assessment of ankle proprioception may clarify sensory contributions to post-stroke balance impairment. Position sense and kinesthesia are complementary, yet their stage-specific cortical correlates remain unclear. We combined joint position reproduction (JPR) and passive movement detection (PMD) within a passive dynamometer-electroencephalography (EEG) framework in 15 healthy middle-aged and older adults. After quality screening, 13 JPR and 14 PMD datasets were analyzed. Position sense was quantified by position matching error (ME), and kinesthesia by movement detection time (MDT). EEG quantified the brain symmetry index (BSI) during position encoding, event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) during reproduction, and movement-evoked N1 during movement detection. Lower parietal BSI was associated with smaller ME across the delta, theta, alpha, and broadband ranges (r = 0.603-0.854, p = 0.001-0.029). During position reproduction, mu/alpha- and beta-band power decreased over sensorimotor regions as the ankle approached the remembered target. Passive movement elicited a frontocentral N1 whose latency was positively associated with MDT at five midline electrodes (r = 0.570-0.803, p = 0.003-0.034). Position accuracy was linked to bilateral parietal organization and sensorimotor processing, whereas movement detection speed was linked to cortical response timing. These findings provide a physiological reference for ankle position sense and kinesthesia in healthy middle-aged and older adults based on averaged EEG features and their associations with behavioral performance, with single-trial reproducibility to be evaluated in future studies.

papers.title: AI-Driven Non-Invasive Scalp EEG Biosensing for Real-Time Seizure Prediction Using Lightweight Gradient Boosting Ensembles.
papers.abstract: Clinical translation of non-invasive scalp electroencephalography (EEG) seizure prediction is severely hindered by patient-dependency, elevated false alarm rates, and excessive computational latency. This study introduces a computationally lightweight, patient-independent machine learning pipeline designed to achieve cross-patient generalization and robust false alarm suppression without requiring subject-specific calibration. Using the continuous multi-channel scalp EEG dataset from the CHB-MIT benchmark (materials/setting), signals underwent dual-stage filtering (1-70 Hz bandpass, 60 Hz notch), artifact removal via Extended FastICA, and Common Average Referencing. Dimensionality was reduced via Principal Component Analysis (12 orthogonal components, >95.4% variance explained). Continuous streams were partitioned into 5 s sliding windows (90% overlap) to extract multi-domain temporal, spectral, and discrete wavelet features, subsequently pruned via ANOVA F-testing to 168 salient predictors. Pre-ictal transitions (20 to 5 min prior to seizure onset, incorporating an excluded 5 min prediction horizon buffer) were classified using a synchronized ensemble of regularized XGBoost and leaf-wise LightGBM models. Dual-model coincidence was governed by a 30 s moving temporal alignment window coupled with 12-epoch persistence smoothing and a 30 min refractory lockout. To prevent intra-subject data leakage, multi-session recordings from the same individual (Cases 01 and 21) were strictly co-located within the training set, and the pipeline was evaluated on an isolated cohort of four completely unseen subjects (Patients 20, 22-24) across 156.5 continuous, unsampled hours. On the independent unseen test cohort, the post-processed framework achieved a primary event-level seizure sensitivity of 100% (34/34 seizures detected; 95% Clopper-Pearson CI: 89.72-100.0%), mathematically bounded by the test sample size, with a false alarm rate of 0.415/h (an 89.5% reduction versus the raw ensemble) and a mean Seizure Prediction Horizon of 17.03 min. Under continuous 0.5 s sliding-window streaming (designed for real-time edge persistence filtering), the framework demonstrated 99.80% operational pre-ictal alert consistency (60,772/60,894 sliding windows; specificity: 98.64%, precision: 91.20%, F1-score: 95.31%). Evaluated on strictly independent, non-overlapping 5 s epochs (N = 6120), the ensemble retained a pre-ictal sensitivity of 99.1%, confirming robust performance independent of window overlap. Execution latency was 0.0057 ms per window, delivering a >1000× speedup over state-of-the-art 3D-CNN and Transformer architectures. By eliminating multi-session data leakage and mitigating clinical alarm fatigue, this pipeline offers reliable cross-patient generalizability, practical intervention timing, and ultra-low computational latency suitable for real-time deployment on low-power wearable closed-loop neurostimulation devices.

papers.title: A Temporally Causal Two-Layer Framework for Wearable EEG Sleep Staging and Short-Horizon Sleep-Transition Forecasting.
papers.abstract: Reliable online sleep monitoring requires sleep-stage estimates and forecasts based only on information available at the time of prediction. This study developed a temporally causal two-layer framework for wearable electroencephalography (EEG) sleep staging and short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting. Using 128 Bitbrain Open Access Sleep (BOAS) recordings from 100 participants, the first layer (M0) performed five-stage sleep classification with causal signal processing and participant-isolated nested validation. The second layer (M1) used strictly cross-fitted histories of M0 stage probabilities to predict transitions from wake or N1 (W/N1) to N2, N3, or REM sleep (N2+) within 60, 90, or 120 s after each observed 30-s epoch. M1 eligibility was determined from M0-predicted stages during training and evaluation, without requiring polysomnography (PSG) stage labels at inference. M0 achieved 0.830 accuracy and 0.704 macro-F1. Under M0-predicted eligibility, M1 achieved AUROC values of 0.801, 0.791, and 0.786 at 60, 90, and 120 s, respectively; complementary PSG-conditioned evaluation yielded 0.814, 0.803, and 0.801. Prediction was stronger during wakefulness than N1, and the benefits of probability history were specific to the future-sleep task. Future-perturbation tests confirmed unchanged pre-boundary outputs under the tested conditions. A frozen M0 replay on three Muse S Gen2 nights further identified stage-specific limitations in cross-device transfer. These findings establish an auditable framework for temporally causal wearable EEG analysis and demonstrate the potential of short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting while identifying its current generalization boundaries.

papers.title: Movement-Based Sleep Estimation Using a Smart Mattress: Adaptation of Cole-Kripke Algorithm and Comparison with a Multimodal Wearable.
papers.abstract: Multimodal consumer wearables such as Garmin smartwatches combine movement with physiological signals to estimate sleep, whereas bed-based sensing largely relies on movement alone. How far movement alone, sensed from the bed, can go in estimating sleep is unclear. We adapted the Cole-Kripke algorithm to the movement signal of a WhizPad, a smart mattress with a 30-zone pressure array, using the original coefficients and one device-specific scale factor. Estimates were compared with those of a Garmin smartwatch, a proprietary comparator rather than a reference standard, across 28 paired nights in four participants. Epoch-level agreement between the two systems was high for sleep (98.08%) but substantially poorer for wake (30.76%; Cohen's κ = 0.346). Over each system's own sleep period, pooled wake after sleep onset (WASO) was 7.3 min lower for the WhizPad and pooled total sleep time (TST) 37.2 min higher, largely through a longer sleep period. The mattress registers bed entry, which Garmin does not export, allowing an exploratory, device-derived estimate of sleep latency that was not independently validated. These findings are descriptive and exploratory, and agreement does not establish the accuracy of either system as no polysomnography (PSG) reference was used. Physiological sensing in the bed and, ultimately, PSG validation are directions for future work.

papers.title: Cross-Patient Epileptic Seizure Labeling via an Unsupervised Hybrid Anomaly Detection Gate.
papers.abstract: Continuous scalp EEG monitoring enables automated epileptic seizure detection, but extreme class imbalance, inter-patient covariate shifts, and intra-subject data leakage heavily hinder clinical deployment. This study introduces an unsupervised, cross-patient feature selection and patient-independent one-class anomaly detection under Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) cross-validation enhanced by a novel One-Class Hybrid (G-Cramer's V) Statistical Gate to resolve these gaps. The architecture models normal baseline neural activity as the solitary learned class, employing a dynamic feature gate that maximizes baseline purity via a One-Class Gini Index and drives robust cross-patient generalization through a Cramer's V filter. To eliminate patient-level data leakage and ensure reliable cross-patient performance, a strict Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) cross-validation protocol is enforced. Benchmarked on the open-source CHB-MIT database against five core unsupervised estimators (OCSVM, kNN, LNND, LOF, IF) and a reference Morlet Wavelet baseline, the proposed Local Outlier Factor (LOF) estimator utilizing a Gated Fourier framework delivers high precision and efficiency. It achieves a mean cohort F1-score of 0.79, a precision of 78%, and a False Alarm Rate of 1.5 alarms per hour on completely unseen patients, while simultaneously yielding a 35.5% reduction in feature-extraction latency.

papers.title: Spectral Differentiation of Vehicle Vibration States Using FFT, ANOVA and Effect Size Analysis.
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to identify vibration frequency bands that most effectively differentiate vehicle operating conditions in real driving. Vehicle vibration signals acquired along three measurement axes and as a resultant signal were analyzed together with synchronized CAN bus parameters. The vibration signals were divided into 5-s segments and analyzed using the fast Fourier transform (FFT). Mean spectra and spectral variability were evaluated for different RPM classes. To quantitatively assess spectral differences, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with False Discovery Rate correction and frequency-dependent Cohen's d effect-size analysis were applied. The results demonstrated that engine operating conditions significantly influence the vibration spectrum across a broad frequency range, with the most diagnostically relevant changes occurring within the 8-12 Hz and 25-35 Hz bands. The strongest spectral separation was observed during the transition from idle to low-RPM operation, yielding very large effect sizes. An additional assessment of the usefulness of the selected descriptors was conducted using a Random Forest classifier, accounting for group-based temporal partitioning and five-fold cross-validation. The classifier achieved an accuracy of 88.28% and a balanced accuracy of 74.51% on a separate test set. The results indicate high recognition rates for the idle state and greater difficulty in distinguishing between low and medium engine speeds. Global spectral descriptors demonstrated the greatest predictive power, whereas the energies of selected narrow frequency bands did not provide significant additional information to the classification model.

papers.title: Associations of Google Pixel Watch 3 Daily Readiness with Autonomic Physiology and Self-Reported Wellness: An Exploratory 14-Day Repeated-Measures Study.
papers.abstract: Consumer smartwatch readiness scores summarise physiological and sleep data, but their relationships with independently measured physiology and self-reported wellness remain uncertain. This exploratory 14-day repeated-measures observational study examined Google Pixel Watch 3 Daily Readiness in 38 participants (410 participant-days; 220 with recorded readiness scores). Morning heart rate variability was measured independently using Polar H10 and Kubios, and daily questionnaires assessed fatigue, stress, body soreness, and sleep quality. Mixed-effects models separated within-person and episode-mean associations; participant-grouped cross-validation tested incremental wellness prediction. Within participants, each 10-point increase in readiness relative to the episode mean was associated with 6.2% higher root mean square of successive differences (95% CI 2.7-11.7%), a 0.15-unit higher parasympathetic index (0.08-0.23), a 0.12-unit lower sympathetic index (-0.25 to -0.05), and 0.99 beats/min lower heart rate (-1.91 to -0.42). Respiratory rate was not associated. Higher readiness was associated with more favourable fatigue (odds ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.03-1.38) and stress (1.26, 1.08-1.47) ratings, but not body soreness or sleep quality after multiplicity correction. No episode-mean association survived correction, although estimates were imprecise. Daily Readiness did not improve out-of-sample prediction. These findings show convergence with one physiological input domain but do not validate the composite or assess its use alongside load metrics.

papers.title: Fibromyalgia and the Gut Microbiome: Current Evidence, Mechanistic Insights, and Research Priorities.
papers.abstract: Fibromyalgia (FM) is a chronic condition characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain, frequently accompanied by fatigue, sleep disturbances, and cognitive dysfunction. Studies have identified differences in gut microbial composition and metabolite profiles in some FM cohorts, but their consistency, clinical significance, and causal direction remain uncertain. This critical narrative review evaluates human observational evidence, experimental models, and microbiome-targeted interventions, distinguishing findings directly relevant to FM from mechanistic insights derived from other conditions. Particular attention is given to short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), tryptophan metabolism, and bile acids as potential mediators of host-microbiome interactions along the gut-brain axis. Human studies are limited by small, predominantly female cohorts, inconsistent findings, and confounding related to gastrointestinal conditions, diet, medication use, and intestinal transit. Although transfer of FM-associated microbiota can induce pain-related phenotypes in experimental animals, these findings do not establish disease causation in humans. Evidence for dietary interventions, probiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation remains preliminary, with unresolved questions concerning efficacy, safety, and durability. We also propose a hypothetical framework of overlapping immune, metabolic, and neuroendocrine or stress-related domains to guide future investigation, not to define validated FM endotypes. Multi-omics and artificial intelligence (AI) may help test these hypotheses, but clinical applications require longitudinal research, independent validation, and adequately controlled trials.

papers.title: Chronovaccinology: Molecular Clock Regulation of Vaccine Timing, Immunogenicity, and Durable Immune Memory.
papers.abstract: Chronovaccinology represents an emerging interface between vaccinology, chronobiology, and immunology, proposing that circadian timing may constitute an underappreciated determinant of vaccine responsiveness. Increasing evidence indicates that molecular clock machinery coordinates immune-cell function, antigen processing, lymphocyte trafficking, and the development of adaptive immune responses, thereby creating temporal windows in which vaccination may elicit distinct immunological outcomes. This review encompasses the molecular and cellular mechanisms linking circadian clocks with vaccine-induced immunity, with particular emphasis on BMAL1/CLOCK-mediated regulation of antigen presentation and the circadian regulation of individual immune-cell populations. We further discuss circadian control of lymphocyte trafficking, T and B cell responses, and the establishment of durable humoral immune memory, focusing on the circadian regulation of germinal-centre formation, affinity maturation, and the overarching immunoregulatory mechanisms that sustain immunological memory. Finally, we critically evaluate the challenges associated with translating experimental evidence into clinical chronovaccination strategies, including interindividual circadian variation, vaccine type, age, sex, disease status, and logistical constraints. Understanding these temporal mechanisms may facilitate the development of biologically informed vaccination schedules, provide a framework for optimizing vaccine immunogenicity and long-term immune protection along with actionable insights for integrating circadian principles into future clinical trial designs and public health immunization programs.

papers.title: REV-ERBα/β Disruption Drives Environmental Tobacco Smoke-Induced Cellular Senescence Associated with cGAS-STING Signaling Promoting Lung Remodeling.
papers.abstract: Cellular senescence and DNA damage are recognized contributors to smoke-induced lung injury. However, how these processes integrate with circadian regulation and innate immune sensing in response to environmental stressors remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify a conserved multi-lineage transcriptional program in murine lungs that we define as the SCPS axis, characterized by Suppressed Clock, Primed Senescence (SCPS), fibrinolytic Shutdown, and cGAS-STING activation. We show that environmental cigarette/tobacco smoke (ETS) exposure induces senescence and SASP factor production in both epithelial and fibroblast populations, even in the presence of an intact molecular clock. Spatial transcriptomic analysis of smoker lungs demonstrates parallel alterations marked by increased expression of senescence-associated genes, activation of DNA damage and innate immune sensors, and repression of core clock genes, particularly within AT2 cells and fibroblasts. Similarly, REVα/β-deficient mice reveal altered lung circadian, cGAS-STING, senescence, and transcriptional programs. Pharmacological clearance of senescent cells effectively reverses these molecular and cellular phenotypes. Together, these findings reveal early epithelial remodeling and fibrotic priming during environmental tobacco smoke exposure and establish a mechanistic link between senescence, circadian disruption, and innate immune activation associated with the cGAS-STING pathway as the SCPS axis for early checkpoint of fibrotic susceptibility.

papers.title: Endogenous Neuronal-like Phenotypic Remodeling of Astrocyte-Associated Cells in the Ischemic Cortex After Stroke.
papers.abstract: Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) induces complex cellular responses in the injured brain, yet the phenotypic plasticity of resident glial cells during post-ischemic repair remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated neuronal-like phenotypic remodeling of resident cells in the peri-ischemic cortex and its potential pharmacological modulation by salvianolic acid A (SAA). A bilateral primary motor cortex photothrombotic ischemia model was established in Male C57BL/6 mice, followed immediately by local injection of RV-EF1α-eGFP to label proliferative cells or an adeno-associated virus expressing mCherry under the astrocyte-associated gfaABC1D promoter. At 30 days after AIS, virus-labeled cells were analyzed by morphology and NeuN/GFAP immunofluorescence, while whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed at 10 days to assess electrophysiological properties. AIS was associated with the emergence of virus-labeled cells exhibiting neuronal-like morphology, and some gfaABC1D-mCherry-positive cells showed reduced or undetectable GFAP expression. These cells generated action potentials and exhibited excitatory postsynaptic currents, indicating partial neuronal-like electrophysiological properties. A single acute dose of SAA increased the proportion of mCherry/NeuN double-positive cells without significantly changing the overall proportions of mCherry-positive or NeuN-positive cells. These findings suggest that ischemic injury is associated with endogenous neuronal-like phenotypic remodeling of astrocyte-associated cells and that this process may be pharmacologically modulated by SAA.

papers.title: The Molecular Potassium Code: Extracellular K+ Sensing, Allosteric Ion Selectivity, KCC2 Thermodynamics, and the Dynamic Control of Neural Inhibition.
papers.abstract: Neuronal excitability can be controlled by the level of potassium (K+) outside a neuron through both its effects on the cell membrane's electrical properties and its influence on ion transport across the membrane. Recent studies have also shown that certain ligand-gated ion-channel receptors can be modulated by the levels of K+ outside the neuron. Therefore, understanding how each mechanism contributes to the generation of inhibitory signals requires the ability to differentiate between them. This study represents a review that integrates evidence using various methods, including electrophysiology, structural studies, thermodynamics, and optical measurements, to propose a framework called the molecular potassium code that explains how neurons respond to varying levels of K+ in their environment. The framework describes three ways that neurons interact with changing levels of K+: how these changes shift their K+ equilibrium potential and membrane voltage; how they alter the thermodynamic driving force for KCC2-mediated cotransport of K+ and Cl-; and how receptor-dependent modulation occurs at specific receptors when documented. Changes in activation, desensitization, pharmacological sensitivity, and permeation characteristics have been measured in Drosophila DmAlka channels; however, the atomic details of K+ recognition by these channels remain unclear. Human GlyRα2 variants engineered or edited to allow for assessment of K+-associated responses under elevated K+ conditions did not provide sufficient evidence for physiological recruitment of these receptors in mammals. Additionally, the presence and function of astrocytes, as well as geometric factors such as size, shape, and orientation, affect local concentrations of K+. Therefore, the framework described here provides multiple approaches that scientists can use to measure and interpret different mechanisms contributing to the generation of inhibitory signals in the nervous system.

papers.title: Identification of Hypoxia- and Circadian Rhythm-Related Prognostic Genes in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Through Integrative Transcriptomic and Single-Cell Analysis.
papers.abstract: Hypoxia perturbs circadian rhythm gene expression in hepatocellular carcinoma, yet prognostic genes associated with both processes remain insufficiently characterized. Data from the liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) cohort in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were analyzed. Candidate genes were identified by intersecting differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with 27 hypoxia- and circadian rhythm-related genes and were further refined using univariate Cox regression and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression; a random survival forest (RSF) risk model was then constructed and validated. Independent prognostic and functional enrichment analyses, immune infiltration profiling, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and immunohistochemistry (IHC) were subsequently performed. Four prognostic genes (ADM, PFKFB3, SERPINE1, and RORA) were identified through integrative computational analysis. The RSF model stratified LIHC patients into the high-risk group (HRG) and the low-risk group (LRG), which had significantly different survival outcomes, and the risk score and tumor stage were combined in a nomogram. The four genes were co-enriched in four pathways; eight immune cell types, including natural killer T (NKT) cells, differed between the risk groups. scRNA-seq identified stem-like/hypoxic malignant cells whose differentiation trajectory showed distinct expression dynamics of the four genes. IHC confirmed significantly higher ADM and PFKFB3 protein expression in LIHC tissues, whereas protein-level evidence for SERPINE1 and RORA was inconclusive. These findings support further prognostic evaluation of LIHC and investigation of the links among hypoxia, metabolic reprogramming, and stemness.

papers.title: LRRC8/VRAC Channels Beyond Volume Regulation: Molecular Mechanisms, Physiological Functions, and Therapeutic Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Volume-regulated anion channels (VRACs) drive regulatory volume decrease and maintain cellular homeostasis in nearly all vertebrate cells. The identification of leucine-rich repeat-containing 8 (LRRC8) proteins as the molecular components of VRAC transformed the field by showing that these channels are heteromers composed of the essential LRRC8A subunit together with one or more LRRC8B-E subunits. Advances in structural biology, electrophysiology, and molecular studies have since improved our understanding of LRRC8 channel assembly, regulation, and function. LRRC8 complexes operate through two distinct functional modalities. The first is substrate permeation through the channel pore: beyond chloride transport, LRRC8 channels mediate the movement of organic osmolytes, amino acids, ATP, glutamate, cyclic dinucleotides, and platinum-based anticancer drugs, with permeability determined by subunit composition. The second is pore-independent signal transduction, in which LRRC8A also acts as a signaling scaffold through its cytoplasmic leucine-rich repeat domain (LRRD), which binds partners such as GRB2 and caveolin-1. Because deleting the protein removes both modalities at once and many reported phenotypes cannot yet be attributed to either alone. Altered LRRC8 channel activity has been linked to cancer, ischemic brain injury, epilepsy, diabetes, inflammatory diseases, and inherited disorders caused by both loss and gain of LRRC8 function. This review discusses recent advances in the molecular architecture, regulatory mechanisms, transport properties, and pore-independent signaling functions of LRRC8 channels. It also examines their physiological and pathophysiological roles across the nervous, cardiovascular, immune, metabolic, renal, epidermal, and reproductive systems, highlighting the strength of the supporting evidence. Finally, the review addresses recent progress in pharmacological targeting, with particular emphasis on the off-target effects of current inhibitors and the lack of subunit-selective modulators. Understanding how LRRC8 channels sense cell volume, assemble into native channel complexes, act through the pore or through the LRRD, and can be selectively targeted will be critical for translating recent discoveries into future therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Clinical and Polysomnographic Correlates of Subsequent Police-Recorded Motor Vehicle Accidents in Obstructive Sleep Apnea Patients: One- and Two-Year Follow-Up After Diagnostic Laboratory Polysomnography.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and excessive daytime sleepiness are associated with motor vehicle accident (MVA) risk, but it remains uncertain whether routinely available clinical and polysomnographic measures characterize subsequent objectively recorded crash risk after diagnostic sleep evaluation. Materials and Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults aged ≥ 20 years who underwent diagnostic attended overnight laboratory polysomnography for suspected OSA at a regional hospital in Taiwan between 2012 and 2016. Clinical and polysomnographic data were linked to police-recorded MVA data and health administrative records using encrypted identifiers. The primary outcome was any all-cause police-recorded MVA within 1 year after polysomnography. An additional 2-year analysis was conducted in a separately selected cohort with complete 2-year ascertainment. Firth penalized logistic regression was used, with ESS and AHI evaluated in separate models adjusted for age and sex. Results: The 1-year cohort included 1233 participants, of whom 30 experienced an MVA. Participants with MVA were younger than those without MVA (39.43 vs. 45.53 years; p = 0.019). In the age-, sex-, and ESS-adjusted model, each 10-year increase in age was associated with lower MVA odds (OR 0.718, 95% CI 0.533-0.946; p = 0.0199), whereas ESS showed an inverse but nonsignificant association (OR 0.933 per point, 95% CI 0.858-1.009; p = 0.0839). In the age-, sex-, and AHI-adjusted model, AHI did not show a positive association with 1-year MVA (OR 0.859 per 10 events/h, 95% CI 0.711-1.006; p = 0.0754). In the 2-year cohort (n = 926; 56 MVA events), ESS showed a statistically significant inverse association (OR 0.921, 95% CI 0.865-0.978; p = 0.0078), whereas AHI was not associated with MVA (OR 1.003, 95% CI 0.899-1.110; p = 0.9488). Conclusions: Age, subjective sleepiness, and AHI showed different relationships with subsequent police-recorded MVA in this clinical OSA population. These measures did not demonstrate a simple positive gradient with real-world crash risk in this selected cohort; these exploratory findings should not be interpreted as evidence that greater sleepiness is protective or that AHI lacks clinical relevance for driving safety.

papers.title: Predominantly Structural Cardiac Differences in Untreated Normal-Weight Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Comprehensive Echocardiographic Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with cardiac remodeling, although the frequent coexistence of obesity complicates interpretation of cardiovascular abnormalities. We investigated the distribution of structural and functional echocardiographic differences across cardiac domains in untreated normal-weight adults with OSA. Material and Methods: In this prospective, single-center, cross-sectional study, 29 untreated patients with OSA and 15 controls without OSA, all with body mass index < 25 kg/m2, underwent respiratory polygraphy and comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography. Left ventricular (LV) mass index (LVMI) was the primary outcome. Results: Most patients with OSA had mild disease (21/29, 72%). Patients with OSA had higher LVMI than controls (79.3 ± 17.1 vs. 64.5 ± 9.1 g/m2; p < 0.001), together with greater interventricular septal and posterior wall thickness and higher LV end-diastolic volume index. In contrast, no consistent between-group differences were observed across conventional indices of LV systolic and diastolic function, atrial structure, or right ventricular function. Standardized effect sizes were largest for LV structural measurements, whereas estimates across functional, atrial, and right ventricular domains were generally smaller and less precise. After adjustment for age, sex, body mass index, and arterial hypertension, the association between OSA and higher LVMI persisted in the primary model (B = 10.56 g/m2; p = 0.047; bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap 95% CI, 1.71-21.16), although sensitivity analysis indicated limited robustness. Conclusions: In untreated normal-weight adults with predominantly mild OSA, comprehensive echocardiographic assessment revealed findings suggestive of a predominantly structural pattern of cardiac differences, centered on the LV, without a consistent parallel signal across conventional functional, atrial, or right ventricular indices. These findings provide a multidomain characterization of cardiac involvement in OSA in the absence of excess body weight and warrant confirmation in larger longitudinal studies.

papers.title: Objective-to-Subjective Sleep Discrepancy in Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Pilot EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Sleep disturbance is common in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but the relationship between subjectively perceived and objectively measured sleep duration remains poorly understood. This pilot study aimed to compare objective and subjective total sleep time (TST) and to explore clinical factors associated with each measure and the difference between them. It also examined the relationship between this difference and nocturnal blood pressure regulation. Materials and Methods: Twenty-two hospitalized patients with RA underwent overnight sleep monitoring using a portable single-channel electroencephalography (EEG) device and provided subjective estimates of TST for the same night in response to a question asked the following morning. Sleep discrepancy was defined as subjective minus EEG-derived TST. Associations with clinical variables were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation analysis with false discovery rate correction. Exploratory regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index were performed. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was available for 20 patients. Results: Subjective TST exceeded EEG-derived TST by a median of 82.75 min (p = 0.0008), and the two measurements were not significantly correlated (ρ = 0.119, p = 0.598). A more positive signed sleep discrepancy was associated with lower serum albumin (ρ = -0.723, q = 0.0020), higher C-reactive protein (CRP) levels (ρ = 0.624, q = 0.0134), glucocorticoid use (q = 0.0462), higher DAS28-CRP (q = 0.0495), and greater functional disability (q = 0.0495). Associations with albumin and CRP persisted in separate exploratory models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Patients with a conventional dipper blood pressure (BP) pattern had a lower signed sleep discrepancy than those with other nocturnal BP patterns (p = 0.0087). Conclusions: In this small exploratory study, subjective sleep duration in patients with RA was generally longer than EEG-derived sleep duration. Furthermore, preliminary associations were observed between sleep discrepancy and inflammatory and clinical characteristics, as well as with nocturnal BP patterns. These findings require confirmation in larger studies, and the clinical significance of sleep discrepancy remains uncertain.

papers.title: Associations Between Sleep Disorders and TMD Symptoms in Adult Patients: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives Sleep disorders (SDs) negatively affect psychophysical well-being and quality of life and may be associated with temporomandibular disorders (TMDs), which involve pain, limited mandibular mobility, and joint sounds. However, their relationship remains unclear. This study aims to investigate the prevalence of TMDs in patients with SDs. Materials and Methods An observational study was conducted following approval by the Ethics Committee of Vita-Salute San Raffaele University (Gnathology TMDs Protocol, approved on 12 March 2025). One hundred patients with a confirmed diagnosis of sleep disorders (39 females and 61 males; mean age 58.6 ± 18.7 years) were recruited at the Neurology-Sleep Disorders Unit of San Raffaele Hospital "Ville Turro" and the Dentistry Unit of Vita-Salute San Raffaele University in Milan, Italy. Participants were selected according to specific inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were collected using validated Diagnostic Criteria for Temporomandibular Disorders (TMDs) (DC/TMD) Axis I and II instruments, including the TMD Pain Screener, DC/TMD Symptom Questionnaire, Graded Chronic Pain Scale (GCPS), Jaw Functional Limitation Scale version 8 (JFLS-8), Patient Health Questionnaire version 15 (PHQ-15), and Oral Behaviors Checklist (OBC). Questionnaires were completed in the presence of a dentist and a sleep medicine physician. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize population characteristics. Continuous variables were compared using Student's t-test or the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, as appropriate, while categorical variables were compared using the Chi-square test or Fisher's exact test. Statistical significance was set at p less than 0.05. Results Statistical analysis showed the prevalence of a TMD sign or symptom in 38% of subjects with SDs. The most common signs and symptoms reported were: TMJ and/or facial pain (57.89%); TMD-related headache (50%); and joint noises (68.42%). The study also showed that subjects with SDs and almost one TMD sign or symptoms have a significantly higher risk of adopting parafunctional habits, as well as higher chronic pain intensity, with respect to the other ones. The more frequent SDs observed in the TMD sub-group were insomnia, OSAS, and Restless legs syndrome (RLS). Conclusions In conclusion, the results of this study suggest a possible association between SD and TMDs, which require further investigation.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Obstructive Sleep Apnea Using Acoustic Signals: Insights from Recent Studies and Future Directions.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Acoustic signals offer accessible inputs for artificial intelligence (AI) methods for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) assessment. This narrative review examines how acquisition, modeling and output construction affect screening, event detection and severity estimation. Materials and Methods: Studies published or available online from 2022 to 29 September 2026 were identified through iterative retrieval, citation checking and supplementary PubMed and Europe PMC searches. Clinical evidence and within-study design comparisons were synthesized qualitatively, with structured appraisal of study quality and applicability. Results: Published meta-analyses reported approximately 90% sensitivity and 87% specificity for overnight audio and 83% for both measures for awake speech (rounded pooled estimates). Evaluation design and disease prevalence were associated with overnight-audio sensitivity; all speech studies used professional microphones in hospitals. A prospective home study testing a previously developed model in a separate cohort obtained complete recordings in 101/117 attempts and reported severe-OSA sensitivity/specificity of 93.3/94.4% on iOS. A multicenter snoring study obtained usable recordings in 121/152 recruits; a severe-OSA area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.964 coexisted with apnea-hypopnea index agreement limits of -41.25 to +23 events/h. Component comparisons linked performance to features, fusion and patient-output construction, although most were internally validated. Conclusions: Acoustic AI may support screening and referral, but routine clinical value depends on recording completion, performance in the intended population and added benefit over accessible clinical tests. Narrative selection and heterogeneous validation preclude a ranking of clinical effectiveness.

papers.title: Nocturnal Pain and Sleep Disorders in Women with Breast Cancer: A Cross-Sectional Study with Multidimensional Assessment in a Brazilian Cohort.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Breast cancer is the most common malignancy among women in Brazil (41.89/100,000 women, 2023-2025) and is associated with high psychosocial morbidity. Sleep disturbances are frequent in this population and pain is a known contributor, but the time of day when pain occurs has rarely been considered, particularly in Latin American cohorts. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of self-reported nocturnal pain and its associations with insomnia, sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) risk, anxiety, and depression in women with breast cancer. Materials and Methods: This is an analytical cross-sectional study with 211 patients under oncological outpatient follow-up at three referral hospitals in Greater São Paulo, Brazil (CEP-FMABC approval No. 7,920,023). Five validated instruments were applied: Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), STOP-Bang, and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS). Comparisons were performed using t-tests and chi-square tests. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) were estimated by multiple logistic regression adjusted for anxiety, depression, age, body mass index (BMI), and menopausal status. Sensitivity analyses added medication burden, comorbidities, and oncological treatment history, and used Firth penalized regression. Results: Nocturnal pain prevalence was 29.9% (n = 63; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 23.8-36.5). The pain group showed significantly worse ISI, PSQI, HADS-Anxiety, and HADS-Depression scores. Nocturnal pain was associated with poor sleep quality (aOR = 3.54; 95% CI: 1.49-8.45; p = 0.004) and clinical insomnia (aOR = 2.16; 95% CI: 1.08-4.33; p = 0.029). Point estimates were stable in sensitivity analyses (aOR 3.40-3.67 for poor sleep quality and 1.92-2.16 for insomnia in conventional logistic models), although the confidence interval for insomnia included unity after additional adjustment for comorbidities. Conclusions: Self-reported nocturnal pain was associated with poor sleep quality and insomnia in women with breast cancer, beyond anxiety and depression symptoms. Given the cross-sectional design, these associations do not establish causality. Asking about pain at night is simple and may help identify patients who need a sleep assessment.

papers.title: Dental Scaling Within the Previous Year and Depressive Symptoms Among Korean Adults: A Nationwide Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Dental scaling may be associated with mental health, but whether this reflects dental care itself or broader healthcare engagement is unclear. We examined the association between dental scaling within the previous year and depressive symptoms among Korean adults and its attenuation after sequential adjustment. Materials and Methods: We analyzed 231,410 adults aged ≥ 19 years from the 2024 Korea Community Health Survey. Scaling was self-reported; depressive symptoms were defined as a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 score ≥ 10. Survey-weighted logistic regression estimated odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Model 2 was the primary confounder-adjusted model, whereas Model 3 (exploratory attenuation model) was additionally adjusted for oral health, healthcare access, and general health. Sensitivity analyses included an alternative PHQ-9 threshold, expanded covariate models, multiple imputation, E-values, and restricted cubic splines. Results: Depressive symptoms were less prevalent among participants reporting scaling than those not reporting scaling (3.2% vs. 5.3%). The crude OR was 0.58 (95% CI: 0.55-0.61); the Model 2 OR was 0.74 (95% CI: 0.70-0.78) and was attenuated to 0.88 (95% CI: 0.83-0.93) in Model 3. Expanded models and multiple imputation yielded similar estimates. The Model 3 E-value was 1.54 (confidence-limit E-value: 1.36). With flexible modeling of age and sleep duration, the Model 3 OR was 0.93 (95% CI: 0.87-0.98). Conclusions: Self-reported scaling within the previous year was inversely associated with PHQ-9-defined depressive symptoms, with attenuation after additional adjustment and flexible modeling. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and these findings do not establish that scaling prevents or treats depressive disorders.

papers.title: Altered Cortisol Dynamics Across Obstructive Sleep Apnea Severity.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is biologically heterogeneous, and neurohormonal change is a recognized dimension of this heterogeneity. Findings on cortisol in OSA are inconsistent, possibly because studies sample different parts of the diurnal rhythm. We examined salivary cortisol and its diurnal slope in relation to OSA severity, collapse pattern at drug-induced sleep endoscopy (DISE), and screening questionnaire performance. Materials and Methods: This cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from a prospective cohort study included 73 patients with moderate (n = 41) or severe (n = 32) OSA undergoing DISE. Salivary cortisol was collected at 07:00-08:00 and 22:00-23:00, and the diurnal slope was calculated as morning minus evening cortisol. Groups were compared with the Mann-Whitney U test and by analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) adjusted for age, BMI, and arterial hypertension. Discrimination of severe OSA by the STOP-BANG questionnaire and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) was assessed by ROC analysis. Results: Morning cortisol (median 8.99 vs. 11.98 ng/mL, p = 0.002) and diurnal slope (6.29 vs. 9.89 ng/mL, p = 0.001) were lower in severe than moderate OSA, while evening cortisol did not differ (p = 0.649). After adjustment for age, BMI, and hypertension, severe OSA remained associated with lower morning cortisol (p = 0.005) and a flatter slope (p = 0.005), and the AHI correlated inversely with both (partial ρ = -0.330 and ρ = -0.359). Patients with complete concentric collapse had higher evening cortisol than those with other patterns (p = 0.045; p = 0.028 after adjustment). The STOP-BANG questionnaire discriminated severe OSA (AUC = 0.667, p = 0.023); the ESS did not (AUC = 0.615, p = 0.118). Conclusions: Severe OSA is associated with lower morning cortisol and a flattened diurnal rhythm than moderate OSA, independent of age, BMI, and hypertension. The association between concentric collapse and evening cortisol is novel but exploratory and requires replication.

papers.title: Associations of Conventional Cigarette Smoking Intensity and Subjective Sleep Quality with Periodontal Status and Oral Health-Related Quality of Life: A Cross-Sectional Clinic-Based Study.
papers.abstract: Background and objectives: Smoking is an established risk factor for periodontitis, whereas periodontitis and poor sleep may adversely affect oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL). This study examined whether conventional cigarette smoking intensity shows differential associations with periodontal status and OHRQoL while accounting for subjective sleep quality and sociodemographic characteristics. Materials and Methods: This cross-sectional study included 504 consecutive adult patients attending a university dental clinic in Bulgaria. Periodontal status was determined according to the 2017 World Workshop classification. Sleep quality and OHRQoL were assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Oral Health Impact Profile-14 (OHIP-14). Multivariable binary logistic regression evaluated the association between smoking intensity and periodontitis, and hierarchical multiple linear regression with bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap confidence intervals evaluated associations with OHIP-14. Analyses of conventional cigarette smoking included 477 participants. Results: Compared with no current smoking, smoking 10-20 cigarettes/day was associated with 5.7-fold higher adjusted odds of periodontitis (OR = 5.726; 95% CI: 1.934-16.956), whereas >20 cigarettes/day was associated with 16.1-fold higher odds (OR = 16.148; 95% CI: 2.127-122.582). Smoking intensity was not associated with PSQI scores. In the OHIP-14 model, smoking intensity increased the explained variance by 4.0% beyond sociodemographic characteristics (p < 0.001), followed by a further 6.4% increase after the addition of periodontal status and PSQI (p < 0.001). Periodontitis (B = 3.986; BCa 95% CI: 1.510-6.473) and higher PSQI scores (B = 0.741; BCa 95% CI: 0.452-1.031) were associated with higher OHIP-14 summary scores in the fully adjusted model. Category-specific adjusted smoking associations with OHIP-14 were heterogeneous and did not increase monotonically with smoking intensity. Conclusions: Higher-intensity conventional cigarette smoking was strongly associated with periodontitis, whereas its adjusted association with OHRQoL was smaller and heterogeneous across smoking-intensity categories. Periodontal status and higher PSQI scores were associated with greater patient-perceived oral health burden after multivariable adjustment. Smoking-related estimates should be interpreted with consideration that the "no current smoking" reference category may have included former smokers because previous smoking history was unavailable.

papers.title: Preconditioning with Menaquinone-7 and Environmental Enrichment Produces Distinct Osteocalcin and Neuroplasticity Responses Following Chronic Social Defeat Stress.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Depression is a growing global health burden, underscoring the need for preventive strategies that complement existing treatments. Environmental enrichment (EE), incorporating physical, cognitive, sensory, and social stimulation, enhances neuroplasticity and stress resilience. Menaquinone-7 (MK-7), a form of vitamin K2, may also support brain health through osteocalcin, a bone-derived hormone involved in cognition and neuroplasticity. This study examined the protective effects of EE and MK-7 preconditioning, alone and combined, against chronic social defeat stress (CSDS), focusing on the osteocalcin-mediated bone-brain axis and structural plasticity. Materials and Methods: Male C57BL/6N mice received MK-7 (100 µg), EE, or both for four weeks before a 10-day CSDS protocol. Depressive-like behavior was assessed using the forced swim and tail suspension tests, while cognition was evaluated using novel object recognition and Y-maze tests. Serum osteocalcin, brain undercarboxylated osteocalcin (ucOC), brain gene expression of Bdnf, Gpr158, and Rbbp4, and protein levels of BDNF, MAP2, and GAP43 were measured. Results: CSDS induced depressive-like behavior and cognitive impairment, accompanied by reductions in serum and brain ucOC, Bdnf expression, BDNF, GAP43, and MAP2. Both MK-7 and EE showed significant main effects on behavioral and cognitive outcomes, while MK-7 exerted broader effects on osteocalcin- and neuroplasticity-related molecular markers. Significant MK-7 × EE interactions were limited to selected outcomes, including FST and brain ucOC, indicating outcome-specific rather than generalized synergy. Conclusions: CSDS disrupts the osteocalcin-mediated bone-brain axis and neuroplasticity-related pathways. MK-7 and EE both improved behavioral and cognitive outcomes, but MK-7 exerted broader effects on ucOC- and BDNF-related molecular markers, whereas their combination produced selective interactions rather than generalized synergy.

papers.title: Advances in Multimodal Imaging and Artificial Intelligence for the Diagnosis and Management of Diabetic Retinopathy: From Biomarkers to Personalized Care.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a leading cause of preventable vision loss. Staging based on colour fundus photography captures only part of a disease that involves the whole neurovascular unit and the retinal periphery. This narrative review summarizes the structural (optical coherence tomography, OCT), vascular (OCT angiography and ultra-widefield imaging) and functional (microperimetry, electrophysiology) biomarkers of DR, grades the evidence supporting each of them, and examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is changing screening, prognostication and treatment selection. Materials and Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for publications from January 2000 to May 2026, giving priority to randomized trials, prospective multicentre cohorts, systematic reviews and externally validated algorithms. Results: Among imaging biomarkers, disorganization of the retinal inner layers, outer retinal integrity and ultra-widefield angiographic non-perfusion have the most consistent prognostic evidence, whereas OCT angiography metrics remain device-dependent. AI has progressed from research classifiers to autonomous systems with regulatory authorization in the United States and the European Union, to prospectively evaluated deployments in national programmes and low-resource settings, and to time-to-event progression models and foundation models. Image-based prediction improves discrimination over clinical risk factors by modest margins, and biomarker-guided treatment of diabetic macular oedema still rests largely on retrospective series. Cross-device standardization of quantitative metrics, representative datasets, prospective outcome trials and health-economic evidence remain the main gaps. Conclusions: Individualized screening intervals are the application closest to routine practice, whereas phenotype-driven therapy and precision monitoring remain promising but unproven.

papers.title: Prevalence of and Factors Associated with Chronic Pain Among Medical Students.
papers.abstract: Background: Chronic pain is a leading cause of disability worldwide, and is highly prevalent among university and medical students; however, data from Jordan are limited, and sleep posture as a potentially modifiable factor remains understudied. Study Design: Cross-sectional study. Methods: A convenience sample of 391 medical students from eight Jordanian universities offering accredited medical programs (two of which contributed only five participants in total) completed a self-administered questionnaire (online and in person) over four months, assessing demographics, lifestyle, the Brief Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (B-PSQI), and usual sleeping postures. Associations were tested using chi-square and logistic regression. Results: The prevalence of chronic pain was 57.8% (n = 226), higher among females than males (64.0% vs. 51.1%, p = 0.009). Regular exercise was associated with lower odds of pain (OR = 0.61, p = 0.037); fair (OR = 3.42, p = 0.001) and very bad (OR = 3.77, p = 0.046) sleep quality, relative to excellent, were associated with higher odds; and prone sleeping posture was associated with higher odds of pain relative to right-side sleeping (OR = 2.85, p = 0.001). The model was significant (p < 0.001) but showed modest explanatory power (Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 = 0.122). Conclusions: Chronic pain is common among Jordanian medical students. Not engaging in regular exercise, suboptimal sleep quality, and prone sleeping posture were independently associated with chronic pain, although the model had modest explanatory power. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal and causal relationships.

papers.title: Association Between Caregiver-Reported ADHD Symptom Categories and Sleep-Related Quality of Life in Primary School Children: A Community-Based Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep problems and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) can substantially affect quality of life (QOL) in children. This study aimed to assess sleep-related QOL using the scores from the caregiver-administered OSA-18 questionnaire among primary school children. The association between ADHD symptom screening categories and caregiver-reported sleep-related QOL, based on the scores, was also examined after adjustment for potential confounders. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among primary school students aged 6-8 years from 10 schools in Bangkok. A caregiver-administered OSA-18 questionnaire was used to assess sleep-related QOL, and the caregiver-administered SNAP-IV was used to screen for ADHD and classify children into ADHD symptom screening categories. Separate multivariable linear regression models examined the association between ADHD symptom screening category and OSA-18 total and subscale scores, adjusting for obesity status, sex, household income, caregiver-reported asthma, and caregiver-reported allergic rhinitis. Results: A total of 2263 children were included. Positive ADHD symptom screening results were identified in 4.8% for inattention, 2.1% for hyperactivity/impulsivity, and 3.2% for children exhibiting both inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms as mutually exclusive symptom categories. Compared with the ADHD symptom screen-negative group, children with inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity, and combined symptoms had significantly higher OSA-18 total scores, with adjusted mean differences of 9.4 (95% CI, 6.9-12.0), 15.0 (95% CI, 11.1-18.9), and 19.3 (95% CI, 16.0-22.5), respectively (all p < 0.001). Similar significant associations were observed across all five OSA-18 subscales, with the largest adjusted mean differences generally among children with a positive screening for combined symptoms. Conclusions: Positive ADHD symptom screening results were significantly associated with higher OSA-18 scores reflecting greater caregiver-reported impact on sleep-related QOL, with the largest difference observed among children with positive screening for combined symptoms. The clinical significance of these score differences warrants further investigation.

papers.title: The Prevalence and Impact of Obstructive Sleep Apnoea and Periodic Limb Movements in Sleep in Adult Parasomnias.
papers.abstract: Parasomnias are abnormal behaviours in sleep. Disorders that can cause microarousals, such as obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) and periodic limb movements in sleep (PLMS) are often considered to trigger parasomnias. However, the prevalence and impact of OSA, and its specific clinical phenotypes, such as REM-related OSA (ROSA) and positional OSA (POSA), as well as PLMS in parasomnias are not fully explored. We analysed the polysomnography reports of 155 patients who were referred to our tertiary service with symptoms of parasomnia. The prevalence of OSA, ROSA, POSA, and PLMS, as well as their severity indices were correlated with the prevalence of specific parasomnias using logistic regression. The prevalence of OSA and PLMS was 48% and 23%, respectively. Whilst OSA and PLMS were inversely related to NREM parasomnias, PLMS was directly related to RBD (p < 0.05). Moreover, there was a significant inverse correlation between the severity of PLMS and the prevalence of NREM parasomnias (β = -0.12, p = 0.03) and a direct correlation with RBD (β = 0.02, p = 0.04). However, following adjustments for age, BMI, and gender, only the inverse relationships between OSA and sleep terrors as well as POSA and sleep-related eating disorder remained significant. The prevalence of OSA and PLMS is high among patients with parasomnia. Due to the exploratory nature of the study, conclusions on the associations need to be validated in interventional trials.
keywords: rapid eye movement sleep-related obstructive sleep apnoea

papers.title: Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Predicting Response and Outcomes After Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of ECG-Based Models.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Up to 40% of patients receiving cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) do not experience significant clinical improvement, highlighting the limitations of conventional selection criteria. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied to electrocardiogram (ECG) and other clinical data to improve patient selection. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the performance and methodological quality of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models using ECG-derived information to predict CRT response and clinical outcomes. Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted in Scopus and Web of Science for studies published between January 2006 and April 2026.
