Eligible studies developed or evaluated ML or DL algorithms primarily using pre-implantation ECG data to predict CRT response, including changes in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) or left ventricular end-systolic volume (LVESV), or mortality. Model performance and prognostic associations were synthesized using random-effects meta-analyses of the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and hazard ratios (HRs), respectively. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the PROBAST+AI tool. Results: We identified 14 eligible studies containing 34 distinct model evaluations. Most models utilized digital 12-lead ECG waveforms or single representative beats. Across 26 model-outcome estimates, the exploratory pooled AUROC was 0.710 (95% CI: 0.660-0.759), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 94.7%; p < 0.001). Across 10 heterogeneous model-outcome estimates, the exploratory pooled HR was 1.75 (95% CI: 1.42-2.15; I2 = 83.3%), although differences in prognostic constructs and endpoints precluded interpretation as a common effect. ML models had a higher pooled AUROC than DL models (0.752 vs. 0.669; exploratory Wald test: difference = 0.084; 95% CI: 0.002-0.165; p = 0.044). Pooled HR estimates also differed (ML: 2.22; DL: 1.46; ratio = 1.51; p < 0.001). These indirect subgroup comparisons were limited by clinical and methodological heterogeneity and potential dependence among estimates. PROBAST+AI assessment identified a high overall risk of bias in 32 of the 34 models, with concerns concentrated primarily in the participants and data sources and analysis domains. Independent geographic external evaluation was reported in only two studies, and these evaluations did not both constitute independent validation of fully specified CRT prediction models. Conclusions: ECG-based ML and DL models demonstrate moderate discrimination for predicting CRT outcomes. However, substantial heterogeneity, high risk of bias and limited independent external validation currently preclude routine clinical implementation. Future research should prioritize standardized outcome definitions, independent external validation, and head-to-head comparisons within the same cohorts to establish incremental predictive and clinical utility. Registration: The review protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261448863).

papers.title: Optically Pumped Magnetometers for Fetal Arrhythmia Evaluation: Clinical Evidence and Implications for Health Technology Assessment.
papers.abstract: Fetal magnetocardiography (fMCG) provides direct non-invasive assessment of fetal cardiac electrophysiology and can resolve atrial and ventricular activation, conduction intervals, and ventricular repolarization. Optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) offer a cryogen-free platform for fMCG, but evidence for their use in fetal arrhythmia remains limited to a few clinical studies. This perspective examines four reports directly relevant to arrhythmia evaluation with OPM-fMCG. Clinical OPM recordings have demonstrated long QT syndrome, T-wave alternans, Torsades de Pointes, atrial flutter, atrial ectopic tachycardia, blocked atrial bigeminy, atrioventricular block, ventricular tachycardia, and ectopy, with close agreement for PR, QTc, and RR intervals in the direct OPM-SQUID comparison. Further developments have enabled simultaneous magnetic and echocardiographic assessment and improved visualization of the low-amplitude P and T waves central to rhythm and repolarization analysis. Collectively, the available reports establish clinical feasibility and show the additional electrophysiological information that OPM-fMCG can provide beyond fetal echocardiography, but they do not yet establish diagnostic sensitivity and specificity for fetal arrhythmia diagnosis. Prospective multicenter validation in larger arrhythmia cohorts is the key next step.

papers.title: Multimodal Detection of Cognitive Impairment in Non-Neurological Rehabilitation Settings: The COGinREHAB Study Protocol.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Cognitive impairment is highly prevalent among hospitalised adults but often remains under-recognised, particularly in non-neurological rehabilitation settings where clinical attention is mainly focused on physical recovery. Undetected cognitive impairment may adversely affect rehabilitation outcomes, functional recovery, and long-term care planning. Methods: A multicentre, prospective, longitudinal study, with a single-group assignment and a diagnostic purpose, will be conducted across three rehabilitation centres of the Don Carlo Gnocchi Foundation (Italy), enrolling 384 patients aged ≥45 years without severe psychiatric or neurological disorders, other than cognitive impairment, admitted to cardiac, pulmonary, orthopaedic rehabilitation, or intermediate care units for non-neurological conditions. At baseline (T0), all participants will undergo standardised clinical and cognitive screening. Individuals with suspected cognitive impairment, operationally defined as an Equivalent Score (ES) of 1 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment-MoCA total score and/or an ES of 0 or 1 on at least one MoCA cognitive domain, including the Memory Index Score (MIS), and a random sample of those without, will undergo a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment. Participants with neuropsychologically defined cognitive impairment, based on objective deficits in the comprehensive neuropsychological assessment, will undergo plasma biomarker testing (GFAP, NfL, pTau-217), APOE genotyping, and brain CT. Participants with a MoCA total ES of 0 will be classified as having cognitive impairment on the basis of screening alone. At two prespecified sites, consecutive consenting participants with neuropsychologically defined cognitive impairment will additionally undergo an EEG vigilance protocol, auditory P300 recording, seven-day actigraphy, and overnight polysomnography. Patients with neuropsychologically defined cognitive impairment at T0 will undergo a 12-month follow-up assessment (T1) of the progression of cognitive impairment and plasma biomarkers; those enrolled in the neurophysiological substudy will additionally repeat the EEG vigilance protocol. Expected Results: The study will provide a conservative (lower-bound) estimate of the prevalence of documented and non-documented cognitive impairment, together with an estimate corrected for partial verification bias, in non-neurological rehabilitation settings. It will further characterise the cognitive profiles and examine their correlations with biomarkers of neurodegeneration (GFAP, NfL, pTau-217), APOE genotype, relative EEG spectral power and sleep intrusion measures, P300 latency and amplitude, actigraphy-derived Sleep Efficiency, and polysomnography-derived sleep stage proportions. Longitudinal data will enable the evaluation of cognitive trajectories and their biological correlates. Conclusions: The COGinREHAB study addresses a critical gap in rehabilitation medicine by implementing a structured, multimodal approach to the identification and characterisation of cognitive impairment in patients with non-neurological conditions. Its findings may facilitate earlier detection of cognitive impairment and inform the development of personalised rehabilitation and care pathways. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07731334.

papers.title: Prevalence of Fatigue in Swedish Patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease, and Factors Contributing to Fatigue-A Mixed-Methods Study.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Fatigue is defined as an overwhelming sense of tiredness, weakness, or exhaustion, which can be physical, psychological, or a combination of both. Evidence suggests that fatigue is more prevalent among patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) than in the general population. The aim of this study was to assess the prevalence of fatigue among Swedish IBD patients. Another aim was to increase our knowledge about factors that may contribute to fatigue, and strategies for managing fatigue. Methods: Swedish IBD patients were asked to complete the IBD Fatigue Scale. Analyses involved both a quantitative and a qualitative approach. Results: A total of 675 patients participated in the study and 44% reported significant fatigue. Fatigue was significantly associated with continuous symptoms, extraintestinal manifestations, and impaired wellbeing. Four categories relating to fatigue were identified: (1) fatigue difficult to define and attribute, (2) fatigue arising from interacting bodily and psychosocial burdens, (3) managing a limited and fluctuating supply of energy, and (4) restoring energy through activity, support and recovery. Participants frequently described fatigue as arising from an interaction between disease activity, comorbid conditions, psychological distress, sleep problems, pain, and everyday life demands. Conclusions: Although fatigue was more severe among participants with continuous symptoms, extraintestinal manifestations and impaired wellbeing, the free-text responses demonstrated that patients frequently perceived comorbidities, disturbed sleep, pain, psychological distress and demanding life circumstances as additional contributors. Management involved balancing rest and activity, planning limited energy, and drawing on supportive relationships and restorative environments. These findings support a holistic and person-centred approach in which fatigue is assessed beyond intestinal disease activity.

papers.title: Quality of Life and Disease Control at First Specialist Assessment in Atopic Dermatitis.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is associated with impaired quality of life and poor disease control. We aimed to describe patients attending their first specialist assessment in a tertiary AD unit and identify factors associated with poorer quality of life and poor perceived disease control. Methods: This single-centre cross-sectional study consecutively enrolled patients with AD and recorded clinical characteristics, treatment history, disease severity and patient-reported outcomes. Multivariable logistic regression assessed factors associated with Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) > 10 and Atopic Dermatitis Control Tool (ADCT) ≥ 7. Complete-case analyses were supplemented by multiple imputation of missing covariates. Results: The study included 255 patients (mean age 37.4 years, 53.9% women). Flexural (33.3%) and diffuse (32.8%) phenotypes predominated, and 57.2% had at least one atopic comorbidity. Previous treatments included oral corticosteroids (44.0%), conventional systemic therapy (26.5%) and advanced therapy (6.9%). Among patients assessed, 25.0% had severe disease according to EASI and 31.9% according to SCORAD. A DLQI score > 10 was observed in 47/155 patients (30.3%) and an ADCT score ≥ 7 in 97/140 (69.3%). Greater itch intensity was associated with both outcomes, and sleep disturbance was associated with an ADCT score ≥ 7. The inverse association between a family history of atopy and a DLQI score > 10 showed a trend towards statistical significance (p = 0.058) after multiple imputation. Conclusions: Poor perceived control was common at the first specialist visit. The findings support assessing itch and sleep alongside clinical severity. The inverse association with a family history of atopy warrants further study.

papers.title: Somatotype and Its Association with Disease Activity and Psychosocial Factors in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Body composition has been suggested to influence disease activity and patient-reported outcomes in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). However, the role of somatotype is not well understood. We aimed to evaluate somatotype characteristics in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and examine their associations with disease activity, function, quality of life, sleep, mood, and fatigue. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, 82 patients with RA (ACR/EULAR criteria) were assessed. Somatotype was determined using the Heath-Carter method and categorized as endomorphic, mesomorphic, or ectomorphic. Disease activity (DAS28), functional status (HAQ), quality of life (SF-12), sleep quality (PSQI), mood (HADS), and fatigue (FSS) were evaluated. Group comparisons, correlation analyses, and BMI-adjusted regression models were performed. Results: Mesomorphic (54.9%) and endomorphic (37.8%) somatotypes predominated, while ectomorphy was uncommon (7.3%). Somatotype groups differed significantly in anthropometric parameters (p < 0.05) whereas no statistically significant group difference were detected in DAS28, HAQ, SF-12, PSQI, HADS, or FSS scores (all p > 0.05). Correlations between somatotype components and clinical measures were weak and none remained significant after adjustment for BMI. Conclusions: Somatotype reflects body habitus in RA. However, no statistically significant associations with disease activity or patient-reported outcomes were identified after adjustment for the measured covariates in this cohort. Given the modest sample size, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and do not exclude potentially clinically relevant relationships.

papers.title: Preoperative Sleep Disturbances, Anxiety, and Depressive Symptoms in Patients with Primary Lung Cancer: Prevalence, Co-Occurrence, and Associated Factors.
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep and mood disturbances are common in patients with cancer, but their prevalence, co-occurrence, and associated factors remain insufficiently characterized in patients undergoing surgery for primary lung cancer. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 69 patients with primary lung cancer evaluated before surgery. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) risk was assessed using the Berlin Questionnaire, insomnia using the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), restless legs syndrome (RLS) symptoms using a standardized screening questionnaire, anxiety using the Beck Anxiety Inventory, and depressive symptoms using the Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale. Daytime sleepiness and functional outcomes were evaluated using the Epworth Sleepiness Scale and Functional Outcomes of Sleep Questionnaire, respectively. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with insomnia symptoms. Results: Insomnia symptoms (ISI ≥ 8) were present in 44.9% of patients, including 13.0% with moderate-to-severe insomnia symptoms (ISI ≥ 15). A high OSA screening risk was identified in 33.3%, and RLS symptoms in 21.7%. Moderate-to-severe anxiety symptoms were present in 18.8%, and moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms in 30.9% (21/68). Coexisting insomnia symptoms and a high OSA screening risk were observed in 18.8% of patients. Anxiety scores were higher among patients with insomnia symptoms. In multivariable analysis (n = 68), higher Beck Anxiety Inventory scores were associated with insomnia symptoms after adjustment for age, sex, and depressive symptom severity (adjusted odds ratio 1.12 per point; 95% CI 1.04-1.21; p = 0.004). Among patients with available functional outcome data (n = 60), greater insomnia severity, anxiety symptoms, and daytime sleepiness were associated with poorer sleep-related daytime functioning. Conclusions: Sleep disturbances and psychological symptoms were common before primary lung cancer surgery and frequently co-occurred. Anxiety symptom severity was associated with insomnia symptoms after adjustment for demographic factors and depressive symptom severity. These findings suggest the potential value of integrated preoperative assessment of sleep and psychological symptoms, although further studies are needed to establish its clinical benefits.

papers.title: Orofacial Myofunctional Therapy as an Adjunct to Mandibular Advancement Devices in Adults with Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Comprehensive Review.
papers.abstract: Background: Mandibular advancement devices (MADs) are an established treatment option for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), particularly in patients with mild-to-moderate disease and those who do not tolerate continuous positive airway pressure. Orofacial myofunctional therapy (OMT) targets functional and neuromuscular abnormalities of the upper airway and has been proposed as a complementary treatment in patients treated with MADs. However, evidence supporting the combination of these two approaches remains limited. Methods: A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) to identify studies evaluating OMT in adults with OSA treated with MADs. The search strategy was initially developed as part of a prospectively registered systematic review. Few eligible studies were identified. We therefore expanded the scope to a comprehensive narrative review and added mechanistic and contextual literature selected by author consensus. Results: Of 558 records initially identified, 366 remained after duplicate removal, and 57 articles underwent full-text assessment. Three clinical publications directly evaluated combined OMT and MAD therapy (one randomized controlled trial and two case reports), and a mechanistic review identified during screening informed the narrative discussion. The single randomized trial (n = 23), judged to be at low risk of bias, did not demonstrate an additional improvement in respiratory event index or minimum oxygen saturation after adding OMT to MAD therapy. Anterior tongue endurance was the only muscle measure that improved significantly compared with sham exercise. The two case reports described clinical improvements in single patients with specific functional problems (nocturnal mouth opening and MAD-related muscular or temporomandibular discomfort); however, co-interventions and the absence of a control condition prevent attributing these changes to OMT. Conclusions: Current evidence is insufficient to establish an additional respiratory benefit of OMT when added to MAD therapy. The effects of OMT on MAD tolerance and adherence remain uncertain. Well-designed prospective randomized trials with larger samples, adequate follow-up, objective adherence monitoring, and predefined functional phenotyping are needed.

papers.title: Injury Profile of Handball Players in Jordan: Prevalence, Associated Factors, and Injury Prevention Beliefs: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Introduction: Handball is a demanding team sport with a high injury rate, yet epidemiological data from Jordan and the Middle East are scarce. Methods: This cross-sectional study surveyed 157 male and female players from the Jordanian Handball League with a self-reported Arabic questionnaire to estimate injury prevalence, describe injury characteristics, explore associated factors, and describe injury-prevention beliefs. The primary outcome was injury in the preceding three months; injury in the preceding 12 months was secondary. Results: Injury was reported by 22.9% (36/157) of players over three months and by 58.0% (91/157) over 12 months. Injuries were mainly lower-limb, contact-related, and frequently recurrent. In bivariate analyses, male sex, lower educational level, poor sleep, and greater training exposure were associated with three-month injury. In exploratory multivariable models, perceived sleep adequacy was associated with lower odds of injury (OR 0.37, 95% CI 0.16-0.88) and cool-down practice with higher odds (OR 5.32, 95% CI 1.43-19.88). Conclusions: Injury prevalence was high in this sample of Jordanian handball players. The associations are exploratory, cannot be interpreted as causal, and require confirmation in prospective studies with exposure-based surveillance.

papers.title: Obesity and Pulmonary Hypertension: A Contemporary Review.
papers.abstract: Obesity and pulmonary hypertension (PH) frequently coexist, but obesity is not a distinct PH group. This narrative review of the literature published through 27 September 2026 appraises the evidence by PH group. Obesity is most clearly linked to PH through intermediate conditions, particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, obstructive sleep apnea, and obesity hypoventilation syndrome, and it can complicate hemodynamic classification because elevated intrathoracic pressure may raise the measured pulmonary arterial wedge pressure. Experimental studies suggest direct pulmonary vascular effects through adipokine imbalance, inflammation, altered estrogen metabolism, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance; however, an independent causal role of obesity in human pulmonary arterial hypertension has not been established. Small, mostly observational studies report lower estimated pulmonary pressures after bariatric surgery, but a benefit of intentional weight loss on invasive hemodynamics or clinical PH outcomes is unproven. Incretin-based therapies produce substantial weight loss and improve symptoms in obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction; acute human hemodynamic data are emerging, but long-term efficacy in PH has not been tested. Higher body mass index has been associated with lower observed mortality in several PH cohorts, possibly reflecting confounding and reverse causation. We distinguish established findings from hypotheses and highlight research priorities.

papers.title: Sleep Disturbance and Psychological Burden in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Comparative Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Background and aims: Sleep disturbances and psychological symptoms are common in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). We compared sleep outcomes in IBD and non-IBD outpatients and explored associations with disease activity. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 155 patients with IBD and 149 non-IBD controls (March-May 2026). Sleep quality, insomnia severity, and psychological symptoms were assessed using the PSQI, ISI, and HADS. Multivariable and sensitivity analyses assessed associations with IBD. Results: Poor sleep quality (PSQI > 5) and moderate-to-severe insomnia (ISI ≥ 15) were more frequent in IBD than controls (50.3% vs. 36.2%, p = 0.015; and 20.0% vs. 8.1%, p = 0.003). However, median PSQI (6 vs. 4; p = 0.056) and ISI (8 vs. 7; p = 0.097) scores did not differ significantly, nor did ISI ≥ 8 prevalence (52.3% vs. 45.6%; p = 0.248). Anxiety (HADS-A ≥ 8: 39.4% vs. 27.5%; p = 0.029) and depressive symptoms (HADS-D ≥ 8: 42.6% vs. 17.4%; p < 0.001) were more frequent in IBD. In primary adjusted models, IBD was associated with poor sleep (aOR 2.00, 95% CI 1.23-3.24) and ISI ≥ 15 (aOR 3.40, 95% CI 1.61-7.18). Sensitivity analyses additionally adjusting for diabetes, hypertension, alcohol use, and BMI supported these associations; continuous-score models identified higher PSQI (β = 1.13; p = 0.008) and ISI (β = 1.52; p = 0.021) scores. Further HADS adjustment yielded nonsignificant, imprecise IBD associations. Continuous disease activity indices were not significantly correlated with sleep outcomes. Conclusions: IBD was associated with more frequent poor sleep and moderate-to-severe insomnia despite nonsignificant median and ISI ≥ 8 comparisons. Disease-activity findings were exploratory; causality cannot be inferred.

papers.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Inflammatory Arthritis: Disease-Specific Evidence and Clinical Implications.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) may complicate fatigue and cardiovascular risk assessment in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), and axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA). We evaluate the strength and clinical applicability of disease-specific evidence. Methods: This expert narrative review uses a documented PubMed/MEDLINE update through 28 October 2026, supplemented by reference-list checking, general OSA trials, and professional guidance. Evidence is appraised qualitatively by ascertainment, selection, adjustment, and directness. Results: RA has the largest but most heterogeneous evidence base: pooled OSA prevalence was 29.8% (95% confidence interval [CI], 15.2-46.7%; I2 = 99.6%), with mixed definitions. In PsA, 21/42 polysomnography (PSG)-tested volunteers had OSA (50%; descriptive 95% CI, 35.5-64.5%), whereas 22/247 clinic patients had a recorded diagnosis (8.9%; 95% CI, 6.0-13.1%). These estimates are not interchangeable. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) findings differ between matched objective testing and administrative cohorts. Adiposity, demographics, medication, and surveillance constrain interpretation. Positive airway pressure has established sleep-related indications; improvements in arthritis activity or arthritis-specific cardiovascular events remain unproven. Tirzepatide evidence concerns adults with obesity and moderate-to-severe OSA. Conclusions: PsA and axSpA evidence remains limited. Shared biology supports a conceptual hypothesis rather than a demonstrated causal axis. Targeted case finding should lead to guideline-concordant objective diagnosis; universal asymptomatic rheumatology screening and disease-modifying effects of OSA treatment are not established.

papers.title: Stress and Neuroendocrine Dysregulation in Colorectal Cancer: Clinical Assessment, HPA-HPT Axis Interactions, and Translational Implications.
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is associated with psychological, metabolic, inflammatory, and endocrine disturbances that may influence patient well-being and clinical outcomes. Psychological distress and circadian disruption can affect hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activity, whereas systemic inflammation, nutritional deterioration, disease burden, and anticancer therapies may alter hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis function. This narrative review critically examines the clinical and translational evidence linking psychological stress, neuroendocrine regulation, systemic thyroid function, and tumor-specific thyroid hormone signaling in CRC. A structured PubMed/MEDLINE search prioritized studies published between January 2020 and July 2026, supplemented by selected earlier landmark studies. Available evidence supports the clinical relevance of psychological distress and suggests that cortisol dynamics and allostatic load may provide complementary information on systemic stress adaptation. Reduced free triiodothyronine (FT3) concentrations and altered FT3/FT4 ratios have been associated with unfavorable outcomes in selected CRC populations, although these associations are influenced by non-thyroidal illness syndrome, inflammation, nutritional status, disease severity, and treatment exposure. Importantly, circulating thyroid hormone parameters do not directly reflect thyroid hormone signaling within the tumor microenvironment, where local hormone metabolism, receptor-mediated pathways, and interactions with stromal and immune cells may contribute to tumor biology. Emerging evidence also implicates neuropeptide signaling in neuroendocrine-tumor communication, although its clinical significance remains uncertain. Collectively, these findings support an integrated approach to assessing psychological, circadian, inflammatory, nutritional, and endocrine alterations in CRC while highlighting the limitations of interpreting isolated biomarkers. Prospective longitudinal studies incorporating standardized neuroendocrine assessments, treatment-related variables, and matched tumor analyses are needed to establish whether integrated neuroendocrine profiles offer prognostic or predictive value beyond established clinicopathological factors.

papers.title: Retreat-Based Support for Ukrainian Psychologists and Psychotherapists During the Ongoing War: A Mixed-Methods Study of Changes in Psycho-Emotional Well-Being and Perceived Supportive Elements.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Ukrainian mental health professionals work under continuous war-related threat. We examined changes in psycho-emotional well-being among Ukrainian psychologists and psychotherapists after a one-week retreat abroad, and the elements they perceived as supportive. Methods: In a mixed-methods study, retreat participants (n = 28) and a non-randomized comparison group (n = 31), all women, completed the WHO-5, CORE-10, BSI subscales, and HAAS before and after the retreat and one month later. Changes were analyzed with linear mixed models. Fourteen interviews were analyzed with qualitative content analysis. Results: From pre- to post-assessment, retreat participants improved more than the comparison group on all seven outcomes (|g| = 0.82-2.08), also after adjustment for age and recent vacation. However, demand characteristics may have inflated these effect sizes. At follow-up, the differences were smaller (|g| = 0.79-1.62) and robust only for psychological distress and well-being. Interviewees described stability, calm, emotional relief, and better sleep, attributed to the interplay of care, nature, safety, voluntary participation, and supportive relationships. Conclusions: A one-week retreat was followed by substantial short-term improvement in psycho-emotional well-being, partly sustained one month after returning to the war zone. The design cannot distinguish the effect of the retreat from that of a week in safety.

papers.title: Determinants of Noninvasive Ventilation Success and Failure in Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome: A Narrative Review Across Acute and Chronic Care.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) is a heterogeneous disorder characterized by obesity, chronic daytime hypercapnia, and sleep-disordered breathing. Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) provides ventilatory support during acute hypercapnic respiratory failure and for persistent hypoventilation in OHS, while continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is appropriate for selected stable patients with coexisting severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This narrative review synthesizes determinants of NIV success and failure across acute and chronic OHS care. Methods: A targeted narrative search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus. Priority was given to OHS-specific cohort studies, randomized trials, individual patient data analyses, and relevant systematic reviews, with broader NIV evidence used cautiously when OHS-specific data were limited. Results: NIV success in OHS is best interpreted as a context-dependent trajectory rather than a single threshold. Acute success involves favorable trends in pH and PaCO2, reduced work of breathing, improved alertness, avoidance of invasive mechanical ventilation, and safe transition from the acute episode. Chronic success is reflected by sustained hypoventilation control, adherence, interface tolerance, symptom improvement, and fewer recurrent decompensations. Failure may reflect persistent physiological derangement, ineffective NIV delivery, or both. Conclusions: Phenotype-guided positive airway pressure (PAP) selection, early reassessment, technical optimization, adherence support, and structured follow-up may support the management of NIV outcomes in OHS. Distinguishing physiological failure from ineffective NIV delivery may help guide clinical reassessment and escalation decisions, although this conceptual framework requires prospective validation.

papers.title: Differential Metabolic Reprogramming by KaiA and KaiC Reveals Distinct Modes of Circadian Regulation in Cyanobacteria.
papers.abstract: The impact of core clock protein dosage on metabolic temporal organization is crucial yet underexplored. In Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942, we independently overexpressed kaiA (kaiA-OE) and kaiC (kaiC-OE), observing mirror-image effects on circadian output and KaiC phosphorylation: kaiA-OE locked the clock output in a persistently elevated state with enhanced KaiC phosphorylation, whereas kaiC-OE suppressed output to a low baseline with accumulation of unphosphorylated KaiC. A 24 h time-course untargeted metabolomic analysis (five time points, six biological replicates per starin) revealed that these two perturbations drove distinct metabolic trajectories. Relative to the phase reference defined by the wild-type metabolome, cosine-fitted phase estimates of metabolite accumulation contracted toward subjective dusk in kaiA-OE, whereas kaiC-OE produced a broadened and fragmented distribution. Pathway-level analysis indicated that kaiA-OE altered the abundance of daytime TCA cycle intermediates and amino-acid-related metabolites and activated nocturnal glutathione metabolism, whereas kaiC-OE preferentially disturbed daytime nucleotide metabolism and nocturnal oxidative pentose phosphate pathway intermediates. Notably, three representative metabolites, glutathione (GSH), α-Ketoglutaric acid (α-KG), and ribose-5-phosphate (R5P), exhibited opposite responses between the two overexpression strains over 24 h. Together, our findings demonstrate that KaiA and KaiC exert differential, dosage-sensitive, and phase-specific control over carbon, nitrogen, and nucleotide metabolism.

papers.title: Behavioral Changes and Absence Seizure Activity Following Low- and High-Glycemic Index Diet Exposure in WAG/Rij Rats.
papers.abstract: Dietary interventions have emerged as promising adjunctive strategies for epilepsy, but the effects of dietary glycemic index on absence epilepsy and associated behavioral outcomes remain unclear. This study investigated spontaneous absence seizures and behavioral outcomes following exposure to low- and high-glycemic index (LGI and HGI) diets in WAG/Rij rats. Thirty male Wistar Albino Glaxo/Rijswijk (WAG/Rij) rats were randomly assigned to control, LGI, or HGI diet groups (n = 10/group) for 21 days. All animals subsequently returned to the standard diet before behavioral and electroencephalographic assessments. Body weight and food intake were monitored. Locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, and depression-like behavior were assessed using locomotor activity, elevated plus maze, and forced swim tests. Electroencephalographic recordings from five animals per group were analyzed for spike-and-wave discharges (SWDs). Body weight and food intake did not differ significantly among groups. The LGI group exhibited fewer SWD episodes than controls in an exploratory pairwise comparison (p = 0.0261), although significance was not retained after correction across EEG outcomes (p = 0.0593). SWD durations did not differ significantly. In the elevated plus maze, the HGI group spent less time in open arms than controls (p = 0.0240) and the LGI group (p = 0.0189). The LGI group showed shorter open-arm entry latency than the HGI group in an exploratory comparison (p = 0.0210). In the forced swim test, the HGI group exhibited longer immobility than controls (p = 0.0233) and reduced active swimming. Dietary glycemic index was associated with subsequent differences in SWD frequency and behavioral outcomes. LGI exposure showed a possible reduction in SWD episodes, whereas HGI exposure was associated with greater anxiety-like and depression-like behavior. Further investigation is warranted.

papers.title: Machine Learning Applications in Adolescent Sports Injury Prediction: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: This review examined machine learning applications to adolescent sports injury prediction. Six databases were searched on 25 May 2026 for publications from January 2021 onward involving participants aged 10-19 years. Two reviewers independently screened studies. Methodological appraisal was conducted using PROBAST+AI, design-specific JBI checklists, or QualSyst, with one reviewer conducting the assessments and the other verifying them. Findings were synthesized narratively. Thirty reports representing 29 studies covered injury prediction, clinical and surrogate outcomes, biomechanical classification, and monitoring or exploratory applications. Thirteen reports provided ROC-AUC values of 0.58-0.94; sensitivity/recall for injury occurrence or recurrence ranged from 25.0% to 94.3%. Features included maturation, anthropometry, clinical history, neuromuscular performance, biomechanics, physiological and metabolic markers, training load, and psychological and sleep-related measures. Among 14 PROBAST+AI reports, performance-related risk of bias was high in 4 and unclear in 10. JBI assessments identified methodological concerns; nine QualSyst scores ranged from 0.50 to 0.80, with one report unscored owing to indeterminate criterion applicability. Evidence is insufficient to establish the generalizability of machine-learning performance because of high or unclear risk of bias and limited external validation. Addressing these limitations may support the future use of machine learning in sports injury risk prediction among adolescents. The review was prospectively registered with OSF (PYE97) and received no external funding.

papers.title: MG-STNet: A Compact Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Network for Adaptive Sleep Staging.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging from polysomnography (PSG) is a core component of objective sleep analysis and plays a crucial role in enabling reliable clinical assessment and downstream physiological interpretation, yet the non-stationary nature of physiological signals poses significant challenges for compact models with fixed temporal receptive fields that cannot adapt to time-varying sleep rhythms. To address this challenge, we propose MG-STNet, a compact multi-granularity spatiotemporal network for adaptive sleep staging. The model first utilizes a Multi-Granularity Feature Learning Module (MFLM) to extract multi-resolution representations via parallel downsampling branches, thereby reducing sequence length and computational redundancy. Building on this compact representation, the Global-Local Feature Recalibration (GLFR) module recalibrates multi-channel PSG features by jointly leveraging global statistics and local temporal interactions, while the Adaptive Spatiotemporal Convolution (ASTC) module dynamically routes among complementary temporal branches to capture evolving sleep rhythms. Furthermore, a Temporal Attention Encoding Module (TAEM) is integrated to model long-range dependencies within each epoch. We evaluate MG-STNet on Sleep-EDF-20 and Sleep-EDF-78 using subject-independent k-fold cross-validation. The four-channel model achieves accuracies of 87.3% and 84.5% with 46.6K parameters and 17.2M FLOPs, while its single-channel counterpart achieves 86.6% and 83.2% with 48.6K parameters and 9.8M FLOPs. Experimental results indicate that MG-STNet achieves competitive accuracy with a substantially smaller parameter footprint than mainstream deep sleep-staging models, offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for automatic sleep staging under computational constraints.

papers.title: Acute Exercise and Food-Related Cognitive Processing in Adults with Overweight or Obesity: An ERP Study.
papers.abstract: Acute exercise can influence cognitive control, but whether different exercise protocols produce distinct effects on food-related cognitive processing remains unclear. This study compared high-intensity interval training (HIIT), moderate-to-vigorous continuous aerobic exercise (MV-CAE), and seated rest in adults with overweight or obesity. Seventeen participants completed all three conditions, contributing 51 experimental sessions in a randomized within-subject crossover design. Participants performed a food-related Flanker task involving food and furniture targets under congruent and incongruent conditions. Behavioral performance and event-related potential (ERP) amplitudes were analyzed using mixed-effects models, with ERP analyses focused on the N2 (180-230 ms), P3 (400-600 ms), and late positive potential (LPP; 700-1100 ms) time windows at Fz. The primary analyses did not identify significant intervention × target category × congruency interactions after Holm correction in the N2 (adjusted p = 0.1635), P3 (adjusted p = 0.5248), or LPP (adjusted p = 0.5248) windows. The HIIT-versus-MV-CAE planned contrast in the N2 window was 1.859 µV (95% CI [0.337, 3.381]; Holm-adjusted p = 0.1532). Behavioral accuracy remained high, with no significant overall intervention effect (χ2(2) = 0.452, p = 0.7978). RT likewise showed no significant intervention effect (p = 0.7221). Sensitivity analyses identified an LPP-related difference after excluding three prespecified high-risk sessions, suggesting that later electrophysiological responses warrant further investigation. These findings suggest potentially task-dependent electrophysiological responses to different acute exercise protocols, although the observed patterns require confirmation in larger studies with more comprehensive EEG quality control.

papers.title: Association Between Obstructive Sleep Apnea Severity, Nocturnal Hypoxemia, and DXA T-Scores in Postmenopausal Women: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) causes intermittent hypoxemia and sleep fragmentation, both of which may affect bone metabolism, yet studies of OSA and bone mineral density (BMD) have produced inconsistent results. We examined whether OSA status and conventional polysomnographic indices of OSA severity and nocturnal oxygenation were associated with lumbar spine and total hip T-scores in postmenopausal women. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study of 101 postmenopausal women with polysomnography (PSG) and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) records; 40 had PSG-confirmed OSA and 61 were controls. Lumbar spine and total hip T-scores were the primary outcomes. The OSA and control groups were compared with linear regression adjusted for age and body mass index (BMI). Four conventional indices (apnea-hypopnea index [AHI], oxygen desaturation index [ODI], mean SpO2, and minimum SpO2) were each examined in a separate model adjusted for age and BMI. Extended models, which added calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase [ALP], vitamin D, and parathyroid hormone [PTH] and entered all four indices together, were treated as sensitivity analyses and were calculated. Women with OSA were older than controls (63.9 ± 7.8 vs. 60.1 ± 7.2 years) and had a higher BMI (36.0 ± 7.0 vs. 30.6 ± 4.9 kg/m2). The unadjusted T-score differences were 0.28 (95% CI -0.30 to 0.86) at the lumbar spine and 0.11 (95% CI -0.34 to 0.56) at the total hip; neither was statistically significant. None of the indices were statistically significant in the extended models. The lumbar extended model was significant overall (p = 0.023), whereas the total hip model was not (p = 0.117). We found no statistically significant associations between the conventional indices and lumbar spine or total hip T-scores. The findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the modest sample size, possible overfitting and collinearity in the extended models, and the lack of data on cumulative hypoxic burden. They do not show that OSA has no effect on bone health. Because fractures were not assessed, these data cannot inform screening or fracture-risk decisions.

papers.title: Electroacupuncture Ameliorates Circadian Rhythm Disruption-Induced Oligoasthenospermia in Mice by Modulating the Sirt1/Nrf2 Antioxidant Signaling Pathway.
papers.abstract: The growing prevalence of shift work and nocturnal light exposure in modern lifestyles has made circadian disruption an underrecognized environmental risk factor for male oligoasthenospermia. The core molecular network underlying circadian disruption-induced spermatogenic impairment remains incompletely understood, and targeted non-pharmacological interventions are limited. This study sought to identify candidate regulatory targets for circadian disruption-related oligoasthenospermia and investigate the protective mechanism of electroacupuncture. Gene sets associated with circadian rhythm and oligoasthenospermia were retrieved from GeneCards, OMIM, and GEO databases. Candidate hub genes and pathways were screened via intersection analysis, functional enrichment, and seven machine learning algorithms. A chronic jet lag mouse model was established and randomly divided into control, circadian disruption, and electroacupuncture groups. Sperm parameters, serum reproductive hormone levels, testicular and hepatic clock gene expression, testicular histology, oxidative stress status, and Sirt1/Nrf2 pathway activity were assessed. Five hub genes linked to both circadian rhythm and oligoasthenospermia (IL1B, NFE2L2, PCNA, DMPK, MYH9) were identified, with functional enrichment highlighting pathways related to oxidative stress, gonadal development, and hormone regulation. In vivo, circadian disruption impaired sperm quality, dysregulated reproductive hormones, downregulated testicular clock genes, disrupted spermatogenic structure, elevated testicular oxidative stress, and suppressed the Sirt1/Nrf2 pathway. Electroacupuncture effectively reversed these pathological changes, restored hepatic clock rhythmicity, and upregulated key molecules of the testicular Sirt1/Nrf2 antioxidant pathway. Electroacupuncture ameliorates circadian disruption-induced spermatogenic impairment in mice. This protective effect is associated with the restoration of peripheral circadian rhythm and activation of the testicular Sirt1/Nrf2 antioxidant pathway.

papers.title: Guipi Tang Combined with Probiotics Ameliorates Sleep Deprivation-Induced Hippocampal Injury and Pentobarbital-Induced Sleep Alterations in Mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbance is a prevalent health problem associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis, chronic inflammation, and neuronal dysfunction. Here, we show that Guipi Tang (GPT) combined with probiotics is associated with improvements in pentobarbital-induced sleep responses and hippocampal injury in mice. Compared with individual treatments, the combined intervention showed improvements in several measured outcomes and was associated with changes in gut microbial composition, inflammatory markers, and hippocampal injury. 16S rRNA (16S ribosomal RNA) sequencing (n = 5 per group) revealed alterations in gut microbial composition following sleep deprivation, while the combined treatment modulated the relative abundance of several bacterial taxa. Furthermore, serum levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α (tumor necrosis factor-alpha) and IL-1β (interleukin-1 beta) differed significantly among groups (n = 5 per group; F (4,20) = 3.959, p = 0.0159 and F (4,20) = 10.26, p = 0.0001, respectively). Western blot analysis (n = 4 per group) revealed significant differences in the expression of autophagy-related markers, including ATG5 (F (4,15) = 8.319, p = 0.0032), Beclin-1 (F (4,15) = 13.62, p < 0.0001), the LC3-II (F (4,15) = 13.56, p < 0.0001), and p62 (F (4,15) = 5.870, p = 0.0048). Compared with the Model group, combined treatment significantly increased ATG5, LC3-II and Beclin-1 expression, while reducing p62 expression. In addition, the Bcl-2/Bax ratio increased significantly following combined treatment (n = 4 per group, p < 0.01 vs. Model), accompanied by a reduction in TUNEL-positive cells. Changes in Akt phosphorylation were also observed, although the relationship between Akt signaling and autophagy requires further investigation. Collectively, these findings suggest that GPT combined with probiotics is associated with improvements in pentobarbital-induced sleep responses and hippocampal injury in sleep-deprived mice, accompanied by changes in gut microbial composition, inflammatory markers, and Akt-associated autophagy-related signaling.

papers.title: Metabolic Signatures of Bipolar Disorder Through a Sex-Informed Lens: Emerging Biomarkers for Precision Psychiatry.
papers.abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a clinically heterogeneous condition for which diagnosis, prognostic assessment, and treatment selection continue to rely predominantly on symptom-based evaluation. Metabolomics offers a promising approach to biomarker discovery by capturing the downstream effects of genetic susceptibility, environmental exposures, lifestyle, disease activity, and pharmacological treatment. Studies using peripheral biofluids, post-mortem brain tissue, and in vivo neurometabolic measures have identified alterations involving lipid metabolism, amino acids, energy production, oxidative stress, one-carbon metabolism, tryptophan-kynurenine pathways, and the gut microbiota-derived metabolome. Reproducibility is limited, and the potential influence of biological sex is frequently neglected or treated merely as a statistical covariate. This narrative review critically examines emerging metabolomic and lipidomic biomarkers in BD through a sex-informed perspective. We discuss their potential applications in differential diagnosis, mood-state characterization, illness staging, prediction of treatment response, and identification of cardiometabolic vulnerability. Particular attention is given to sex hormones, reproductive transitions, body composition, immune-metabolic regulation, circadian biology, and sex-dependent pharmacometabolic effects. Major methodological limitations, including small samples, medication exposure, inconsistent mood-state characterization, and insufficient sex-stratified validation, are also considered. Integrating sex as a biological variable into longitudinal, multi-omic, and clinically deeply phenotyped studies may improve biomarker reproducibility and support more individualized approaches to BD.

papers.title: Resilience Medicine and Metabolic Adaptation in Healthy Aging.
papers.abstract: Healthy aging is defined not only by the absence of disease but by the capacity to maintain function and to recover from physiological stress. This integrative review proposes and specifies resilience medicine as a framework that moves beyond static descriptions of aging by linking metabolic adaptation to functional recovery across eight interconnected domains: inflammatory regulation, mitochondrial function, metabolic flexibility, musculoskeletal function, vascular regulation, microbiome-associated processes, neurocognitive function, and circadian organization. The framework separates an individual functional profile-baseline function, reserve, stress response, and recovery-from formulation-specific evidence profiles for nutritional and nutraceutical interventions. Representative trials show why this separation matters: contrasting cardiovascular outcomes with different omega-3 formulations, together with studies of muscle function, cognition, and vascular surrogate endpoints, demonstrate that formulation, population, comparator, and outcome determine what an intervention can claim. We introduce the Multi-System Resilience Activity construct and conditional resilience breadth as transparent reporting tools that map evidence across domains while keeping mechanistic, surrogate, functional, and clinical-event findings distinct, and apply them to published trial data. Finally, we define a validation agenda built on standardized challenge-recovery protocols, repeated metabolic measurements, and patient-relevant functional endpoints. Resilience medicine thereby provides a testable pathway from metabolomic discovery to clinically meaningful evidence in healthy aging.

papers.title: Leukocyte Regulation by Exercise and Complementary Lifestyle Factors in Cardiovascular Health.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of death worldwide, underscoring the need for effective preventive and therapeutic strategies. Chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation contribute to CVD development, with leukocytes linking systemic immune responses to vascular and myocardial injury. Regular exercise is a cornerstone of non-pharmacological cardiovascular prevention and exerts immunomodulatory effects beyond conventional risk-factor control by regulating leukocyte production, trafficking, immunometabolism, and effector functions. Diet, sleep, circadian rhythms, and psychological stress also influence leukocyte-mediated immune regulation through interconnected metabolic, neuroendocrine, and microbiota-related pathways. This review integrates mechanistic evidence on how these lifestyle factors shape leukocyte-mediated immunity in cardiovascular health and disease. Acute exercise induces transient catecholamine-mediated leukocyte mobilization and redistribution, with responses generally increasing with exercise intensity and duration, whereas regular training may produce more sustained changes in hematopoiesis, immunometabolism, and inflammatory function. These adaptations are influenced by cumulative training load and recovery, with experimental studies implicating adipose-derived leptin signaling and myeloid metabolic reprogramming as potential mechanisms. Importantly, transient changes in circulating leukocyte counts do not necessarily indicate sustained functional adaptations, and whether leukocyte regulation directly mediates cardiovascular benefits remains uncertain, particularly in humans. We further identify key mechanistic and translational gaps that must be addressed to develop more targeted lifestyle strategies for CVD prevention and management.

papers.title: Circadian Rhythms, Exercise, and Metabolic Remodeling in MASLD: From Chronometabolism to Muscle-Preserving Care.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) links hepatic lipid accumulation with insulin resistance, disturbed sleep, and impaired muscle health. This critical narrative review integrates clinical, metabolomics, and mechanistic evidence identified through a structured multi-database search and citation-tracing workflow covering PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar to 30 September 2026, focusing on circadian regulation, exercise, and muscle-preserving care. Hepatic clocks coordinate nutrient handling, bile-acid signaling, mitochondrial metabolism, and redox balance. Sleep and meal-timing disruption are associated with adverse metabolic phenotypes, although MASLD-specific causal evidence remains limited. Exercise improves liver and metabolic outcomes, but no universal optimal session time has been established. Time-restricted eating should be evaluated alongside energy intake, diet quality, protein distribution, sleep, and adherence. Complex lipids, acylcarnitines, bile acids, ketone bodies, and amino acids offer complementary research signals; their interpretation requires standardized sampling, analytical quality control, and external validation. Circulating concentrations should not be equated with tissue flux or treatment benefit. Clinical care should integrate fibrosis and cardiometabolic risk assessment with sustainable weight management, progressive resistance and aerobic exercise, adequate protein, and sleep assessment. Future trials should pair repeated, timed metabolite measurements with liver, body-composition, strength, and physical-function outcomes to establish whether these signatures improve clinical decisions.

papers.title: Pediatric Obesity and Cardiometabolic Health: Integrating Metabolomic Signatures, Biological Mechanisms, and Early-Life Exposures.
papers.abstract: Pediatric obesity is increasingly recognized as a biologically heterogeneous metabolic condition associated with early alterations in cardiometabolic health. Traditional clinical markers provide limited resolution for characterizing this heterogeneity, underscoring the need for more integrative approaches. Metabolomics has emerged as a powerful tool for identifying molecular phenotypes that reflect the interplay between excess adiposity, environmental and lifestyle exposures, and cardiometabolic dysfunction. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on pediatric obesity and cardiometabolic health, with particular emphasis on metabolomic signatures, potential biological mechanisms, and early-life and lifestyle determinants. Studies using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and mass spectrometry have identified coordinated alterations in lipoprotein subclasses, triglyceride-rich particles, fatty acids and complex lipids, branched-chain and aromatic amino acids, acylcarnitines, and pathways involved in energy metabolism. These metabolic profiles are associated with insulin resistance and other adverse cardiometabolic traits. Proposed links with adipose tissue dysfunction, inflammation, mitochondrial substrate utilization, and hepatic lipid dysregulation draw partly on adult and experimental mechanistic evidence. Early-life and lifestyle exposures, including maternal health, infant feeding, dietary patterns, physical activity, sleep, and environmental factors, may further shape these metabolic phenotypes. Integrating metabolomic information with clinical and environmental data may improve the characterization of metabolic heterogeneity and help identify biological pathways associated with early cardiometabolic dysfunction. However, classification of current metabolic phenotypes does not establish prediction of future disease. Independent prospective validation, methodological harmonization, and demonstration of incremental clinical utility remain necessary before metabolomic profiling can be incorporated into routine pediatric risk assessment.

papers.title: Abdominal Obesity, Brain Glymphatic Function, and LH-dlHPC Appetite Regulation: Current Evidence, Potential Links, and Implications for Metabolic Health.
papers.abstract: Abdominal obesity is closely associated with adverse metabolic outcomes, but how visceral fat accumulation affects central feeding regulation remains incompletely understood. This narrative review integrates research on visceral adipose tissue (VAT), brain glymphatic processes, and lateral hypothalamus-dorsolateral hippocampus (LH-dlHPC) feeding regulation to examine potential links among peripheral metabolic signals, the brain microenvironment, and circuit function. Human imaging studies suggest associations of obesity-related phenotypes with changes in LH-dlHPC connectivity and glymphatic imaging markers; animal experiments provide mechanistic clues to adipose-derived signals affecting hippocampal synaptic plasticity. We propose that VAT-related inflammatory and extracellular vesicle signals may act on barrier and perivascular glial interfaces, contributing to feeding circuit changes through altered local transport and microenvironmental homeostasis. Current evidence supports parts of this model but has not established a causal relationship in which altered transport mediates dysfunction in specific feeding circuits. We also discuss the influences of sex, hormonal status, and sleep, and outline longitudinal and interventional approaches combining assessments of fat distribution, regional transport, circuit function, and feeding behavior to test these mechanisms and their implications for metabolic health.

papers.title: Effects of Morning Versus Late-Day Exercise on Cardiovascular and Metabolic Outcomes in Different Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Background: Exercise timing may influence cardiovascular and metabolic responses, but the available evidence varies across populations, exercise protocols, and assessment periods. Objectives: To compare the cardiovascular and metabolic effects of morning and late-day exercise in individuals with and without specified cardiometabolic diagnoses. Methods: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library databases were searched for relevant published literature. We included randomized controlled trials and randomized crossover trials comparing exercise performed within prespecified morning and late-day time windows. Eligible populations included individuals without target cardiometabolic diagnoses and patients with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, or metabolic syndrome. Studies were synthesized quantitatively when outcomes were sufficiently comparable for pooling and otherwise summarized narratively. Random-effects models were used for the primary meta-analyses. Results: Thirty-seven studies involving 1150 participants were included. In parallel group trials involving participants without the target diagnoses, late-day exercise was associated with lower blood glucose and triglyceride levels than morning exercise; both estimates were based on two studies and rated as low-certainty evidence. In randomized crossover trials, mean platelet volume was higher after morning exercise both immediately after exercise and during recovery, whereas most other cardiovascular, metabolic, and exercise-response outcomes showed no statistically significant difference between exercise timings. In patients with hypertension and diabetes, pooled analyses did not demonstrate significant differences in the available outcomes, although the evidence was limited and imprecise. Evidence for coronary artery disease and metabolic syndrome was sparse, comprising two and one trials, respectively. Conclusions: Current evidence is insufficient to establish a universally optimal exercise time or demonstrate that differences in acute biomarkers translate into long-term clinical benefit or harm. Although some individual outcomes differed according to exercise timing, the available evidence is limited by the small number of studies, methodological heterogeneity, and limited evidence in populations with cardiometabolic diseases. Larger, well-designed trials with standardized exercise timing protocols and outcome measures are needed to determine whether exercise timing has clinically meaningful effects on cardiovascular and metabolic health.

papers.title: Effects of Superficial Microcurrent Neuromodulation on Sleep and Behavioral Dysregulation in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Quadruple-Blind Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and behavioral dysregulation are common in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This trial evaluated superficial microcurrent neuromodulation (NESA) for prespecified sleep outcomes and explored behavioral effects. Thirty-four children with ASD were randomized to active NESA (n = 16) or sham treatment (n = 18), alongside usual care, for 20 sessions (NCT06417450). Sleep disturbances (SDSC), sleep habits (CSHQ), behavioral dysregulation (ABC-C), and parental stress (PSI-SF) were assessed before and after treatment. Baseline-adjusted ANCOVA estimated between-group differences; a sensitivity analysis included children aged ≥5 years. Parental PSQI responses were excluded because questionnaire completion was unreliable. No significant adjusted between-group effects were observed for sleep disturbances (SDSC, p = 0.274), sleep habits (CSHQ, p = 0.630), or parental stress (PSI-SF, p = 0.355). The secondary ABC-C outcome favored active treatment (adjusted difference, -12.03 points; 95% CI, -22.45 to -1.62; nominal p = 0.025). This finding would not withstand a four-outcome Bonferroni correction and was attenuated in the age-restricted analysis (n = 23; p = 0.283). No between-group benefit was demonstrated on analyzable sleep outcomes. The favorable behavioral signal remains exploratory and requires confirmation in larger, age-appropriate trials.

papers.title: Sex-Stratified Associations Between Sleep-Stage-Specific Respiratory Indices and Metabolic Parameters in Children with Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: To examine whether sex modifies associations between whole-night and sleep-stage-specific respiratory indices and metabolic parameters in children with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This retrospective cross-sectional secondary analysis included a previously reported cohort of 514 children (330 boys, 184 girls) referred for suspected sleep-disordered breathing. Whole-night, rapid eye movement (REM), and non-rapid eye movement (NREM) obstructive apnea-hypopnea index (OAHI) and oxygen desaturation index (ODI) were examined in sex-stratified and pooled interaction models adjusted for age and body mass index z-score. Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied across 30 interaction tests. Sleep architecture was also assessed. After false discovery rate (FDR) correction, triglycerides (TG) were positively associated with all six respiratory indices in both sexes. Sex interactions were significant for TG with whole-night OAHI (standardized β = -0.509; 95% CI, -0.737 to -0.281) and NREM OAHI (β = -0.582; 95% CI, -0.813 to -0.350; both q < 0.001), indicating stronger associations in girls (boys minus girls). No other interactions survived FDR correction. Sex-related heterogeneity was confined to selected TG-OAHI associations. Independent prospective validation is needed to assess reproducibility and clinical relevance.

papers.title: Positional Obstructive Sleep Apnoea and Discordance Between Symptom-Based Screening and Polysomnography in Children.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Paediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ) symptom scores can be discordant with polysomnography (PSG)-defined obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). We characterised this discordance and examined whether positional OSA (POSA) was associated with PSQ-negative status across OSA severity. Methods: This secondary cross-sectional analysis pooled prospective data from two studies of 2-17-year-olds referred for clinically indicated PSG at two Canadian sites. PSQ sleep-related breathing disorder score < 0.33 defined PSQ-negative status; obstructive apnoea-hypopnoea index (OAHI) ≥ 1.5 and ≥5 events/h defined OSA and moderate-to-severe OSA. POSA required a supine-to-non-supine OAHI ratio ≥ 2 and ≥30 min in supine and non-supine positions. Results: Of 475 participants, 141 were PSQ-negative; 101/141 (71.6%) had OSA and 44/141 (31.2%) had moderate-to-severe OSA. Discrimination was limited (area under the curve [AUC]: OSA, 0.518; moderate-to-severe OSA, 0.569). There was no clear association between POSA and PSQ-negative status (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 1.20, 95% CI 0.71-2.00). A post hoc interaction analysis indicated variation by the presence of moderate-to-severe OSA (ratio of ORs 5.37, 95% CI 1.87-15.4). Within moderate-to-severe OSA, PSQ-negative participants showed no clear evidence of lower PSG-defined severity. POSA occurred in 54.8% of PSQ-negative versus 28.1% of PSQ-positive participants and remained associated in the OAHI-adjusted model (OR 2.94, 95% CI 1.38-6.38). Conclusions: PSQ-negative status did not preclude moderate-to-severe OSA among referred children. Within moderate-to-severe OSA, POSA was associated with PSQ-negative status after accounting for overall OAHI and measured covariates. Prospective studies should determine whether positional characteristics measurable before PSG can help characterise symptom-PSG discordance and complement symptom-based assessment.

papers.title: Persistent Insufficient Sleep from Toddlerhood to Early Childhood: A Longitudinal Actigraphy Study.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Sleep in early childhood is essential for healthy development, yet insufficient sleep remains highly prevalent. This study aimed to characterize longitudinal changes in objectively measured sleep patterns, to compare actigraphy-derived sleep measures with parental reports, and to identify predictors of insufficient sleep. Methods: In this longitudinal cohort study, healthy children were assessed at 18-29 months (T1) and 30-41 months (T2). Sleep was objectively measured using wrist actigraphy over 72 h, while parent-reported sleep habits were collected through structured questionnaires. Agreement between actigraphy-derived sleep parameters and parental reports obtained through the Sleep Habits Questionnaire (SHQ) was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and Bland-Altman analyses. Logistic regression models were used to examine whether insufficient sleep at T1 predicted insufficient sleep at T2. Associations between behavioral factors and sleep outcomes were assessed using generalized linear models with repeated measures. Results: A total of 185 children were assessed at T1 and 176 at T2. Mean ± SD total sleep time (TST) remained stable between assessments (10:07 ± 63 min vs. 10:10 ± 62 min), although both bedtime and wake-up time occurred later at T2 (p = 0.003 and p = 0.005, respectively). Children with insufficient sleep at T1 had increased odds of insufficient sleep at T2 (adjusted OR = 3.21; 95% CI: 1.40-7.37; p = 0.006). Moderate agreement between parental reports and actigraphy was observed for bedtime and wake-up time, whereas agreement for TST was poor, since parents consistently overestimated TST and underestimated nocturnal sleep fragmentation (p < 0.001). Nighttime milk intake was associated with lower sleep efficiency and more awakenings, while exposure to blue light before bedtime was associated with shorter TST and higher sleep latency. Conclusions: Insufficient sleep persisted over time. Nighttime feeding and blue light exposure were associated with less favorable sleep outcomes. Early identification of at-risk children and objective sleep assessment may support targeted interventions.

papers.title: Modifiable Factors Associated with Adolescent Mental Health: Evidence from the Spartanburg County Youth Risk Behavior Survey.
papers.abstract: Background: This study examined demographic, school, behavioral, social, and academic factors associated with adolescent mental health and assessed in an exploratory analysis whether the association between academic performance and persistent sadness differed by sex. Methods: We analyzed data from 1112 adolescents participating in the 2022 Spartanburg County Youth Risk Behavior Survey. Survey-weighted logistic regression models examined persistent sadness and suicide planning, and survey-weighted ordinal logistic regression examined poor mental health. Models adjusted for demographic characteristics, bullying, school connectedness, feeling unsafe at school, physical activity, sleep, screen time, caring-adult support, and academic performance. Results: Female and bullying exposure were associated with higher odds across all three mental health outcomes, whereas longer sleep duration and greater caring-adult support were associated with lower odds across all three outcomes. Greater school connectedness was associated with lower odds of suicide planning and poor mental health, but not significantly with persistent sadness. Feeling unsafe at school was associated with persistent sadness and suicide planning, while greater screen time was associated with persistent sadness and poorer mental health. Academic performance was not independently associated with the outcomes overall. However, its association with persistent sadness differed by sex (p = 0.014). Higher academic performance was associated with lower odds of persistent sadness among female students, but not among male students. A sensitivity analysis combining sparse academic-grade categories showed a similar directional pattern, although the interaction did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.060). Conclusions: These findings identify potentially modifiable factors across school, behavioral, and relational contexts and illustrate how locally administered Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) data can inform school- and community-based adolescent mental health prevention planning and future research, while recognizing the observational nature of the findings.

papers.title: Hybrid EEG-EOG Brain-Computer Interface for Virtual-Reality Powered Mobility Training in Children with Severe Neuromotor Disabilities: A Multiple-Case Feasibility Study.
papers.abstract: Background: Developing Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) for children with severe neuromotor disabilities remains challenging due to developmental neurophysiology and the high cognitive demands of motor imagery. Hybrid BCIs integrating electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) can overcome these limitations by combining continuous motor-related control with reliable discrete commands. This multiple-case study investigated the feasibility of a hybrid EEG-EOG BCI integrated with a virtual reality (VR) powered wheelchair simulator for mobility training. Methods: Six participants (mean age: 13.00 ± 3.52 years; 1 female, 5 males) with severe neuromotor disabilities (i.e., Central Core Myopathy, LAMA2 related Congenital Muscular Dystrophy, Spinal Muscular Atrophy Type II, and Cerebral Palsy) completed repeated sessions using a self-paced BCI. The system combined continuous kinesthetic motor imagery (KMI) for steering and EOG-detected voluntary blinks for discrete commands. We evaluated online classification performance (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity), user workload (NASA-TLX), and simulator-related discomfort (MSAQ) under fully and semi-immersive VR conditions. Results: Across the selected session-level evaluations, mean online classification accuracy was 67%, increasing to 77% when considering only successful evaluations. Four of the six participants completed the experimental protocol, whereas two discontinued after T3 because sufficiently stable BCI control could not be achieved. NASA-TLX scores indicated increasing perceived workload but generally low frustration, while low MSAQ scores suggested good VR tolerability. No participants withdrew because of VR-related discomfort or adverse effects. Conclusions: This exploratory study provides preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility of hybrid EEG-EOG BCI control within a VR-based powered mobility simulator for children and adolescents with severe neuromotor disabilities. Although simulated navigation was feasible for four participants, substantial variability in BCI control highlights the need for further technological refinement and validation in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chatbots to Promote Health Behaviors in Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Adolescence is a critical developmental period for establishing health behaviors that shape long-term well-being and chronic disease risk. However, many adolescents do not meet recommendations for physical activity (PA), diet, screen time, or sleep. This review examines the use of AI chatbots to promote adolescents' health behaviors. It synthesizes the existing literature on the use of AI chatbots to promote adolescents' health behaviors, with a focus on four areas: design, feasibility, impact, safety and ethics. Methods: This narrative review synthesized adolescent-focused studies and relevant studies involving children, young adults, mixed-age samples, or unspecified populations when their findings were applicable to adolescent health behavior interventions. The evidence was organized around chatbot design, feasibility, behavioral outcomes, and safety and ethical issues. Results: Selected studies reported favorable usability, satisfaction, or engagement during brief evaluations. Adaptive personalization, contextual prompting, and theory-guided dialogue were reported design features, but their contributions to sustained engagement or behavioral outcomes remain uncertain. However, evidence of behavioral impact of AI chatbots remains limited and uneven across behavior domains (i.e., PA, dietary intake, screen time, and sleep). Safety and ethical concerns include accuracy and misinformation, privacy and data governance, and clear escalation and safety protocols. Conclusions: AI chatbots warrant further investigation for adolescent health behavior promotion. Current evidence does not establish general acceptability, sustained engagement, or behavior change efficacy, and further research should evaluate these outcomes alongside safety and ethical safeguards.

papers.title: Clinical and Genetic Characterization of Preschool Girls with Autism Spectrum Disorder: Insights from Copy Number Variants and X-Chromosome Inactivation.
papers.abstract: Females remain underrepresented in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) research. We characterized clinical and genetic profiles of preschool girls with ASD, focusing on copy number variants (CNVs) and X-chromosome inactivation (XCI). Thirty-two girls with ASD (mean age 3.18 ± 0.85 years) underwent standardized assessment, chromosomal microarray analysis, FMR1 testing, and XCI evaluation using a methylation-sensitive androgen receptor assay. Clinical features were compared between participants with at least one reportable CNV and those with no reportable CNV detected. Identified CNVs were retrospectively reassessed according to ACMG/ClinGen standards. Multiple-testing correction and a sensitivity analysis comparing pathogenic/VUS CNV carriers with participants showing no reportable CNV or only likely benign CNVs were performed. Developmental impairment was frequent, with 24/32 participants (75.0%) showing a GMDS-III developmental quotient below 70. At least one reportable CNV was identified in 14/32 participants (43.8%), and 18/32 (56.3%) had none. Following expert reassessment according to ACMG/ClinGen standards, 17 CNVs were classified as pathogenic (n = 2), variants of uncertain significance (n = 7), or likely benign (n = 8). Pathogenic CNVs were identified in two participants (6.3% of the cohort). Among 25 participants informative for XCI, 24 (96.0%) showed non-markedly skewed XCI and one (4.0%) showed highly skewed XCI (7:93). In primary analyses based on original reportable-CNV status, nominal differences were observed for ADOS-2 symptom severity and sleep difficulties, but these did not remain significant after false discovery rate correction. Continuous GMDS-III, VABS-II, and DP-3 scores did not differ significantly between groups. Primary cross-sectional phenotype-CNV associations did not remain significant after multiple-testing correction. In the exploratory CBCL 6-18 follow-up analyses, differences in Externalizing Problems, Total Problems, and DSM-oriented Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Problems remained significant after FDR correction under the original reportable-CNV grouping, but none remained significant in the sensitivity analysis based on CNV reclassification. Highly skewed XCI was uncommon in this cohort, whereas pathogenic CNVs were identified in a minority of participants despite the relatively high frequency of reportable genomic findings. Primary cross-sectional clinical differences did not survive multiple-testing correction, and phenotype-CNV associations were further attenuated after CNV reclassification. These findings underscore the heterogeneity of female ASD and support a cautious interpretation of genotype-phenotype associations based solely on the presence of reportable CNVs.

papers.title: Socioeconomic and Clinical Outcomes Following Eat Sleep Console Implementation in Appalachia.
papers.abstract: Infants exposed to opioids in utero are at risk of neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS). We compared clinical, family-related, and classification-derived resource outcomes before and after implementation of Eat, Sleep, Console (ESC) in an Appalachian hospital. This single-center retrospective cohort study compared outcomes of opioid-exposed neonates assessed with Finnegan Scoring system (FNASS) (Epoch 1, N = 252) versus the Eat, Sleep, Console (ESC) method (Epoch 2, N = 100). Multivariable logistic regression and gamma generalized linear models with log links evaluated outcomes after adjustment for gestational age and maternal tobacco, fentanyl, and methamphetamine exposure. ESC was associated with lower adjusted odds of NOWS classification (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 0.32, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 0.19-0.54), rescue morphine (aOR 0.36, 95% CI 0.17-0.75), and morphine taper (aOR 0.32, 95% CI 0.12-0.85). Adjusted mean length of stay was lower (ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.54-0.79).
