For the Siena database, the model demonstrated a sensitivity of 95.71 ± 7.87% and a false prediction rate of 0.028 ± 0.036/h. Furthermore, this study achieved patient-independent experiments for prediction evaluation. Conclusions: The proposed model effectively achieves the fusion of multiple features and significantly enhances the prediction performance through multiple deep learning methods. For patient-independent experiments, the excellent prediction performance demonstrates the strong generalization ability.

papers.title: Exploratory Assessment of Portable EEG- and PPG-Derived Indices Following High-Intensity Exercise Under Partial Sleep Restriction in Young Men.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: This exploratory study investigated associations between partial sleep restriction and portable device-derived prefrontal EEG and PPG indices, heart rate recovery (HRR), and perceived exertion (RPE) after high-intensity exercise in young men. Methods: Forty healthy men were randomly assigned to a normal sleep group (NSG; ~8 h, n = 20) or a sleep-restricted group (SRG; ~4 h, n = 20). Participants performed the Harvard Step Test (HST). Prefrontal EEG (Fp1 and Fp2) and single-site PPG were recorded for 1 min before and immediately after exercise using a portable consumer-grade device. Heart rate (HR), HRR, RPE, and physical fitness were assessed. Data were analyzed using mixed-design analysis of variance, t-tests, and supplementary linear mixed-effects models with Holm correction. Results: The theta-to-beta ratio (TBR) showed a significant group × time interaction (Holm-adjusted p = 0.034), increasing only in the SRG (p = 0.0014), whereas spectral edge frequency at 90% (SEF-90) showed no interaction (p = 0.781). Significant interactions were observed for the heart rate variability (HRV) index (p = 0.0085), sympathetic-related index (p < 0.001), and parasympathetic-related index (p = 0.0063). The HRV index decreased and the sympathetic-related index increased only in the SRG, whereas the parasympathetic-related index decreased in both groups. During recovery (1-3 min), the SRG had higher HR and lower HRR than the NSG (all p < 0.05). RPE was also higher in the SRG (p = 0.013). All reported p-values were Holm-adjusted. Conclusions: Partial sleep restriction was associated with changes in prefrontal EEG and exploratory PPG-derived indices, lower early HRR, and greater perceived exertion. The selective TBR response suggests index-dependent EEG changes. These findings warrant caution because of limited EEG spatial coverage, brief recordings, potential artifacts, and unvalidated proprietary algorithms. Device-derived changes do not directly establish altered central or autonomic neural activity.

papers.title: Sensorimotor Beta Power Modulation with Functional Electrical Stimulation to Enhance Reactive Balance Among People with Chronic Stroke-A Preliminary Study.
papers.abstract: Background: People with stroke (PwS) fall nearly twice as often as healthy counterparts, which may reflect deficits in reactive balance control. Those with greater motor impairment fall more often and tolerate lower perturbation intensities, so they may need supplemental agents within perturbation-based training. Our recent work showed that functional electrical stimulation (FES) during unpredicted stance slips immediately improved reactive balance biomechanics and reduced laboratory falls. Whether these peripheral and behavioral effects are accompanied by cortical changes remains unknown. Using mobile brain imaging via electroencephalography (EEG), we examined sensorimotor beta power during slips with and without FES. Methods: Nineteen participants (75.35 ± 12.62 years) with moderate-to-high motor impairment (Chedoke McMaster Leg ≤ 4/7) experienced two unpredicted stance slips in a randomized order: one with FES to the paretic quadriceps 50-500 ms after perturbation onset and one with sub-sensory sham stimulation (Sham-FES). Fifteen participants had artifact-free recordings. Primary outcomes were beta power in the 400 ms windows before and after perturbation onset. Secondary outcomes were laboratory falls and reactive stability; tertiary outcomes were compensatory step length, initiation time, and execution time. We compared conditions using McNemar and paired t-tests. Results: Pre-perturbation beta power was similar across conditions (p > 0.05). Beta power increased from the pre- to the post-perturbation window in both conditions (p < 0.01). Post-perturbation, PwS showed lower sensorimotor beta power during slips with FES than with Sham-FES (p < 0.05), accompanied by fewer laboratory falls, higher reactive stability, and shorter step initiation time. Conclusion: FES to the paretic quadriceps was accompanied by lower post-perturbation sensorimotor beta power and improved reactive balance control, with no pre-perturbation differences. These preliminary findings suggest a promising role for FES in reactive balance recovery among PwS and support further mechanistic study.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Features for Distinguishing VS/UWS from MCS: A Comprehensive Univariate Evaluation with Exploratory Multivariate Analysis.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Consciousness assessment in Disorders of Consciousness (DoC) lacks reliable biomarkers. The relative utility of different EEG feature families for distinguishing Vegetative State/Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome (VS/UWS) from Minimally Conscious State (MCS) remains unclear. This study systematically compares their discriminative capacity. Methods: Resting-state EEG was recorded from 53 VS/UWSs, 55 MCSs, and 48 healthy controls (HCs). Ten feature families were extracted: spectral power/ratios, Mean Microstate Duration (MMD), Microstate frequency of occurrence (MFO), Microstate coverage (MC), microstate transitions, nonlinear complexity, weighted Phase-Lag Index (wPLI) connectivity, Autocorrelation Window (ACW), and aperiodic 1/f parameters. Features were screened for between-group differences with monotonic trends across VS/UWS, MCS, and HC, correlated with Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R) scores. To obtain unbiased performance estimates and address potential circularity, an exploratory Sparse Group Lasso (SGL) analysis was embedded within a strict nested cross-validation (CV) framework, where all univariate screening, standardization, and hyperparameter tuning were performed exclusively within each outer training fold. Results: Of 101 initial features, 35 wPLI-based metrics were excluded after quality control, leaving 66; of these, 29 showed significant monotonic between-group differences. Partial correlations suggested EEG-CRS-R associations were primarily driven by between-group differences. Microstate transition probabilities showed the strongest univariate discrimination, with the highest AUC for D to A (0.708; sensitivity 60.0%, specificity 77.4%). In the nested CV, the SGL linear predictor achieved a mean outer-fold AUC of 0.632 ± 0.107 (median 0.636) across 37 valid folds, and a nested stable-feature logistic regression yielded a comparable AUC of 0.638 ± 0.099. Notably, family-level selection was highly consistent: Complexity and Microstate Transition families were selected in 74% of outer training folds, followed by MFO (70%) and MMD (70%). Conclusions: Although individual EEG features showed limited discriminative power, and the nested-CV multivariate model did not outperform the best single-feature AUC (0.708), SGL analysis within a nested CV framework identified microstate dynamics and nonlinear complexity as the most robust feature families for distinguishing VS/UWS from MCS. Furthermore, partial correlation analyses indicated that EEG-CRS-R associations were driven by between-group differences, positioning this framework as state-discriminative rather than recovery-monitoring. These findings are exploratory and require further validation in independent external cohorts.

papers.title: Is Peripheral Nerve Hyperexcitability More Common in Adults with ADHD? A Hypothesis-Generating Perspective.
papers.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adults involves heterogeneous alterations of catecholaminergic signalling and inhibitory motor control. Dopamine and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) interact within cortical and subcortical networks, while transcranial magnetic stimulation studies suggest altered cortical inhibition in some ADHD populations. These observations raise a separate, unresolved question: could adults with ADHD have a higher prevalence of peripheral nerve hyperexcitability (PNH) than adults without ADHD? This perspective critically distinguishes central motor disinhibition from spontaneous peripheral motor-axonal activity and examines clinical phenotypes, electrophysiological findings, medication effects and rare genetic disorders. The literature identified provides indirect mechanistic support and isolated clinical observations but does not establish an increased prevalence of electrophysiologically confirmed peripheral nerve hyperexcitability in typical adult ADHD. Negative cortical findings, non-uniform GABA measurements and substantial confounding further constrain interpretation. Three alternative explanatory models are considered: independent coexistence, shared biological predisposition, and indirect influences mediated by treatment, sleep or stress. A testable research framework combines standardised clinical phenotyping with electromyography, peripheral nerve stimulation and, where feasible, complementary central and axonal excitability measurements. The epidemiological hypothesis must be tested before neurotransmitter mechanisms are inferred. Appropriately controlled studies, particularly involving medication-naïve adults, are required; the present hypothesis does not justify routine electrophysiological screening of all adults with ADHD.

papers.title: Is Swimming Training Experience Associated with Better Sensorimotor Control in Water? An Exploratory Study of Upper-Limb Joint Position Sense, EEG Activity, and Subjective Workload.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study examined whether swimming experience is associated with better sensorimotor control in water by comparing joint position sense, cortical activity, and subjective workload across training backgrounds and environments. Methods: Thirty-six participants (12 swimmers, 12 Chinese Wushu (Wushu) athletes, and 12 untrained individuals) performed continuous shoulder and elbow joint-position-reproduction tasks on land and in water. Joint-angle errors, resting-state and task-related α- and β-band EEG power, and NASA Task Load Index scores were assessed using cluster-based permutation tests and mixed analyses of variance with multiple-comparison correction. Results: Environment affected left-elbow absolute error (p = 0.0015) and constant error at all four joints (all corrected p ≤ 0.0028), without a swimming-specific accuracy advantage. Wushu athletes had lower signed left-shoulder and left-elbow constant errors than swimmers. Swimmers showed a greater water-land increase in resting-state α power than untrained participants before right-side tasks (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0048). Task-related α desynchronization was weaker in water during left-shoulder and left-elbow tasks; no corrected training-related effects emerged for task-related α or β power. Physical demand and perceived performance showed group × environment interactions (both corrected p = 0.0458); swimmers reported lower physical demand than untrained participants in water. Conclusions: Swimming experience was associated with distinct pre-task resting-state α responses, but not better joint-position accuracy or distinct task-related cortical activity modulation. Long-term training in different environments appeared to reduce the physical demand of sensorimotor tasks performed in the familiar environment. These findings provide limited support for swimming-specific sensorimotor advantages in water.

papers.title: Hypothalamic Orexin Neurons Modulate Sleep-Wake States and Seizure Burden in a Kainic Acid-Induced Mouse Model of Chronic Temporal Lobe Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Sleep-wake states strongly influence seizure susceptibility, but the circuit mechanisms linking arousal regulation to seizure burden in chronic temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) remain unclear. This study investigated whether hypothalamic orexin neurons regulate sleep architecture, spontaneous seizures, and epileptic network activity in a kainic acid (KA)-induced chronic TLE model in male mice. Methods: Continuous video-EEG/EMG recordings were used to quantify sleep-wake states, circadian seizure distribution, and seizure burden. Orexin neurons were bidirectionally manipulated in KA-treated Hcrt-Cre mice using Cre-dependent hM3Dq or hM4Di chemogenetic tools. Orexin receptor 1 signaling was pharmacologically blocked with SB334867. Power spectral density and phase-amplitude coupling analyses were performed across wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement sleep, and rapid eye movement sleep. Results: Spontaneous seizures occurred predominantly during wakefulness and non-rapid eye movement sleep, with no seizures observed during rapid eye movement sleep. Seizure occurrence was greater during the dark phase and remained higher during wakefulness after correction for state occupancy. Chemogenetic activation of orexin neurons increased wakefulness, reduced sleep, and increased seizure count and total seizure duration, whereas chemogenetic inhibition produced opposite effects. SB334867 promoted sleep and reduced seizure count and total seizure duration. Chronic KA mice showed state-dependent spectral remodeling and enhanced delta-high-gamma coupling, which was partially attenuated by SB334867 during non-rapid eye movement and rapid eye movement sleep. Conclusions: These findings suggest that orexin signaling is associated with sleep-wake regulation, abnormal network coupling, and seizure burden in chronic TLE. Modulating orexin signaling may represent a potential direction for future therapeutic investigation aimed at improving sleep disruption and reducing seizure burden.

papers.title: Clinical Translation of Optically Pumped Magnetometer-Based Magnetoencephalography: Current Evidence, Implementation Challenges, and Future Pathways.
papers.abstract: Optically pumped magnetometer-based magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) enables cryogen-free, on-scalp recordings with wearable, individually configurable sensor arrays. These features may expand access to MEG for patients poorly accommodated by fixed-helmet superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) systems. This review evaluates current clinical evidence, implementation barriers, and priorities for clinical translation. This narrative review synthesizes OPM-MEG studies in presurgical epilepsy evaluation and functional mapping, alongside exploratory applications in other neurological and psychiatric conditions. Evidence is considered in relation to clinical performance, validation endpoints, and requirements for acquisition, analysis, and implementation across different clinical settings. Patient-based evidence includes comparative and prospective studies of presurgical evaluation in drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Studies support interictal epileptiform discharge detection and localization, with broad concordance with SQUID-MEG and intracranial electrophysiology; early reports also demonstrate ictal recordings. Pediatric and motion-tolerant recordings represent promising applications. Motor mapping has progressed to small patient cohorts with limited intraoperative validation, while language mapping is supported mainly by small studies and case reports. Applications in neurodegenerative, headache, psychiatric, and developmental disorders remain exploratory and currently lack established clinical indications for MEG. Common translational priorities include standardized performance benchmarks, acquisition quality control, motion management, co-registration, analysis, reporting, and personnel training. OPM-MEG shows promise for extending clinical MEG, supported by patient-based feasibility and comparative studies in presurgical epilepsy evaluation. Multicenter prospective studies should establish performance and reproducibility for defined indications. New applications and claims of additional benefit require evaluation of their effects on clinical management and patient outcomes, supported by standardized workflows across systems and centers.

papers.title: Clinical Outcomes and Corticomotor Excitability After Accelerated High-Frequency rTMS in Refractory Trigeminal Neuralgia: A Prospective Comparative Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Objective: The objective of this study is to evaluate three-month changes in corticomotor excitability, assessed by motor-evoked potential (MEP) amplitudes, following accelerated high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) of the primary motor cortex (M1) in patients with refractory trigeminal neuralgia (TN), and to determine whether chronological age modifies neurophysiological and clinical outcomes. Methods: This prospective, non-randomized, parallel-group comparative cohort study enrolled 192 patients with refractory classical TN, diagnosed according to the International Classification of Headache Disorders, third edition (ICHD-3). The active rTMS group (n = 108) received 10 intensive sessions over five consecutive days (two sessions per day, 40 min interval) using combined 10 Hz and 20 Hz sub-protocols targeting the M1 facial motor representation contralateral to the symptomatic side, guided by international 10/20 electroencephalography (EEG) landmarks and functional MEP optimization. The control group (n = 84) received optimized standard pharmacological care (carbamazepine and/or gabapentin). We assessed Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) and Quality-of-Life Pain (QoLp) scores at baseline (T0), one month (T1), and three months (T3) in both cohorts to evaluate the sustainability of the analgesic effect without maintenance therapies. Longitudinal MEP monitoring was performed exclusively in the active rTMS cohort to trace trajectories; no direct between-group MEP comparisons were performed, and follow-up was fixed at three months. Results: At 3 months, mean facial MEP amplitudes decreased within the active rTMS group (58.11 ± 12.77 μV to 49.77 ± 12.49 μV; p < 0.001), indicating a temporal association with reduced local cortical excitability. This neurophysiological shift paralleled robust clinical improvements: cumulative BPI scores dropped from 96.60 ± 24.88 to 32.88 ± 24.75 (p < 0.001), representing a 65.96% pain reduction, and QoLp scores rose from 4.32 ± 1.85 to 8.57 ± 1.36 (p < 0.001), indicating substantial elevation in functional independence. The control group showed statistically significant but clinically modest changes (p < 0.001, consistent with tabulated estimates), substantially lower than those in the active cohort (group-by-time interaction, p < 0.001). Mixed-design ANCOVA indicated that therapeutic benefits were not modified by chronological age (age-by-time interaction, p > 0.05), despite the active rTMS group having an older baseline age profile (54.69 ± 16.27 vs. 43.17 ± 17.27 years; p < 0.001) due to protracted clinical pharmacoresistance. Conclusions: Accelerated dual-frequency rTMS over the contralateral M1 facial representation may produce measurable reductions in corticomotor excitability that strongly co-occur temporally with clinical remission at 3 months among patients with refractory TN. Significance: These findings may indicate preserved cortical neuroplastic capacity in older, highly treatment-resistant populations, potentially supporting accelerated M1 rTMS as an age-resilient therapeutic strategy for chronic neuropathic pain, although a direct causal relationship remains to be established and extensive randomized trials are required.

papers.title: Behavioral and Neural Measures of Auditory Distraction Are Not Associated with Tinnitus Severity.
papers.abstract: Individuals with chronic tinnitus perceive a phantom sound that imposes either a bothersome and irrepressible distraction throughout waking hours or a relatively mild nuisance that often fades into subliminal awareness. The difference in tinnitus salience may reflect a general difference in inhibitory control over any distracting sound, whether externally or internally generated. In this exploratory study, we tested whether tinnitus burden, assessed using the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI), was associated with behavioral and neural responses to external auditory distraction. Thirty adults with chronic tinnitus completed behavioral and electroencephalographic (EEG) testing. Participants with lower and higher THI scores were similar in age and hearing thresholds. Data from twenty-three neurotypical adults provided an additional reference cohort. Participants classified sequences of amplitude-modulated tones as random or repeating during behavioral testing or combined behavioral and EEG recording sessions. Competing noise or melodic distractors imposed lower and higher levels of distraction, respectively. Melodic distractors reduced response accuracy more than noise distractors, with comparable effects in the lower- and higher-THI groups. Neural synchronization to changes in the target sequence also decreased more with melodic distractors, but this effect did not differ between groups. Other measures of synchronization to target and distractor features showed no significant group differences. Behavioral and neural measures were sensitive to external auditory distraction but did not distinguish participants with lower and higher tinnitus burden. These findings do not support a general deficit in suppressing external auditory distractors as an explanation for greater tinnitus burden under the conditions tested.

papers.title: Electrophysiological Evidence of Cognitive Dysfunction After tSAH: An ERP Study Based on Three Different Stimulation Paradigms.
papers.abstract: Objectives: This study aims to investigate the characteristics of event-related potentials (ERP) in patients with traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (tSAH) during the clinical stable phase, with the aim of obtaining neuroelectrophysiological indicators that can objectively assess cognitive dysfunction caused by this injury. Methods: A total of 16 healthy volunteers and 33 tSAH patients in the stable phase were recruited. Demographic and clinical data were collected, MMSE assessments were completed, and EEG data for P300, mismatch negativity (MMN), and contingent negative variation (CNV) were recorded using a 32-lead ERP system. ERP analysis was performed by comparing the tSAH group with the healthy control (HC) group and by further dividing the tSAH group into a cognitive impairment subgroup (CI, n = 18) and a normal cognition subgroup (NC, n = 15) based on MMSE scores, with a focus on the mean amplitude and peak latency within specific time windows and their correlation with cognitive behavioral measures. Results: The results showed no significant differences in demographic characteristics between the two groups, while the MMSE scores of the tSAH group were significantly lower than those of the HC group. Compared with HC, the mean amplitude of P300 in response to the target stimuli was significantly reduced in multiple brain regions in the tSAH group and attenuated the negativity of mean CNV amplitudes across multiple brain regions, while no significant differences in mean MMN amplitudes were detected across electrodes and no significant differences were observed in peak latencies of P300 and MMN. The CI group was slightly older than the NC group; after controlling for the effect of age, the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores of the CI group were significantly lower than those of the NC group, but no significant differences were found between the two groups in mean amplitudes and peak latencies of P300 and MMN or in mean CNV amplitudes. Conclusions: This study indicates that tSAH may be one of the relevant risk factors for post-traumatic cognitive dysfunction. ERP findings suggest that the allocation of relevant cognitive resources is attenuated in this population, but no differences were detected in the temporal sequence of neural processing. No significant abnormalities were observed during auditory deviance detection corresponding to the MMN time window, and no significant differences in ERP characteristics were found among the subgroups. This study found that tSAH can cause selective cognitive electrophysiological impairment, but ERP electrophysiological changes do not fully match cognitive impairment classified based on clinical scales.

papers.title: Working Memory Disruption and Altered Alpha Dynamics in Misophonics.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Misophonia is characterized by disproportionate emotional and physiological responses to specific "trigger" sounds, often accompanied by self-reported difficulty maintaining focus. Here, we seek to provide objective evidence of such cognitive disruptions by combining behavioral measures of auditory working memory with electroencephalographic (EEG) indices of neural processing. Methods: Fifty-five participants (23 misophonic, 32 control) completed a pitch-matching working memory task under three distractor conditions: individualized trigger sounds, neutral sounds, and silence. EEG was analyzed using a time-frequency approach to assess alpha (8-12 Hz) oscillatory activity during working memory retention at the source level; this was carried out using Independent Component Analysis (ICA). Results: Behaviorally, misophonic participants exhibited reduced overall working memory performance compared to controls, with no difference between neutral and trigger conditions, suggesting a general deficit in distractor inhibition. In exploratory analyses, EEG results showed lower alpha power across all conditions in the misophonia group, consistent with diminished ability to inhibit sound processing rather than trigger-specific effects. This lower alpha appeared to occur for sources in parietal and somatomotor areas, with group differences becoming apparent via alpha suppression around distractor onset. Conclusions: The results are consistent with claims made in the literature that misophonics show impaired attentional control and motor regulation, but conflict with findings that suggest that these issues are specific to triggers.

papers.title: Natural Dopamine: Nature's Seven DIURNAL Environmental Enrichment Properties in Changing Visual Complexity.
papers.abstract: Time spent in unchanging environments is associated with poorer brain, cognitive and mental health outcomes, while environmental enrichment for humans is measured by how much nature is present rather than how it changes. This study quantified nature's changing visual complexity using a large-language-model scoring method validated against a deep-learning complexity metric previously tested using event-related potentials. Photos were taken of a natural scene, a tree, and the sky across minutes, days, and seasons (1115 photographs; 2024 to 2026). The analysis identified seven quantitative properties describing nature's dynamic environmental enrichment in changing visual complexity: Dichotomy, Inclination, Unpredictability, Renewal, Net balance, Amplitude, and Level (DIURNAL). A quantitative simulation then showed that a natural view offers more change than indoor and urban views, consistent with the argument that unchanging environments are detrimental to the brain, which is hypothesised here to act through a dopaminergic pathway. DIURNAL raises questions for biophilic design and for how neurotypical and neurodivergent brains respond to change in visual complexity in nature, digital environments and built environments.

papers.title: Participant-Specific Adaptive Label Smoothing Using Subjective Workload Responses for Cognitive Workload Classification from EEG.
papers.abstract: Background: Cognitive workload classification from electroencephalography is affected by interindividual variability in EEG signals and subjective workload responses. We propose participant-specific adaptive label smoothing, in which the change in perceived workload between resting and task conditions controls the target confidence, while the experimental class remains unchanged. Methods: The method was evaluated on the STEW dataset and compared with five alternative supervision strategies. Two classification models were used: a feature-based convolutional neural network and a multi-scale Swin Transformer network (MST-Net) operating on time-frequency representations. Global and participant-specific stratified normalization were evaluated using participant-disjoint cross-validation. The participant-specific approach used normalization statistics estimated from each unseen participant's own unlabeled EEG data. Results: Under stratified normalization, adaptive label smoothing produced the highest macro F1 for both models, with values of 0.768 and 0.796, and ROC AUC values of 0.844 and 0.878, respectively. It also maintained high recall for both classes. Conclusions: The findings suggest that participant-specific subjective workload responses can be used to modulate target confidence, with the most consistent benefit observed under participant-specific normalization. As the strategies differ in target definitions and no hard rest/task or fixed label-smoothing control was evaluated, the differences are descriptive.

papers.title: Stimulus Dependence of Peripheral Flanker Effects During a Central Task: An EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Surrounding stimuli affect the visual processing of a target; however, whether this effect varies across stimulus types when peripheral targets do not need to be actively discriminated remains unclear. Methods: We recorded EEG activity from 20 participants during a central color judgment task while they viewed peripheral Gabor patterns, vertical stripes, letters, and numbers that were irrelevant to the task. Flankers appeared 1000 ms before targets in the flanked condition, providing an existing visual background. In the unflanked condition, only the fixation point was present before target onset. We compared event-related potentials (ERPs) and beta power between these conditions. Results: A spatiotemporal cluster permutation test revealed a significant interaction between stimulus type and flanker condition in the ERP results, with a cluster spanning 146-252 ms after target onset. Further comparisons revealed that flanker effects on ERP amplitude differed between Gabor patterns and vertical stripes. Within each stimulus condition, ERP changes were observed over different time ranges and scalp locations. Beta power was lower in the flanked condition for Gabor patterns, vertical stripes, and numbers, but no significant interaction was detected for beta power. Central color judgment responses were faster in the flanked condition, whereas accuracy did not differ significantly between conditions. Conclusions: These findings suggest that an existing flanker background can affect EEG responses after target onset without active discrimination of peripheral targets. Differences in flanker effects across stimulus types were supported by the ERP results, while beta power provided additional evidence of changes within stimulus conditions.

papers.title: Evaluating Autonomic and Cognitive Responses to Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation as a Countermeasure for Sleep Deprivation.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Acute sleep deprivation impairs cognitive performance in safety-critical occupations, highlighting a demand for effective countermeasures. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has been explored as an alternative noninvasive neuromodulatory approach to mitigating performance decline. Groups have also capitalized on the ability of biosignals like heart rate variability (HRV) to continuously track performance decline during extended wakefulness, but whether fatigue interventions like tDCS shift the autonomic measures used in such tracking during sleep deprivation remains unknown. This study examined whether tDCS affects autonomic function and cognitive performance during sleep deprivation. Methods: Nineteen participants underwent 26 h of continuous wakefulness with repeated cognitive assessments and electrocardiogram monitoring. After 19 h awake, participants received 30 min of verum (n = 10) or sham (n = 9) tDCS targeting the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in a double-blind design. Performance and HRV were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction, including 5 min windowed analyses of the Multi-Attribute Task Battery-II (MATB). Results: Stimulation had no significant main effect on any cognitive performance or HRV outcome. Exploratory analyses revealed stimulation × window interactions within the MATB for system monitoring reaction time, resource management performance, and absolute high-frequency HRV power. Verum participants reported lower sleepiness at a single post-stimulation round without a corresponding performance benefit. Conclusions: In this exploratory sample, a single tDCS session produced no detectable group-level effects on cognitive performance or HRV, and apart from one exploratory within-task interaction, no systematic stimulation-related shift in autonomic measures was observed. Effect size estimates and exploratory findings within tasks provide a basis for adequately powered studies examining individual variability in tDCS response.

papers.title: From Lesion to Dysmaturation: The Evolving Neuropathological Landscape of Encephalopathy of Prematurity.
papers.abstract: Encephalopathy of prematurity (EoP), a complex neurodevelopmental disorder encompassing brain injury and dysmaturation in preterm infants, has undergone a major conceptual shift over the past several decades. While early neuropathological studies emphasized focal cystic periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), contemporary cohorts predominantly present with diffuse white matter injury (DWMI). The hallmark features of DWMI include hypomyelination or delayed myelination driven by differentiation failure of oligodendrocyte (OL) lineage cells, accompanied by axonopathy and reactive gliosis. Recent insights have broadened this framework beyond isolated white matter abnormalities, demonstrating widespread dysmaturation of neurons, glia, and neural circuits across both white and gray matter structures. At the cellular and molecular levels, diffuse injury is underpinned by the selective vulnerability of pre-OLs to oxidative stress, excitotoxicity, and proinflammatory cascades, which cause differentiation arrest and persistent hypomyelination rather than progenitor cell depletion. Concurrently, activated microglia and astrocytes interact with these oxidative, excitotoxic, and inflammatory pathways, resulting in the disruption of dendritic arborization, interneuron migration, and synaptic pruning, thereby impairing neural circuit assembly. Consequently, EoP is increasingly conceptualized as a multi-factorial neurodevelopmental disorder shaped by the dynamic interplay among destructive injury, developmental dysmaturation, compensatory neuroplasticity, and endogenous repair. These mechanistic insights provide critical implications for therapeutic development. While conventional neuroprotective and neurorestorative strategies remain essential, targeting inhibitory signaling and extracellular matrix barriers to promote OL differentiation and myelination, while concurrently fostering neural plasticity through multimodal interventions, such as gut-brain axis modulation and environmental enrichment, offers unprecedented opportunities to improve functional outcomes.

papers.title: Source-Level Multiscale Granger Causality from Preictal Scalp EEG Identifies Candidate Seizure-Onset Zones in Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Precise localization of seizure-onset zones (SOZs) from noninvasive electroencephalography (EEG) remains challenging in the presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant focal epilepsy. We investigated whether cortical source reconstruction combined with multiscale spectral Granger causality (GC) analysis of preictal scalp EEG could identify candidate SOZ regions. Methods: Sixteen participants underwent presurgical evaluation; two were excluded for excessive EEG artifacts, leaving 14 participants (seven resected with Engel class I outcomes and seven unresected). A clinically representative 20 s preictal EEG segment was cleaned using independent component analysis, EEG source solutions were reconstructed with sLORETA on a template head model, and the EEG source activities were then parcellated into 68 Desikan-Killiany cortical regions. Nonparametric GC using Janashia-Lagvilava spectral matrix factorization was estimated in four bands (1-12, 13-30, 30-45, and 55-95 Hz). Regional causal inflow, outflow, and net flow were calculated. Candidate SOZ regions were defined as those exceeding the 95th percentile of absolute net-flow values. Concordance was assessed against clinically determined SOZ localization and, in resected cases, postoperative surgical outcome. Results: Using beta (13-30 Hz) as the primary band, we found that candidate SOZ regions were concordant with clinical localization in 6/7 resected participants (85.7%; exact 95% CI, 42.1-99.6%) and 3/5 scorable prospective participants (60.0%; 14.7-94.7%), yielding 9/12 overall (75.0%; 42.8-94.5%). Two prospective participants lacked sufficient clinical localization for assessment. Three resected participants with left mesial temporal epilepsy showed reproducible left parahippocampal dominance across beta, gamma, and high-gamma bands, with variable entorhinal co-involvement. Top-ranked candidate SOZ regions consistently exhibited net causal inflow. Conclusions: In this small, heterogeneous cohort, source-level net-flow mapping of preictal scalp EEG identified clinically plausible candidate SOZ regions; these exploratory findings suggest a potential noninvasive adjunct to presurgical evaluation. The inflow-dominant pattern supports a receiver-like role of the SOZ. Larger prospective studies with individualized head models, multiple seizures, and intracranial EEG validation will help establish robustness and clinical utility.

papers.title: Dynamical Analysis of Abnormal Oscillatory Activity in the BG and PPN Associated with Sleep-Related Alterations in Parkinson's Disease and Its Modulation by DBS.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder in which over 80% of patients experience severe sleep disorders. Understanding the neural dynamical mechanisms underlying these sleep disturbances is essential for developing targeted therapeutic strategies. We construct a basal ganglia-thalamocortical-pedunculopontine nucleus (BGTC-PPN) network model by combining Hodgkin-Huxley and Izhikevich neuron models to simulate both healthy and PD network dynamics. We systematically compare the discharge patterns, synchronization indices and power spectral densities of key nuclei between healthy and PD conditions. In addition, we use coherence analysis to characterize the frequency-dependent coupling between the PPN and basal ganglia nuclei, and investigate deep brain stimulation (DBS) modulation effects on the PD network using rectangular-wave stimulation at three target nuclei. Under the PD condition, neuronal activity in the GPi and STN is increased but synchronization in the GPe and PPN is enhanced. β band oscillations are increased, and low-frequency activity in the PPN is disrupted. Coherence analysis reveals frequency-dependent coupling between the PPN and basal ganglia during PD-related network states. Comparison of different DBS targets demonstrates distinct effects. Within our 5-Hz-resolution frequency sweep, STN-DBS broadly suppresses β oscillations and, at approximately 70 Hz, minimizes the deviation of both the δ and β bands from the healthy reference; PPN-DBS enhances δ band activity at low stimulation frequencies or suppresses β synchronization at high frequencies, but these two effects do not co-occur within a single frequency window; GPi-DBS yields a larger increase in δ band power relative to the PD baseline near 55 Hz and suppresses β power in the GPi and PPN, yet the STN β deviation remains elevated across the scanned frequencies. PD-related pathological changes extend beyond motor circuitry and alter BGTC-PPN network dynamics that may be relevant to sleep. The target-dependent and frequency-dependent effects of DBS indicate that STN-DBS at approximately 70 Hz concurrently minimizes the deviation of both the δ and β bands from the healthy reference, whereas GPi-DBS and PPN-DBS modulate the two bands in a frequency-decoupled manner within our 5 Hz resolution frequency sweep. These findings provide a computational framework for optimizing DBS intervention strategies for PD-related sleep dysfunction.

papers.title: Afternoon Spectral Reddening of Daylight as a Candidate Physical Cue for Sundowning Syndrome: A Computational Hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Sundowning syndrome-recurrent late-afternoon agitation, disorientation and anxiety in people with dementia-is widely attributed to disturbed light exposure. Existing accounts remain qualitative, specifying neither which property of the ambient light field changes nor when, and so yield no prediction varying with latitude, season or sky conditions. This article is a computational hypothesis: it contains no patient data and is intended to make a light-based account specific enough to be tested. Methods: We combine standard solar geometry, an analytic clear-sky radiance model and the CIE photometric and CIE S 026 melanopic weighting functions to compute the spectral composition of the light reaching an observer as a continuous function of time, for single sky directions, for vertical (corneal) planes integrated over the whole sky, for turbidities 2-6, and for an observer indoors near a window, at three European latitudes over a full year. Results: The melanopic daylight efficacy ratio at the eye falls from about 1.33 at solar noon to about 1.02 at a solar altitude of 10° and about 0.89 at 2° (turbidity 2), while modelled total illuminance changes much less (by 3-10%). The decline is a function of solar altitude alone to within 0.005 across sites and dates, is flattened but not removed by aerosol loading and, in a modelled side-lit room with interreflections, by electric light. The Sun passes 10° altitude 51-107 min before sunset, at clock times that vary by 3-6 h over the year. These are model estimates of spectral composition, least certain close to the horizon, and not measures of physiological melanopic stimulation. Conclusions: We propose that afternoon spectral reddening-rather than darkness itself-is a candidate physical cue for sundowning, possibly mediated by the diminished short-wavelength drive to melanopsin-expressing retinal ganglion cells. The proposal yields testable predictions, including an experimental design that separates spectral composition from light level, and implies that lighting interventions should be timed to local solar conditions rather than the clock.

papers.title: A Multi-View Graph Convolutional Network with Context Gating for Frequency-Aware Sleep Stage Classification.
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep staging is important for assessing sleep architecture and supporting the diagnosis of sleep-related disorders. Manual scoring is time-consuming and subject to inter-scorer variability, while joint modeling of EEG channel relationships and frequency characteristics remains challenging. Methods: We propose DCMG-Net (dual-branch CNN and context-gated multi-view graph network), a frequency-aware network combining multi-view graph convolution with context gating for five-class sleep staging using EEG alone. Multiscale convolutions and attention extract channel features. Functional, globally learnable, and four physiological frequency-band adjacency matrices define six graph views, whose representations are adaptively fused by context gating. Results: On Sleep-EDF-20, ISRUC-S3, and the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS), overall accuracies were 91.2%, 90.0%, and 86.3%; macro-F1 scores were 84.4%, 88.7%, and 77.2%; and Cohen's κ values were 0.88, 0.87, and 0.81, respectively. Macro-F1 exceeded the highest values reported by the compared literature methods by 1.9, 4.2, and 0.7 percentage points, respectively. In the ablation experiments, gating improved macro-F1 over direct concatenation by 6.1 and 2.3 percentage points on ISRUC-S3 and SHHS. Conclusions: Frequency-band topology and context gating jointly exploit EEG frequency information and channel relationships to improve multi-view classification, providing a methodological basis for portable sleep monitoring and computer-assisted clinical scoring.

papers.title: Parent-Reported Sleep Disturbance Profiles in Children with Epilepsy: A Cross-Sectional Study Using the Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children (SDSC).
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: It is unclear whether sleep disturbances differ between epilepsy phenotypes defined by current International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) criteria. We explored parent-reported sleep disturbances in children with idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) and other epilepsies. Methods: Parents of 127 children with epilepsy completed the Polish Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children (SDSC). We compared IGE (n = 31) with other epilepsies by epilepsy type, etiology, and category, using non-parametric tests with false discovery rate (FDR) correction and linear regression adjusted for age and sex. Results: Children with IGE had lower total SDSC scores than children with other epilepsies (median 39 vs. 44), but this difference was small and not robust in sensitivity analyses. Compared with IGE, structural epilepsy (n = 18) was associated with higher scores for difficulties initiating and maintaining sleep (DIMS; β = 4.3, 95% CI 1.5 to 7.0) and epileptic encephalopathies (n = 15) with higher sleep hyperhidrosis (SHY) scores (β = 1.5, 95% CI 0.33 to 2.7); after FDR correction, both were at or near the threshold of significance (q = 0.053 and q = 0.047). Lower sleep-wake transition scores in IGE were explained by older age. Conclusions: Children with IGE may have milder parent-reported sleep disturbances. The DIMS and SHY findings are exploratory, and age should be considered when interpreting SDSC subscales.

papers.title: Geometric Positional Encoding and Dynamic Weight Fusion for EEG-fNIRS Emotion Recognition.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Driven by the neurovascular coupling mechanism, electroencephalogram (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) capture shared underlying neural activity from electrophysiological and hemodynamic perspectives and thus complement each other. Emotional processing relies on functional synergy across brain regions recorded via EEG and fNIRS channels. Functionally similar channels are co-activated and adjacent in functional space. Nevertheless, existing EEG-fNIRS emotion recognition methods characterize inter-channel synergy using physical distances or graph structures. They fail to quantify channel-relative positions in functional space and capture synergies between functionally similar channels. Furthermore, these methods overlook dynamic modality contributions during fusion, rendering predictions susceptible to low-quality signals. Methods: To tackle these limitations, we propose the Geometric Positional Encoding and Dynamic Weight Fusion Network (GDWF-Net). The EEG branch adopts functional-space geometric distances as positional cues and embeds them into attention via rotary positional encoding to model inter-channel functional synergy. The fNIRS branch extracts spatiotemporal features using lightweight modules. The fusion module computes dynamic weights from modality contributions, suppresses noisy low-quality modalities via negative learning, and models cross-modal interactions within a mixed-curvature space. Conclusions: Evaluated on the ENTER dataset, GDWF-Net achieves accuracies of 81.63% and 65.71% in subject-dependent and cross-subject settings, surpassing state-of-the-art baselines. Ablation experiments and visualizations verify the effectiveness and interpretability of each proposed module.

papers.title: Diffusion-Prior Guided Channel Gating for Interpretable Patient-Specific Seizure Prediction.
papers.abstract: Background: Patient-specific seizure prediction remains challenging because preictal EEG patterns and channel relevance vary substantially across individuals. Methods: We propose a CNN-GCN-Diffusion Network (CGD-Net) integrating channel-wise temporal encoding, montage-informed graph modeling, bag-level aggregation, and diffusion-prior-guided soft channel gating. The patient-specific channel prior was estimated exclusively from training data. CGD-Net was evaluated on 19 CHB-MIT recording cases using seizure-group-aware chronological training, validation, and test partitions. Robustness was assessed using random seeds 42, 52, and 62. Results: Across the three seeds, mean accuracy ranged from 74.84% to 75.87%, and mean AUC ranged from 81.82% to 82.01%. In the seed-42 component comparison, the full model achieved the highest mean accuracy, AUC, F1-score, and specificity. Recording-case-level Wilcoxon tests with Holm correction showed significant improvements in accuracy, AUC, and F1-score over the No bag, No diffusion, and No prior configurations, whereas differences from Random graph were not significant after correction. Channel-importance patterns were highly stable across seeds, with a mean pairwise Spearman correlation of 0.9819 and a mean Top-5 Jaccard index of 0.8730, while hub importance showed moderate patient-dependent stability. Conclusions: These results support the combined use of temporal aggregation, montage-informed graph modeling, and prior-guided channel modulation for retrospective preictal-versus-interictal classification. The explanations represent model-level attributions rather than clinically validated seizure-onset regions. Event-level sensitivity and false-alarm rates were not evaluated, and continuous-recording validation is required before clinical warning-system deployment.

papers.title: EEG Emotion Recognition Based on Azimuthal Equidistant Projection and a Multiscale Residual Temporal Network.
papers.abstract: Background: In most existing EEG-based emotion recognition studies, the spatial configuration of electroencephalography (EEG) electrodes is not adequately preserved, and conventional single-scale convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have limited ability to capture both local and global spatial patterns. To address these limitations, an EEG emotion recognition framework integrating azimuthal equidistant projection (AEP) with a multiscale residual temporal network (MRTNet) is proposed. Methods: Differential entropy (DE) features are first extracted, and the three-dimensional electrode coordinates are projected onto a two-dimensional plane to construct AEP-based DE (AEP-DE) feature maps that preserve the spatial topology of the electrode layout. MRTNet then combines multiscale depthwise separable convolutions with a long short-term memory (LSTM) network to extract spatial features at multiple receptive-field scales and model temporal dependencies across EEG segments. Results: Experimental results show that MRTNet achieves average accuracies of 95.1% for four-class classification on the Database for Emotion Analysis using Physiological Signals (DEAP) and 93.1% for three-class classification on the SJTU Emotion EEG Dataset (SEED). Conclusions: Grad-CAM visualizations further indicate that the model responses are concentrated in spatially localized frontal and temporal regions, providing qualitative support for the spatial interpretability of the proposed method.

papers.title: Associations Between Individual Differences in Cognitive Control Capacity and Multitasking Performance.
papers.abstract: Cognitive control capacity (CCC) describes the maximum volume of information an individual can reliably process per unit time, a key cognitive factor of multitasking performance. While sustained high-load multitasking is known to induce cumulative cognitive impairment, it remains untested whether CCC is associated with vulnerability to this decline across subjective, behavioral, and neural levels. This study systematically characterized how individual differences in CCC relate to multitasking processing ability and examined whether a higher CCC is associated with smaller cognitive fatigue during extended operations. CCC was assessed in 313 college students via the adaptive MFTA_A paradigm. Participants scoring in the upper and lower 27% of the CCC distribution formed the high-CCC group (n = 42, 3.65 ± 0.33 bps) and the low-CCC group (n = 41, 2.04 ± 0.28 bps). All participants completed a 1 h multitasking information-processing test comprising tracking, instrument monitoring, and listening subtasks. Alertness was measured with the Psychomotor Vigilance Task before and after the test, subjective workload was rated across four Visual Analogue Scale dimensions, and continuous task-state EEG was recorded to analyze spectral power and microstate dynamics. Relative to low-CCC participants, the high-CCC group showed smaller post-test alertness declines, consistently higher multitasking scores across all blocks, and sustained higher theta/alpha ratios and parietal beta power throughout the task. High-CCC participants also exhibited descriptively stronger activation of microstate C and a late rebound pattern in microstate D transitions, while the low-CCC group showed early stabilization of D-state dynamics without compensatory adjustment. Subjective workload ratings rose equivalently across time in both groups, with no significant between-group differences. CCC is strongly associated with multitasking efficiency. Higher CCC is associated with larger information-processing capacity and better sustained performance during high-load work. This association may be supported by more efficient neural resource allocation and more robust cognitive control network engagement, with exploratory evidence of adaptive brain network reorganization under fatigue. CCC is associated with both immediate multitasking performance and alertness maintenance capacity during prolonged operations.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Auditory Electrophysiological Biomarkers in Alzheimer's Disease and Hearing Loss: A Critical Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with a long preclinical phase, making early biomarker discovery essential for timely diagnosis, risk stratification, and intervention. Hearing loss has increasingly been recognized as a clinically important and potentially modifiable factor associated with cognitive decline and dementia risk. Beyond peripheral auditory impairment, accumulating evidence suggests that central auditory dysfunction, altered auditory processing, and electrophysiological abnormalities may emerge during the course of AD and related cognitive disorders. Auditory electrophysiological signals, including electroencephalography (EEG), auditory event-related potentials (ERP), auditory evoked cortical potentials (AECP), auditory brainstem response (ABR) recordings, cochlear microphonics (CM), and distortion product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) measures, provide objective and repeatable measurements of peripheral and central auditory pathway function. However, conventional analysis based on peak latency, amplitude, spectral power, and manually engineered features may not fully capture subtle disease-related alterations distributed across time, frequency, and waveform morphology. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new opportunities to extract high-dimensional and physiologically informative representations from auditory and neural signals. Machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), self-supervised learning (SSL), explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and multimodal modeling can support data-driven biomarker discovery, especially in settings where labeled datasets are limited and electrophysiological changes are subtle. This critical narrative review synthesizes current knowledge at the intersection of hearing loss, AD, auditory electrophysiology, and AI. We discuss traditional signal processing, supervised ML, deep neural networks, self-supervised representation learning, explainable models, and multimodal integration strategies. We also identify major methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, heterogeneous acquisition protocols, insufficient external validation, limited interpretability, data leakage risks, and challenges in translating animal-model findings to human disease. Finally, we propose future directions for trustworthy, interpretable, and multimodal AI systems capable of advancing auditory electrophysiological biomarkers for AD and hearing-related neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Continuous Biosignal Analysis in Anesthesia and Critical Care: Detection, State Assessment, and Adverse-Event Prediction: A Critical Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Continuous biosignals contain physiological information that artificial intelligence (AI) may use for adverse-event forecasting, concurrent detection, anesthesia-state classification, and nociception assessment. This critical narrative review examined the technical and clinical evidence for AI-driven biosignal analysis in perioperative and critical care settings. PubMed and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, supplemented by Google Scholar and citation searching. The documented initial selection retained 18 studies from 529 records. One additional eligible study was added, yielding 19 studies for detailed synthesis: 15 clinical patient cohorts, 3 healthy-volunteer experiments, and 1 EEG architectural benchmark. Performance was heterogeneous and not directly comparable across tasks, horizons, prevalences, and validation designs; reported AUROC values ranged from 0.731 to 0.990. A descriptive, PROBAST-informed appraisal of the 18 task-relevant studies identified recurrent methodological concerns, particularly in analysis and validation; applicability was considered separately. Principal limitations included inconsistent outcome definitions, class imbalance, incomplete calibration and clinical-utility assessment, leakage risks, sensor-related bias, and limited prospective evaluation. Translation requires explicit task definitions and prediction horizons, patient-level validation, representative data, appropriate discrimination and calibration assessment, prospective multicenter evaluation, and evidence of clinical utility.

papers.title: Cross-Subject Generalization and Few-Calibration Learning for Fine Motor Imagery BCIs: Evidence Boundaries, Evaluation Recommendations, and a Research Agenda.
papers.abstract: Fine motor imagery (FMI) is a demanding paradigm for scalp EEG brain-computer interfaces, yet most cross-subject and few-calibration methods have only been validated on coarse-grained motor imagery, so their transfer to FMI is unproven. This targeted, evidence-graded review separates direct FMI studies from candidate evidence drawn from upper-limb motor imagery, mixed motor execution/imagery, and coarse-grained tasks. We formalize cross-subject, cross-session, few-shot, zero-calibration, inductive, and transductive settings; assess five candidate method families (data-level alignment, domain adaptation, meta-learning, self-supervised pretraining, and subject-conditioned representation learning); and propose a reproducible leave-one-subject-out evaluation framework with repeated calibration draws, per-subject uncertainty, and explicit hardware metadata. The review shows that the evidence does not permit a ranking of method families for FMI, that no FMI-specific cross-subject benchmark is available in the searched literature although direct individual-finger decoding evidence exists, and that class confusion is a substantial contributor to FMI decoding difficulty, while its dominance over subject shift remains an untested hypothesis. We identify the evidence gaps requiring task-matched, multi-dataset validation before reliable FMI claims can be made and provide a staged research agenda.

papers.title: EEG Functional Connectivity for Consumer Preference Prediction: Statistical Network Analysis and Stable Connectivity Signatures.
papers.abstract: Background: Electroencephalography (EEG) is increasingly used to investigate consumer preferences; however, most predictive studies rely on local spectral or temporal features, and the predictive and statistical relevance of functional connectivity remains underexplored. This study evaluated the statistical significance, predictive performance, and feature-selection stability of EEG functional connectivity measures associated with consumer preference. Methods: Phase Locking Value (PLV) and Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) were computed for the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma frequency bands using product-related EEG recordings from the NeuMa dataset. Subject-level paired statistical analyses were performed with false discovery rate correction. PLV, NMI, and early feature-level PLV+NMI fusion were evaluated using LASSO-based feature selection and five machine-learning classifiers under stratified 10-fold and subject-independent leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation. Feature-selection stability was assessed under both validation strategies. Results: Preferred-product viewing was associated with widespread reductions in functional connectivity for both PLV and NMI, with NMI showing particularly extensive differences in the delta band. PLV and NMI yielded broadly comparable predictive performance, with the highest balanced accuracy of 0.699 achieved by PLV combined with Naive Bayes under both stratified 10-fold and LOSO validation. Early PLV+NMI fusion did not improve predictive performance. In contrast, NMI-derived features dominated the fused stability ranking, accounting for 18 of the 20 highest-ranked stable features, predominantly in the delta band. Conclusions: EEG functional connectivity provides complementary information about consumer preference at the statistical, predictive, and feature-stability levels. PLV combined with Naive Bayes provided the highest balanced accuracy, whereas NMI exhibited greater statistical sensitivity and feature-selection stability. These findings highlight low-frequency, particularly delta-band, connectivity as a relevant target for further investigation and demonstrate the importance of evaluating EEG representations beyond classification performance alone.

papers.title: Incremental Value of EEG Beyond EMG for Participant-Independent Forecasting of Bilateral Lower-Limb Joint Angles.
papers.abstract: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) may contain gait information without improving forecasts beyond electromyography (EMG). We evaluated this increment in 163 treadmill trials from 57 healthy participants (145,885 prediction origins). Six bilateral lower-limb angles were forecast approximately 124.6 ms ahead on the released grid using two-second EEG band powers and EMG features, ridge regression, and 5 × 4 participant-disjoint nested validation. Shared-penalty fusion produced no false-discovery-rate-significant gain over EMG-only and reduced R2 for the left knee (ΔR2 = -0.0260, q = 0.0072) and left ankle (ΔR2 = -0.0390, q = 0.0222). Its descriptive mean increment was -0.0156 (95% CI -0.0312 to 0.0004). Separate penalties did not establish an advantage (mean ΔR2 = -0.0009, 95% CI -0.0123 to 0.0084). An additional C3/Cz/C4 analysis likewise did not establish mean improvement within its fixed exploratory grid (mean ΔR2 = -0.0006, 95% CI -0.0074 to 0.0058). Extending EEG penalties downward left selected models and predictions unchanged. Current-angle, speed-adjusted, and low-gamma-excluded comparisons revealed no reliable gain; EEG-only did not reliably outperform the training mean. These findings apply to the tested predictors in healthy walking. They do not establish equivalence, identify a neuroanatomical cause, or assess intention decoding in patients with weak, unreliable, or spastic activation.

papers.title: MSST-TCN: A Spatially Adaptive Multi-Scale Temporal Convolutional Network for Resting-State EEG-Based Depression Recognition.
papers.abstract: Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) exhibits complex spatial correlations, nonstationarity across multiple scales, and substantial individual differences. Effective extraction of discriminative spatiotemporal features therefore remains a major challenge in automated depression recognition. To address these issues, this study proposes MSST-TCN, a depression recognition model that integrates spatial adaptive filtering with multi-scale temporal modeling. First, the Spatial Adaptive Filtering (SAF) module combines learnable spatial projection, electrode-topology information, and channel recalibration to optimize spatial feature representations of multichannel EEG. The Multi-Scale Dilated Convolution (MSDC) module then extracts dynamic features at different local temporal scales. Finally, the Temporal Attention Pooling (TAP) module combines attention weighting with global average pooling to adaptively aggregate temporal features. The model was evaluated using 53 participants from the MODMA dataset (24 patients with MDD and 29 healthy controls) under a stratified five-fold cross-validation protocol with mutually exclusive training, validation, and test participants. MSST-TCN achieved a mean window-level accuracy of 84.71 ± 2.49% and a participant-level accuracy of 81.13% (43/53; Wilson 95% CI: 68.64-89.41%), improving mean window-level accuracy by 6.41 percentage points over the single-scale TCN baseline. Core-module ablations showed that the complete model outperformed the baseline in all five test folds. In the fine-grained ablation comparisons, some configurations achieved favorable performance point estimates; however, all corresponding participant-paired 95% confidence intervals included zero, and statistically reliable independent performance gains from individual internal components could not be established. Sensitivity analyses further demonstrated relatively consistent classification performance under the examined participant partitioning, window segmentation, and normalization settings. These findings indicate that jointly modeling spatial feature representations, multi-scale local temporal dynamics, and temporal information aggregation can improve EEG-based depression recognition under the current participant-independent evaluation conditions. MSST-TCN thus provides a spatiotemporal feature-learning approach with potential for further application-oriented exploration in EEG-based assisted depression recognition.

papers.title: Auditable Multiscale EEG Fusion for Offline Cognitive Workload Decoding in COG-BCI.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Provenance checks and target-data access are often poorly documented in cross-participant electroencephalography (EEG) workload studies. An auditable multiscale decoder is evaluated for the 0-back versus 2-back contrast in the public COG-BCI dataset. Methods: Multiscale spectral, covariance, and bilateral features were selected from training data alone. Linear discriminant analysis and support vector machines were then combined. Identical N-back signal files were found under two nominal identifiers during a source audit. One identifier was excluded. Nominal-unit-held-out evaluation covered 23 test units, 10,682 windows, and 138 recordings. Each test unit was excluded from all supervised steps. Unlabeled target data were available for alignment. Results: Mean window balanced accuracy (BA) was 80.70% (SD, 11.23 points; median, 80.39%; range, 55.48-99.36%; descriptive 95% bootstrap interval, 76.15-85.18%). The mean unit area under the curve (AUC) was 0.8770, and pooled recording BA was 86.96%. A re-centered Riemannian minimum-distance-to-mean comparator reached 68.21%. BA fell by 16.39 points without target alignment. No reliable difference was observed for single temporal widths or linear-margin control. Conclusions: The audited pipeline supports offline, transductive decoding within one cohort. Because the cohort informed development, the estimates are internal and post hoc. Independent-cohort validation and evaluation with a fully causal processing pipeline are required.

papers.title: Infraslow Activity in Hybrid Brain-Computer Interfaces: Signals, Derived Measures, and Validity Conditions for Wearable State Characterization.
papers.abstract: Hybrid brain-computer interfaces (hBCIs) combine EEG with optical and peripheral channels and are increasingly worn outside the laboratory for passive state characterization. Activity below 0.5 Hz is largely excluded from such systems, though brain-body coupling is reported to occur there. This review asks what can be rigorously measured in that range. Some of the analytical conventions imported from faster bands assume a stable characteristic frequency that slow signals often lack. We argue that the absence of periodicity does not preclude rigorous tracking and state characterization. Analyses are organized into three tiers by the temporal assumption each makes: stable frequency, recurrence without stable frequency, and neither, with admissibility often established by test for a given recording rather than assumed from a band label. We review candidate channels by generator character, wearability, and required stillness. We set out the estimators available without phase, including directional ones. We also specify hardware-related acquisition requirements for two possible approaches to analyzing the infraslow band: band-limited envelopes and DC-coupled potentials. In the absence of population norms, we propose individual referencing and identify the reporting minimum a slow-band result requires.

papers.title: A Proof-of-Concept CFD Study of Intranasal Airflow Under Different Breathing Routes and Airway Collapse Conditions.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is closely associated with nasal obstruction, breathing route, and upper-airway collapsibility, yet how changes in breathing route interact with airway collapse to redistribute aerodynamic loading remains incompletely understood. This proof-of-concept study developed a patient-specific computational fluid dynamics (CFD) framework to compare nasal and oronasal breathing under baseline and simulated collapsed upper-airway conditions. Airflow velocity, regional pressure drop, and wall shear stress (WSS) were evaluated across the nasal cavity and downstream pharyngeal regions. Switching from nasal to oronasal breathing consistently reduced intranasal airflow velocity and nasal pressure drop under both airway conditions. Oronasal breathing reduced the cycle-maximum local WSS within the nasal cavity by approximately 42-45%, with reductions exceeding 50% across most turbinate regions. In contrast, the pressure response was strongly region-dependent: oronasal breathing reduced pressure loss across the nasal cavity and uvular region but increased pressure drop at the tongue root. Airway collapse produced a more localized aerodynamic response, most notably increasing posterior nasal velocity and markedly increasing the pressure drop across the uvular region during nasal breathing. These findings indicate that breathing-route alteration and airway collapse do not uniformly increase or decrease upper-airway aerodynamic loading; instead, they redistribute airflow and pressure losses among different anatomical regions. Although based on a single patient-specific model, the proposed CFD framework demonstrates the feasibility of quantifying breathing-route-dependent nose-pharynx aerodynamic interactions and provides a methodological basis for future patient-specific and cohort-based investigations of OSA.

papers.title: PHQ-9-Guided Ordinal Contrastive Learning for Severity-Aware EEG Depression Representation Learning.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based depression detection studies commonly reduce clinical severity scores, such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), to binary diagnostic labels, thereby discarding ordinal information that may be useful for representation learning. This study proposes PHQ-9-guided ordinal contrastive learning (CE+OC), a training objective that uses PHQ-9 scores as privileged ordinal supervision during training while requiring only EEG at inference. PHQ-9 severity distances guide contrastive pair selection and scale the embedding separation margin, using clinical distances to guide the latent EEG space without an explicit patient-ranking objective. The method was evaluated on the Multi-modal Open Dataset for Mental-Disorder Analysis (MODMA) using strict leave-one-subject-out cross-validation across 53 subjects with 128-channel resting-state EEG. The primary representation finding was improved full-cohort PHQ-9 recoverability: a cross-validated held-out PHQ-9 probe showed that CE+OC increased recoverable PHQ-9 rank correlation from 7.8% to 33.6% (paired two-sided permutation p=0.031), an absolute gain of 25.7 percentage points, and reduced mean absolute PHQ-9 error from 27.8% to 22.8% of the 27-point PHQ-9 range (18.1% relative reduction; paired two-sided Wilcoxon p=0.011; bootstrap 95% CI for Δρ: 3.0% to 49.6%). CE+OC also showed descriptive diagnostic differences on MODMA: AUC increased from 59.8% to 69.3%, balanced accuracy from 59.5% to 66.0%, specificity from 69.0% to 86.2%, precision for major depressive disorder (MDD) from 57.1% to 73.3%, and MDD-F1 from 53.3% to 56.4%. False positives decreased from 31.0% to 13.8% of healthy subjects, although sensitivity decreased from 50.0% to 45.8%. A separate LOSO diagnosis evaluation on the independently acquired Mumtaz cohort achieved an AUC of 85.1%; it provides secondary evidence that the pipeline is feasible in a second cohort, but it is not a cross-dataset transfer experiment. A true-diagnosis-only control achieved ρ=0.502 and MAE 2.142 points, and within-MDD probe correlation remained negative (ρ=-0.424). The findings support increased full-cohort PHQ-9 recoverability relative to CE-only, not established information beyond diagnosis; diagnostic difference intervals include zero, and the model is not validated for stand-alone screening.

papers.title: Machine Learning Decoding of Dystonic States from EEG-LFP Signals in GPi-DBS: A Multimodal Case Study.
papers.abstract: Programming Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) for pediatric dystonia remains largely empirical, as no validated electrophysiological biomarker currently guides parameter selection, and most studies treat each signal modality separately rather than exploiting their joint structure. In a single pediatric patient with generalized dystonia and bilateral globus pallidus internus (GPi) DBS implantation, we synchronized electroencephalography (EEG), local field potential (LFP), and electromyography (EMG) recordings across seven sessions spanning stimulator-OFF and multiple stimulation intensities. Dystonic muscle activity labels were derived from a validated quantitative EMG pipeline. Regularized logistic regression classifiers, trained on EEG-only, LFP-only, and combined EEG-LFP feature sets, were evaluated under four validation schemes: within-OFF cross-validation, OFF-to-ON generalization, a mixed leave-one-recording-out (LORO) scheme, and generalization to unseen stimulation intensities. The Combined model performed best in the mixed LORO scenario (balanced accuracy 0.74, sensitivity 0.78, specificity 0.70), inheriting a favorable trade-off from the complementary biases of EEG (sensitivity-dominated) and LFP (specificity-dominated). LFP-derived Hjorth mobility, the beta/gamma power ratio, EEG central alpha power, and central-temporal gamma coherence ranked among the most consistent candidate predictive features across scenarios. Generalization to unseen stimulation intensities preserved a similar, moderately degraded performance profile (balanced accuracy 0.66-0.70). These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence that multimodal EEG-LFP decoding can identify epochs of dystonic muscle activity in paediatric dystonia.

papers.title: Multidimensional Electrophysiological Responses to TMS on the Primary Motor Cortex: A TMS-EEG Characterization of Immediate Cortical Responses.
papers.abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) combined with electroencephalography (EEG) enables millisecond-scale characterization of cortical responses, but direct multidimensional comparisons across stimulation protocols remain limited. In a randomized within-subject crossover study, 17 healthy adults received 10 Hz repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), 1 Hz rTMS, and intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) over the left primary motor cortex in separate sessions. TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs), power spectral density (PSD), and EEG microstate dynamics were assessed before and immediately after stimulation. Following 10 Hz rTMS, group-level P30 amplitude increased from 0.17 to 0.89 μV, while N45 became less negative from -1.73 to -0.82 μV; PSD increased significantly across 15.5-45 Hz. In contrast, 1 Hz rTMS reduced P30 from 0.68 to 0.39 μV and increased P60 from 0.31 to 1.65 μV, with significant PSD reductions at 12.7-31.7 Hz and 32.2-45 Hz. iTBS reduced the magnitude of N45 from -2.76 to -1.93 μV and decreased P60 from 1.41 to 0.47 μV. These findings demonstrate protocol-specific multidimensional electrophysiological profiles across temporal and spectral measures. This framework facilitates systematic comparison across stimulation protocols and provides a basis for further investigation of TMS-induced cortical responses and individualized neuromodulation.

papers.title: Effects of Intermittent Theta-Burst Stimulation over the Left Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex on Executive Function During Sustained Simulated Flight Operations: A Randomized Crossover Study Using a Flight-Cognitive Dual-Task Paradigm.
papers.abstract: Sustained flight operation load may compromise executive control in complex human-machine interaction environments. Intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) holds potential for modulating executive function, yet its effects on different executive components under sustained operational load remain unclear. This study employed a randomized, balanced, within-subject crossover design, enrolling 25 healthy male participants. Each participant completed three intervention conditions: Active iTBS, Sham iTBS, and No-stimulation. Each experimental session consisted of stimulation delivery, a 60-min cruising simulated flight, and a 30-min flight-cognitive dual-task phase. Primary outcomes were behavioral performance on the Go/No-Go, 3-back, and number-rule switching tasks; EEG microstates and prefrontal relative oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO) changes during the dual-task phase served as exploratory neurophysiological indices.
