Results showed that condition differences were concentrated in working memory updating and rule switching: compared with No-stimulation, Active iTBS shortened 3-back reaction time and reduced switch cost; compared with both No-stimulation and Sham iTBS, Active iTBS improved 3-back accuracy and number-rule switching accuracy; the switch-cost difference between Active and Sham iTBS did not reach significance (pBonferroni = 0.055). No significant condition effect was observed for the Go/No-Go task. EEG microstate analysis revealed task-specific changes: under the Active iTBS condition, the occurrence rate and temporal coverage of microstate D increased during the 3-back task; temporal coverage of microstate D increased during the number-rule switching task; no significant microstate changes were observed during the Go/No-Go task. Exploratory fNIRS analysis indicated that left-hemisphere and all-channel prefrontal HbO under Active iTBS was higher than under Sham iTBS in planned pairwise comparisons (pBonferroni < 0.03), but the corresponding condition main effects (p ≥ 0.065) and condition × hemisphere interaction (p = 0.919) were non-significant, and channel-level effects did not survive multiple-comparison correction. These findings suggest that, within the flight-cognitive dual-task paradigm, Active iTBS over the left DLPFC is associated with improvements in working memory and rule switching performance, accompanied by changes in microstate temporal organization during certain tasks. The microstate and fNIRS results provide exploratory neurophysiological observations and cannot establish causal relationships with the behavioral improvements.

papers.title: Neural State Geometry: Unifying Amplitude Landscapes, Coherency Geometry and Information Geometry for EEG State Estimation.
papers.abstract: Brain-state engineering requires measurement and modulation through interpretable, physics-informed coordinates of EEG state structure, change and intervention response. Applications include cognitive fatigue monitoring, neuromodulation readout and progress toward adaptive closed-loop neurotechnology. We introduce Neural State Geometry (NSG), which is a sensor-space framework derived from the complex analytic EEG field rather than a biophysical neuronal model. NSG integrates a Neural Amplitude Landscape (NAL), mapping analytic-amplitude distributions to statistical temperature, internal energy, entropy and heat capacity through exact canonical statistical thermodynamics; pairwise Stokes/coherency geometry representing inter-channel organisation using electromagnetic coherence theory; and quantum-information-inspired state-space geometry quantifying selected-basis organisation. We evaluate NSG through controlled synthetic tests, outcome-blind human-EEG amplitude-model comparison, a single-participant cognitive fatigue example, and a single-investigator transcranial focused ultrasound (TUS) neuromodulation feasibility case. Synthetic tests established descriptor selectivity and common-source sensitivity of zero-lag second-order geometry. NAL/generalised-gamma improved participant-balanced held-out prediction over Rayleigh, Nakagami and gamma but not lognormal. The cognitive fatigue example showed predominantly positive PRE-POST NAL shifts with spectral and second-order deformation. In the fixed-order TUS case, the largest reference-stable NAL displacement occurred at the application site alongside broader sensor-space deformation. NSG provides an interpretable layer for comparing natural and intervention-associated EEG states, supporting future biomarker and target-engagement validation, mechanistic investigation and closed-loop neural engineering.

papers.title: The Effects of Neurotransmitters in Chondrocytes and Cartilage Biology.
papers.abstract: Neurotransmitters are key factors for cell communication within the central and peripheral nervous systems. Recent evidence indicates that they also regulate the function of non-neuronal tissues, including cartilage, as chondrocytes express neurotransmitter receptors, transporters, and other signaling molecules, enabling them to respond to neurochemical cues affecting homeostasis and disease. This review synthesizes the current literature on the roles of major neurotransmitters in chondrocytes and cartilage biology, focusing on norepinephrine, glutamate, γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), acetylcholine, and serotonin. Specifically, we conducted an extensive literature review within major databases such as PubMed and Scopus, which led to 2748 papers being screened based on various inclusion/exclusion criteria. A total of 42 relevant manuscripts were further selected and are presented to describe the role of neurotransmitters in chondrocytes/cartilage. The data demonstrate that neurotransmitter signaling regulates diverse aspects of chondrocyte biology, including proliferation, differentiation, endochondral ossification, mechanotransduction, extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammation, apoptosis, autophagy, and osteoarthritis (OA). Norepinephrine is the most extensively studied neurotransmitter and exhibits context-dependent effects on cartilage development, OA progression, and repair through adrenergic receptor signaling and neuroendocrine pathways. Glutamatergic signaling, particularly through N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, is implicated in mechanotransduction, inflammatory activation, circadian regulation, and OA-associated phenotypic changes, whereas GABAergic signaling primarily regulates growth plate maturation and chondrogenesis. Finally, acetylcholine signaling appears to promote chondrocyte survival and anti-inflammatory responses, while serotonin is linked to altered calcium signaling, inflammatory mediator production, and cartilage catabolism. The biological effects of these neurotransmitters are highly dependent on receptor subtype, disease stage, inflammatory status, and mechanical environment, highlighting the complexity of neuro-cartilage communication. Although significant knowledge gaps remain regarding receptor-specific mechanisms and translational significance, current data support neurotransmitter signaling as an important regulator of cartilage and a promising avenue for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for OA.

papers.title: Clinical, Genetic, and Non-Genomic Biological Factors Associated with Treatment Outcomes in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Clinical, genetic, and non-genomic biological factors may be associated with treatment outcomes in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We examined whether this evidence supports prognosis, treatment selection, monitoring, or safety assessment. Methods: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, with the final search reported on 30 July 2026. Eligibility covered English-language original reports first published online from 2020-2025. Narrative synthesis used QUIPS-informed risk-of-bias domains, ICEMAN interaction credibility questions, and PROBAST + AI-informed prediction-model assessment. Source-linked data and explicit selection rules are supplied for each selected analysis record. Primary outcomes and adjusted models were prioritized, retaining distinct null findings. Results: Twenty-eight reports contributed 58 selected factor-outcome analysis records. Clinical associations varied across interventions and outcomes. Genetic findings showed inconsistent multiplicity-adjusted support and lacked independent replication. Post-treatment prolactin and EEG changes represented process or pharmacodynamic correlates. A combined clinical-genetic model achieved nested-cross-validation AUC = 0.632 without external validation. Certainty was low for restricted placebo-prognosis associations and very low for other questions. Conclusions: No marker or model in this evidence set establishes a sufficiently validated routine ASD treatment-selection rule.

papers.title: Beyond CBD and THC: Cannabigerol (CBG) as an Emerging Neuropsychiatric Drug Candidate.
papers.abstract: Cannabigerol (CBG) is a non-intoxicating phytocannabinoid under investigation as a neuropsychiatric drug candidate. Although historically studied primarily for its role in cannabinoid biosynthesis, CBG has a multitarget pharmacological profile distinct from those of cannabidiol (CBD) and Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC). Experimental studies implicate cannabinoid receptors, α2A-adrenoceptors, 5-HT1A receptors, transient receptor potential channels, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ, and voltage-gated sodium channels, alongside effects on neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, neuronal survival, and excitability. These findings support investigation across several neuropsychiatric conditions, but their clinical relevance remains uncertain. Human studies have begun to characterize oral pharmacokinetics, the influence of food and formulation on systemic exposure, and acute tolerability. A single-dose controlled study of healthy adults reported preliminary effects on anxiety and stress, whereas a repeated-dose randomized trial in participants with problematic sleep found no superiority over placebo on its primary outcome. Brain exposure, target engagement, exposure-response relationships, drug interactions, therapeutic dosing, and long-term safety remain insufficiently defined. This review critically evaluates the pharmacological, preclinical, and human evidence for CBG and identifies the barriers to clinical translation. Despite a plausible experimental rationale, efficacy has not been established for any neuropsychiatric disorder.

papers.title: Circadian Disruption and the 24-Hour Blood Pressure Phenotype in Arterial Hypertension.
papers.abstract: Arterial hypertension is not only a disorder of blood pressure level but also of its temporal organization. This review examines circadian disruption as a multidimensional determinant of the hypertensive phenotype and proposes the 24 h blood pressure profile as an integrated downstream physiological phenotype rather than a direct measure of intrinsic clock dysfunction. Nocturnal hypertension, non-dipping, reverse dipping, morning blood pressure transition, and short-term variability are related but non-equivalent phenotypes with different determinants and imperfect reproducibility. Controlled human studies support causal effects of acute circadian misalignment on selected cardiovascular and metabolic processes, whereas free-living evidence is predominantly observational and confounded by coexisting sleep, metabolic, occupational, and behavioral exposures. Emerging evidence on sleep regularity, social jetlag, nighttime light, meal timing, and time-restricted eating identifies potentially modifiable pathways, but their independent contribution remains difficult to separate from energy balance, weight loss, sleep, and behavioral regularity. Randomized trials do not support universal bedtime antihypertensive dosing. We therefore frame circadian-informed hypertension care around multidimensional phenotyping, with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring as the established cardiovascular output and upstream sleep, behavioral, metabolic, environmental, and, where feasible, endogenous circadian measures. The key translational question is whether reproducible temporal phenotypes can guide interventions that improve cardiovascular and renal outcomes beyond conventional hypertension management.

papers.title: The Role of Circadian Blood Pressure Patterns in Long-Term Mortality in Hypertensive Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) is valuable for assessing circadian blood pressure patterns in hypertensive patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). This study aimed to evaluate the association between circadian blood pressure patterns and long-term mortality and cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events in hypertensive patients with T2DM. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 78 hypertensive patients with T2DM followed who underwent ABPM between 2009 and 2010 at the Diabetes Outpatient Clinic of Haydarpasa Numune Training and Research Hospital, Istanbul, Türkiye. Circadian blood pressure patterns were determined using 24-h ABPM, and participants were classified as dippers or non-dippers. All-cause mortality and cardiovascular/cerebrovascular events were assessed over a 16-year follow-up period. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis cause-specific Cox proportional hazards regression, and Fine-Gray competing-risk regression were performed. Results: A non-dipping blood pressure pattern was identified in 67.9% of patients. During a follow-up period of up to 16 years, 13 deaths and 38 cardiovascular/cerebrovascular (CVD/CeVD) events occurring after baseline ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) were recorded. All-cause mortality occurred in 3 of 25 patients in the dipper group and 10 of 53 patients in the non-dipper group. The estimated 16-year survival probabilities were 88.0% and 81.1%, respectively, with no statistically significant difference between the Kaplan-Meier survival curves (log-rank p = 0.415). In the multivariable Cox proportional hazards model for CVD/CeVD events, non-dipping status was not significantly associated with event risk (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 0.787, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.390-1.587; p = 0.503). In contrast, each 1-percentage-point increase in baseline HbA1c was associated with a higher hazard of CVD/CeVD events (adjusted HR 1.369, 95% CI 1.066-1.757; p = 0.014). Similarly, each additional antihypertensive agent was associated with an increased event hazard (adjusted HR 1.421, 95% CI 1.034-1.954; p = 0.030). In a subgroup analysis restricted to patients without CVD/CeVD at baseline, 34 incident events were observed, and the association between HbA1c and subsequent CVD/CeVD events persisted. Conclusions: The non-dipping blood pressure pattern was not significantly associated with all-cause mortality in hypertensive patients with T2DM. Higher baseline HbA1c was associated with subsequent cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events in both the cause-specific Cox model and the Fine-Gray model.

papers.title: Atherogenic Lipid Profile in Non-Obese Adults with Untreated Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with dyslipidemia, but obesity is a major potential confounder. We investigated whether untreated OSA is associated with an adverse atherogenic lipid profile in non-obese adults. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 104 eligible non-obese adults selected from 703 consecutive patients undergoing respiratory polygraphy; 76 had OSA and 28 did not. Fasting lipid measurements obtained during routine clinical care were retrospectively retrieved from medical records. The Atherogenic Index of Plasma (AIP) was the primary lipid outcome, with additional analyses of conventional lipid components and supportive atherogenic indices. The primary model adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and statin therapy. Results: AIP was higher in participants with OSA than in those without OSA (-0.104 ± 0.303 vs. -0.266 ± 0.296; p = 0.020). After adjustment, OSA remained associated with higher AIP (β = 0.150; 95% CI, 0.009 to 0.290; p = 0.038). OSA was also associated with lower HDL cholesterol (adjusted β = -7.89 mg/dL; 95% CI, -15.03 to -0.76), whereas LDL cholesterol and total cholesterol showed no clear differences. No clear relationship emerged between AIP and conventional measures of OSA severity. Conclusions: In non-obese adults, untreated OSA was associated with an adverse atherogenic lipid profile characterized by higher AIP and predominantly lower HDL cholesterol. These findings suggest that lipid alterations may accompany OSA even without overt obesity, without a clear relationship with conventional measures of OSA severity.

papers.title: CCL4 Enhances Left Stellate Ganglion Sympathetic Activity and Aggravates Ventricular Arrhythmias After Myocardial Ischemia Reperfusion.
papers.abstract: Background: Excessive left stellate ganglion (LSG) activity contributes to ventricular arrhythmias (VAs) after myocardial ischemia reperfusion (I/R). C-C motif chemokine ligand 4 (CCL4) is an inflammatory chemokine involved in neuroimmune signaling. However, whether CCL4 contributes to LSG activation and VAs after myocardial I/R remains unclear. Methods: We enrolled 98 patients with acute myocardial infarction undergoing emergency percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and assessed circulating CCL4, norepinephrine (NE), heart rate variability, and 24-h VAs. In beagles, CCL4 or CCL4 plus a neutralizing antibody was locally microinjected into the LSG before myocardial I/R. LSG neural activity and function, myocardial sympathetic and inflammatory indices, ventricular electrophysiology, and VAs were evaluated. C-C chemokine receptor type 5 (CCR5) expression and localization, together with local immune inflammatory changes, were assessed within the LSG. Results: Patients who developed VAs during post-PCI monitoring had higher circulating CCL4 levels both before PCI and at 1 h after PCI reperfusion, and the increase in CCL4 from pre-PCI to 1 h post-PCI was significantly greater. CCL4 at 1 h post-PCI correlated with sympathetic-related indices and 24-h ventricular premature beat burden, and remained independently associated with VAs after multivariable adjustment. In beagles, myocardial I/R increased endogenous CCL4 mRNA expression in the LSG. Local CCL4 administration enhanced LSG neural activity and function, increased myocardial TH-positive area and pro-inflammatory cytokine mRNA expression, shortened effective refractory period and action potential duration at 90% repolarization, and promoted VAs, whereas CCL4 neutralization attenuated these effects. CCR5 partially colocalized with tyrosine hydroxylase-positive sympathetic neurons. CCR5 expression and c-Fos activation were increased after I/R and further enhanced by CCL4. CCL4 also increased the numbers of Iba1-, CD3-, and CD11c-positive cells and inflammatory responses within the LSG. Conclusions: Clinically, circulating CCL4 was associated with VAs after PCI. In the canine I/R model, local CCL4 administration enhanced LSG sympathetic activity and ventricular arrhythmia susceptibility, potentially involving CCR5-related and local inflammatory processes.

papers.title: The Effects of Progressive Muscle Relaxation Exercise and Kinesio Taping on Stress, Depression, and Sleep Quality in University Students with Premenstrual Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study evaluated progressive muscle relaxation (PMR), Kinesio taping (KT), and their combination for premenstrual symptoms, perceived stress, depressive symptoms, and sleep quality in university students meeting a PMSS-based screening criterion. Methods: In this four-arm randomized trial, 180 students were initially assigned to PMR, KT, PMR + KT, or control (45/group). Fourteen discontinued after baseline, before intervention initiation, and were replaced. Primary longitudinal mixed-effects analyses retained the originally randomized cohort; replacements were included only in sensitivity analyses. Outcomes were measured at baseline, post-intervention, and one-month follow-up. Pairwise comparisons were Bonferroni-adjusted. Registration was retrospective (NCT07791121). Results: Premenstrual symptom severity showed a significant group-by-time interaction (Wald χ2(6) = 199.20, p < 0.001), with lower PMSS scores in all intervention groups versus control at post-intervention and follow-up (all adjusted p < 0.001). The depressive symptom interaction was nominally significant (p = 0.045); only PMR versus control at post-intervention remained significant after adjustment (MD = -3.90; adjusted 95% CI, -7.59 to -0.20). This finding was sensitive to missing-data assumptions. No significant interactions were observed for stress or sleep quality. Conclusions: All interventions were associated with lower premenstrual symptom severity than control. Evidence for depressive symptoms was limited; stress and sleep outcomes showed no significant differential effects. These findings may also have broader relevance to women's health and to efforts aligned with SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being).

papers.title: Effects of Lipoabdominoplasty on Pulmonary Function and Sleep Apnea Risk in Obese Participants.
papers.abstract: Background: The rising global prevalence of obesity has led to an increased demand for lipoabdominoplasty. Obesity is known to impair pulmonary function. In addition, obese patients have an increased risk of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). However, the long-term effects of lipoabdominoplasty on pulmonary function and sleep apnea are unknown. In our study, we aimed to evaluate pulmonary function and OSA risk 3 months after lipoabdominoplasty. Methods: Our single-center, prospective study was conducted at a university hospital between July 2022 and January 2024 and included participants who underwent lipoabdominoplasty. Demographic data, spirometric parameters, modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnea scores, Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) and STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, blood pressure, body mass index, age, neck size, gender) scores were recorded before and 3 months after the lipoabdominoplasty procedure. Results: Of the 31 participants, 24 completed the study. Body mass index (BMI) decreased significantly after lipoabdominoplasty (p < 0.001). Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), forced vital capacity (FVC), and peak expiratory flow (PEF) increased significantly, while mMRC dyspnea scores decreased significantly compared with preoperative values (p < 0.05). ESS and STOP-Bang scores significantly decreased compared to the preoperative period (p < 0.001). The decreases in ESS and STOP-Bang scores were correlated with the decrease in BMI (r = 0.416, p = 0.045; r = 0.459, p = 0.024). Conclusions: Lipoabdominoplasty may be associated with improved spirometric parameters and lower OSA risk scores at 3 months in participants with obesity.

papers.title: Cannabinoids in Psoriasis: From Cutaneous Endocannabinoid Biology to Emerging Clinical Evidence.
papers.abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disease whose management remains limited by treatment costs, routes of administration, and suboptimal adherence, despite major advances in biologic therapies targeting the interleukin-23 (IL-23)/T helper 17 (Th17) axis. In this context, the cutaneous endocannabinoid system has emerged as a promising therapeutic target because of its involvement in keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, local immune regulation, inflammation, pruritus, and neuroimmune signaling. This narrative review synthesizes evidence retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science regarding the role of the cutaneous endocannabinoid system in psoriasis and the therapeutic potential of phytocannabinoids derived from Cannabis sativa. Preclinical studies indicate that cannabinoids can exert anti-inflammatory, antiproliferative, antipruritic, and neuroimmunomodulatory effects through multiple molecular targets relevant to psoriatic pathophysiology. However, these compelling biological findings have not yet been consistently translated into clinical efficacy. The available randomized controlled trials are limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous formulations and routes of administration, and divergent findings concerning objective disease severity, although potential benefits for symptoms such as pruritus and sleep disturbances have been reported. Overall, cannabinoid-based interventions represent a biologically plausible therapeutic strategy under investigation for psoriasis, particularly as adjunctive or symptom-oriented interventions. Nevertheless, adequately powered clinical trials using standardized formulations, well-defined cannabinoid compositions and dosing regimens, clinically appropriate routes of administration, and longer follow-up periods are urgently needed to establish their efficacy, safety, and role in clinical practice.

papers.title: Cholinesterase Inhibitors in the Management of Canine Cognitive Dysfunction: A Review on the Mechanisms of Action, Current Evidence from Experimental and Clinical Studies, and Future Directions.
papers.abstract: Canine cognitive dysfunction is a progressive, age-related neurodegenerative disorder that shares several clinical and neuropathological features with human Alzheimer's disease, although important differences exist between the two conditions. The central mechanisms underlying the pathophysiology of canine cognitive dysfunction include the accumulation of amyloid-β plaques, cytoplasmic deposits of phosphorylated tau protein with rarely observed neurofibrillary tangles, cortical brain atrophy, and disturbances in neurotransmitters, particularly within cholinergic pathways. Compared with those in age-matched, cognitively unimpaired and young cohorts, the number of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain in old, cognitively impaired dogs is significantly lower. However, cholinergic deficit does not correlate directly with cortical amyloid-β load. These neurochemical and structural changes contribute to the characteristic cognitive and behavioral deficits of canine cognitive dysfunction. Cholinesterase inhibitors, which increase synaptic acetylcholine levels by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase and/or butyrylcholinesterase, have emerged as a promising pharmacological strategy. This review critically evaluates current evidence from experimental studies investigating the effects of cholinesterase inhibitors on age-associated cognitive performance in laboratory beagle dogs, as well as clinical studies involving client-owned dogs diagnosed with canine cognitive dysfunction; describes their mechanistic basis; and outlines currently available symptomatic pharmacological interventions, such as the monoamine oxidase B inhibitor selegiline (L-deprenyl), and non-pharmacological interventions, including environmental enrichment, regular exercise, diet, and nutritional supplements. Furthermore, it identifies knowledge gaps and proposes future research directions that could support the translation of cholinesterase inhibitors into effective therapeutic interventions for improving cognitive function and quality of life in aging dog populations.
papers.journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI

papers.title: The Causes of Homelessness Among Dogs and the Role of Shelters in Its Prevention.
papers.abstract: Animal shelters play a vital role in providing care for homeless animals and preparing them for adoption; however, homelessness still poses a significant challenge to the animal welfare system. In the case of dogs, the success of the adoption process is strongly influenced by their behaviour, which is shaped by both their previous life experiences and the shelter environment. The aim of this study was to evaluate the significance of behavioural problems in shelter dogs for the adoption process, with particular emphasis on the relationship between welfare, animal behaviour, the preferences of prospective adopters and the behaviour of the dogs following adoption. This review proposes that the effectiveness of adoption should be considered not only quantitatively, i.e., in terms of the number of animals leaving the shelter, but also qualitatively, i.e., regarding the suitability of the dogs to their new environment and the longevity of the relationship with their owners. The adoption process can be supported by improving welfare, reducing stress and enriching the environment in the shelter, and by conducting individual behavioural assessments, preparing the dog for life in a home environment and presenting the animal appropriately; it is also recommended to educate prospective owners and offer support where necessary. By following a comprehensive approach that promotes dog welfare and employs a responsible adoption process, it is more likely that the animal will find a permanent home with less risk of being returned to the shelter. Hence, to ensure the effective functioning of animal shelters within the animal welfare system, animal behaviour and welfare should be treated as integral elements of strategies to combat dog homelessness.
papers.journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI

papers.title: Research Progress on Peripheral Physiological Responses and Central Neural Activity Characteristics of Competitive Anxiety.
papers.abstract: Competitive anxiety is a core psychological factor constraining athletes' competitive performance. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on its peripheral physiological responses and central neural activity characteristics. At the peripheral level, the autonomic nervous system has been associated with a dual imbalance of sympathetic dominance and parasympathetic suppression. Nonlinear heart rate variability indices have been proposed to be more sensitive than linear indices in one small BMX study, but this remains preliminary and requires replication. Anticipatory cortisol elevation in the HPA axis has been interpreted within the inverted-U hypothesis, with high-trait-anxiety individuals showing delayed recovery dynamics in preliminary studies. Temporal characteristics of catecholamines in the SAM system may be more predictive of performance than absolute concentrations. Oxytocin and progesterone have been proposed as protective neuropeptide mechanisms, whereas sustained elevation of β-endorphin may mask fatigue perception and suppress immunity; these mechanisms remain largely hypothetical. Gut-brain axis research suggests anxiety-associated microbiota restructuring, and probiotic interventions have been associated with improved EEG activity and cognitive function in preliminary trials. At the central level, the Neurovisceral Integration model has been proposed as a framework for peripheral-central interactions. Prefrontal-limbic circuit dysfunction has been proposed to contribute to cognitive interference and somatosensory amplification. Frontoparietal attentional network imbalance may contribute to shortened quiet eye periods and impaired executive function. Cortical neural oscillations have been characterized by enhanced β-band activity with suppressed α/θ activity in some studies. Dysregulation of 5-HT/NE/DA neurotransmitter systems has been proposed to contribute to functional reorganization of the triple brain network through BDNF-mediated synaptic plasticity alterations; this remains a hypothetical integrative pathway. It should be emphasized that many findings derive from heterogeneous designs, small samples, and non-athlete or non-competitive populations; conclusions should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Future research should integrate wearable monitoring, ecological momentary assessment, and machine learning to develop individualized interventions based on neurobiological phenotypes, pending validation of the proposed biomarkers.

papers.title: Exploring Changes in Students' Subjective Sleep Quality, Sleep Beliefs, and Pre-Sleep Arousal After Attending a Curriculum-Embedded University Course on Sleep.
papers.abstract: Good sleep is essential for health, yet sleep is often overlooked due to academic, occupational, and social demands. This non-randomized exploratory study examined changes in sleep-related beliefs, subjective sleep quality, and pre-sleep arousal among students attending a mandatory curriculum-embedded university course on sleep. Seventy-five volunteers (40 female, age = 21.2 ± 2.24) completed the Dysfunctional Beliefs and Attitudes about Sleep (DBAS), the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and the Pre-Sleep Arousal Scale (PSAS) before attending a 3-month curriculum-embedded course in Sleep Psychology (N = 50, 22 females, age = 21.5 ± 2.40) or in History of Psychology (N = 25, 18 F, age = 20.7 ± 1.82). At the end of each course, the same questionnaires were administered. Group × Time interactions were significant for the PSQI subjective sleep quality and sleep disturbances component, PSAS cognitive arousal, DBAS global score, and DBAS consequences component, indicating different pre-post changes between groups. The PSQI global score showed no significant Group × Time interaction, despite a reduction within the Sleep Psychology group. Attending a sleep course was associated with selected sleep-related outcomes. Besides the exploratory nature of this study, our findings highlight the potential value of integrating sleep education into university curricula to promote students' health and well-being.

papers.title: Delayed Declarative and Procedural Memory Performance Following Interference: A Comparison of a 90-Min Midday Nap, Quiet Rest, and Active Wake.
papers.abstract: Newly formed memories are vulnerable to interference. Although sleep can stabilize memories and increase resistance to interference, whether quiet rest provides comparable delayed benefits remains unclear. This study compared the effects of a midday nap, quiet rest, and active wake on delayed declarative and procedural memory performance following interference learning. Post-interference performance served as the baseline. Thirty-seven habitual nappers (29 females and 8 males; mean age = 20.21 ± 3.04 years) were randomly assigned to nap (n = 13), quiet rest (n = 12), or active wake (n = 12) conditions, with polysomnography recorded during the assigned condition. Analyses of percentage change from the post-interference baseline revealed no significant group effects or group × time interactions for declarative or procedural memory. Procedural memory accuracy and speed showed greater improvement at next-day noon than in the evening. Exploratory Holm-corrected one-sample Wilcoxon tests showed improved procedural accuracy relative to the post-interference baseline in the nap group in the evening and in the nap and active wake groups at next-day noon, when speed improved in all three groups. These within-group changes do not establish between-group differences. In the nap group, frontal N2 slow spindle density was positively associated with next-day declarative memory accuracy, while slow spindle peak-phase coupling during N2 and N3 sleep was significantly associated with next-day changes in declarative memory accuracy. Greater REM sleep duration and percentage were associated with less improvement in evening procedural memory speed, whereas frontal N3 fast spindle phase-amplitude coupling was negatively associated with evening gains in procedural memory accuracy. No significant EEG-memory associations emerged during quiet rest. Overall, no significant nap-specific or quiet-rest behavioral advantage was detected. The EEG-memory associations were exploratory and do not establish a sleep-specific consolidation mechanism.

papers.title: Differentiated Neurocognitive Profiles in Problematic Social Media Use: Evidence of Left Frontal Alpha Power, Parietal Activity, and Neural Flexibility in an Adapted Go/NoGo Paradigm.
papers.abstract: There is growing evidence to suggest that problematic social media use reflects a variety of neurocognitive profiles. This study examined differences in absolute alpha and beta spectral power using electroencephalography across three usage profiles: Compulsive Use Profile (CUP), Distress-Associated Profile (DAP) and Functional Profile (FP), derived from a prior cluster analysis. Activity was recorded during three experimental phases: baseline rest, an adapted Go/NoGo task with social media stimuli, and recovery. A 32-channel EEG was recorded from 42 young adults (x¯ = 19.62 years) during the 3 phases mentioned. Absolute spectral power (Welch method) was calculated for the alpha and beta bands in frontal and parietal regions. Mixed ANOVAs, Mann-Whitney U pairwise comparisons and Friedman tests were performed to assess neural modulation. A cluster effect approaching, but not reaching, conventional significance was found for left frontal alpha power (p = 0.057); a direct test of the Profile × Phase interaction for this variable was not significant (p = 0.837), indicating this trend was not specific to any one experimental phase. Pairwise comparisons revealed that the CUP showed significantly lower left frontal alpha power than the FP during the task phase (p = 0.012), with no differences at rest or during recovery. The DAP group showed lower left parietal alpha power during the task (p = 0.036) and lower right parietal alpha power at rest (p = 0.034) compared with the FP group. Only the FP group exhibited significant modulation of alpha power (neural flexibility) across phases (p = 0.035). Problematic social media use is not a uniform phenomenon. The CUP and DAP show distinct neural patterns in the frontal cortex for compulsivity and in the parietal cortex for emotional vulnerability, supporting the use of differentiated neurocognitive models and the need for tailored clinical interventions.

papers.title: The Relationship Between Sleep Disturbance Symptoms, Anxiety, Stress and Risky Headphone-Use Behaviors in Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbance symptoms are common during adolescence and may be associated with affective difficulties and health-related behaviors. This cross-sectional study examined sleep disturbance profiles in relation to anxiety and stress symptoms and risky headphone-use behaviors among 2828 middle- and high-school students in Lianyungang, China. Participants were recruited using stratified multistage cluster sampling. Latent profile analysis identified profiles of nighttime sleep disturbance and daytime dysfunction. Multiple linear regression models estimated adjusted associations with the study outcomes. Three latent profiles were identified. Anxiety and stress symptom scores increased from Profile 1 to Profile 3. Risky headphone-use scores were higher in Profiles 2 and 3 than in Profile 1, with no significant difference between Profiles 2 and 3. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the temporal ordering of these associations.

papers.title: Composite Lifestyle Patterns and Perceived Resilience in Young Adults: A Cross-Sectional Analysis.
papers.abstract: Introduction: Psychological resilience is shaped by behavioral and social factors, thus far most studies have evaluated lifestyle habits in isolation rather than as coordinated patterns. However, it remains unclear whether resilience relates to individual behaviors or to wider behavioral organization. This study examines associations between demographic characteristics, lifestyle behaviors, and perceived resilience, and to test whether clustered behavioral patterns differentiate resilience levels. Methods: A cross-sectional anonymous online survey was completed by 440 young adults, predominantly university students (mean age, 21.96 ± 6.95 years; 90.0% students). Resilience was measured using the Brief Resilience Scale. Lifestyle variables included sleep duration, diet quality, substance use, and physical activity. Ordinal logistic regression was used to evaluate independent predictors of resilience level (Low, Normal, High). Principal component analysis (PCA) identified higher-order behavioral patterns, and group differences were tested using nonparametric comparisons. Results: Higher resilience was associated with male gender (OR = 2.48, p < 0.001) and doctoral degree level (OR = 4.90, p = 0.018); transgender-male participants showed an elevated but non-significant association (OR = 3.12, p = 0.102), and physical activity was not independently associated with resilience after adjustment for other lifestyle behaviors (OR = 1.39, p = 0.127). PCA identified two components representing distinct patterns of covariance among the measured lifestyle indicators (diet category, sleep duration, exercise status, and substance use). Component scores were subsequently compared across resilience categories. PC2 represented a general lifestyle pattern dominated by diet quality and exercise, whereas PC1 reflected a distinct pattern characterized primarily by exercise status, sleep duration, and substance use. PC1 did not differ significantly across resilience levels (p = 0.369). In contrast, PC2 differed significantly and increased monotonically across resilience categories (p = 0.001; η2 = 0.026). Post hoc testing identified significant differences between the Low and Normal resilience groups and between the Low and High resilience groups, but not between the Normal and High resilience groups. Conclusions: Resilience in young adults was associated with a difference in a composite lifestyle pattern, primarily reflecting diet quality and physical activity, rather than with individual lifestyle behaviors considered separately. These findings suggest that the measured lifestyle indicators may exhibit different patterns of covariation across resilience categories, and that the specific behavioral combination associated with resilience may be sensitive to the composition of the analytic sample. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish the direction or mechanisms of this association.

papers.title: Coping with Poor Sleep at University: A Qualitative Study of Student Perspectives and Implications for Personalised Interventions.
papers.abstract: Although it has been established that poor sleep is common in university students, there is some evidence that this has worsened in the post-pandemic era, where irregular sleep patterns and reliance on technology became widespread in young people. This qualitative study explored the experiences of young people who were experiencing poor sleep. Using purposive sampling, 13 undergraduate students reporting sleep difficulties were recruited from academic institutions in the UK, Italy, and Portugal. In-depth interviews were conducted between July 2022 and January 2023, and data were analysed using thematic analysis. Four themes were constructed: (I) Feeling unable to shake off the lingering effects of COVID lockdown, (II) Hypnotic effects of smartphone usage, (III) Being stuck in a loop of poor sleep and low mood, and (IV) Desperately trying to regain control over sleep. Students were eager to remedy their lack of sleep, but some behaviours, such as excessive social media use and late-night rumination contributed to a vicious cycle of negative emotions further disrupting their sleep, which in turn, worsened these feelings. The normalisation of some sleep-related behaviours among young people contributed to their maintenance. In order to develop effective sleep interventions, it is important to recognise the complex and interconnected factors associated with poor sleep in this population. The findings may inform the development of personalised, targeted interventions that address both the psychological and behavioural factors associated with sleep difficulties in university students.

papers.title: Developmental, Contextual, and Profile-Based Heterogeneity in K-12 Students' Artificial Intelligence Literacy.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in students' learning and everyday lives, making AI literacy an important competence in K-12 education. However, large-scale evidence remains limited on AI literacy differences, associated factors, and student profiles. This cross-sectional study used survey data from 141,988 students in Grades 6, 9, and 11 in Changchun, Northeast China. The study addressed three research questions: whether AI literacy differed by grade and student background; which family, academic, lifestyle, and media-use factors were associated with it; and whether profiles emerged across AI understanding, use, evaluation, and ethical awareness. Group comparisons, correlation and hierarchical regression analyses, and latent profile analysis were conducted. AI literacy was higher among students in the upper grades, urban students, and students from higher-socioeconomic-status families, while gender differences were small. Family socioeconomic status, academic achievement, discretionary time, sleep duration, physical activity duration and habit, online gaming habit, and mobile phone usage pattern were positively associated with AI literacy. Online gaming time and mobile phone use time were not independently associated with AI literacy. Four latent profiles were identified: overall low-level, overall high-level, high-exposure-low-reflection, and low-exposure-high-reflection. These findings support equitable, stage-appropriate AI literacy education that considers students' backgrounds and profiles.

papers.title: Associations Between Sleep Quality and Anxiety Among Undergraduate Engineering Students: A Longitudinal Panel Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep is important to university students' mental health, but longitudinal evidence on associations between sleep and anxiety is limited among engineering undergraduates. Using a three-wave balanced panel of 281 engineering undergraduates (W1-W3) at a Chinese university, this study examined longitudinal associations among sleep quality, sleep duration, and anxiety symptoms using a cross-lagged panel model, complemented by individual fixed-effects and adjacent-wave change-score analyses. Anxiety symptoms and sleep-quality problems were descriptively higher at W2 and W3 than at W1, while average sleep duration changed little. Poorer sleep quality at W2 was significantly associated with higher anxiety at W3, and higher anxiety at W2 was significantly associated with poorer sleep quality at W3. Average paths in both directions across the two adjacent-wave intervals were significant; interval-specific reciprocal prospective associations were statistically detectable only from W2 to W3. Independent cross-lagged associations between sleep duration and anxiety were generally weak. Complementary analyses showed significant contemporaneous within-person associations and synchronous changes between deteriorating sleep quality and increasing anxiety. These findings advance the understanding of the relationship between sleep quality and anxiety and may inform further research on sleep support and anxiety risk identification in demanding educational contexts.

papers.title: Effects of Acute Partial Nocturnal Sleep Restriction on Mental Fatigue and Cognitive Control.
papers.abstract: This study examined how one night of 5 h partial sleep restriction affects mental fatigue and cognitive control and compared the magnitude of change between subjective and objective measures. In a within-subject crossover design, 32 healthy university students completed the Stanford Sleepiness Scale (SSS), a visual analog scale (VAS) of fatigue, the brief Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT-B), and a modified Stroop task under a normal-sleep condition and a one-night 5 h sleep-restriction condition. Data were analyzed with linear and generalized linear mixed models. Sleep restriction significantly increased subjective sleepiness and fatigue (both p < 0.001; ηp2 = 0.69 and 0.71, respectively), and these increases were already present before the task. It also produced a small decline in Stroop accuracy for congruent trials (95.94% vs. 93.86%; OR = 0.65, p < 0.001) and special trials (80.40% vs. 76.62%; OR = 0.80, FDR-corrected p = 0.038), with no significant change in incongruent-trial accuracy or reaction time. Objective vigilance and overall reaction time did not change significantly. One night of mild sleep restriction was therefore sufficient to induce subjective mental fatigue; the only objective effect detected was a small decline in accuracy for congruent and special trials, whereas objective vigilance and overall reaction time showed no significant change. The early effects of mild sleep loss appear subjectively sensitive, while the objective cognitive effects, if any, are small and confined to congruent- and special-trial accuracy.

papers.title: Temporal Dynamics of Moral Semantic Processing in Chinese: An ERP Study of Word Categorization.
papers.abstract: Morality serves as a universal code of behavior and a foundation for social value systems. To investigate the cognitive architecture of moral information processing, the present study adopted event-related potentials (ERPs). We used Chinese moral words as stimuli to characterize the temporal neural dynamics of moral processing. Fifty-four participants completed a one-way repeated-measures lexical categorization task with four conditions (moral, immoral, neutral, and pseudowords), including response mapping as a between-subjects factor. Behavioral responses and electroencephalography (EEG) activity were recorded simultaneously. Behavioral analyses yielded robust response latency disparities: participants categorized moral words most rapidly, followed by neutral words and immoral words; pseudowords elicited the slowest responses. ERP analyses revealed graded neural signatures across stimulus categories. During the P2 window (150-250 ms), immoral words elicited the largest amplitudes. At the N3 component (250-350 ms), real words showed attenuated negativity compared with pseudowords, and moral words also differed from neutral words, suggesting that N3 reflects lexical-semantic categorization with additional moral-relevance effects. At the LPP (400-800 ms), immoral words evoked the largest responses, significantly larger than those for neutral and pseudowords, whereas the moral-immoral contrast was not significant. Collectively, these results are consistent with an affective-moral salience account: moral words show a behavioral recognition advantage, and immoral words elicit heightened early and late neurocognitive sensitivity. The findings highlight the utility of ERP analysis for mapping moral semantic processing within the logographic Chinese writing system, and may inform future cross-cultural neurocognitive research and semantic decoding in brain-computer interface paradigms.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Sleep-dependent reduction of glutamate in thalamocortical circuits measured by magnetic resonance spectroscopy at 7T.
papers.abstract: Sleep is crucial for cerebral metabolic homeostasis, yet the processes associated with its restorative effects remain incompletely understood. The synaptic homeostasis hypothesis posits that sleep renormalizes synaptic strength potentiated during wakefulness, thereby promoting energy conservation and optimizing neural efficiency. However, human studies remain limited because conventional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) cannot adequately resolve glutamate from glutamine. Leveraging the superior spectral resolution of ultra-high-field 7‑Tesla MRS, we quantified metabolites in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and thalamus of 20 healthy adults before and after natural sleep. Glutamate concentrations decreased after sleep by 4.8% in the PCC and 5.8% in the thalamus, whereas glutamine and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) showed no significant differences between the two sessions. Higher before-sleep thalamic GABA correlated with increased wake after sleep onset. The lower after-sleep glutamate concentrations are consistent with the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis. The thalamic association suggests a potential role for GABA in compensatory inhibitory regulation in individuals with poorer sleep continuity. These findings reveal regionally consistent sleep-associated differences in glutamate and a region-specific association between thalamic GABA and sleep continuity, highlighting the utility of 7T MRS for resolving metabolite- and region-specific patterns in glutamatergic and GABAergic systems in relation to sleep.
papers.journal: Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism

papers.title: Sedentary behaviour change: barriers and strategies reported by individuals with type 2 diabetes during a multi-component intervention.
papers.abstract: Engaging in high volumes of sedentary behaviour increases the risk of adverse health outcomes, especially for individuals with Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Understanding likely influences on behaviour and effective strategies for reducing sedentary time, as explored in this study, can inform future intervention development and implementation. A randomised controlled feasibility trial was undertaken to evaluate a remotely delivered sedentary behaviour intervention in adults with T2DM. As part of the process evaluation, intervention participants (n = 35) were asked to report the barriers they experienced, and strategies adopted, in their efforts to reduce sitting time. Using template analysis, 44 statements of barriers (from n = 18) and 99 statements of attempted behaviour change strategies (from n = 17) from two time periods were analysed. Themes were similar across 3- and 6-month data for barriers [fatigue/sleep (e.g., feeling drowsy), disability/health, work-related (e.g., work tasks and facilities), and context (social or environmental contextual barriers)]. The themes for strategies reflected behaviours associated with ways to break up sitting, increasing incidental physical activity, and adding in purposeful physical activity. Barriers reflected various individual and contextual factors, while change strategies centred on breaking up sitting through substitution of other behaviours and the use of different types of physical activity. Such information may prove useful in future interventions to reduce sedentary behaviour.
papers.journal: Journal of activity, sedentary and sleep behaviors

papers.title: Proportion of 3- and 4-year-old children meeting individual and combinations of 24-hour movement guidelines across five Canadian provinces: a SUNRISE study.
papers.abstract: Surveillance of children's sleep, physical activity (PA), and sedentary behaviour is a cornerstone of movement behaviour and health research, providing key information for guiding future health promotion policies, programs, and services. Systematic monitoring of these behaviours in preschool-aged children is lacking, particularly for certain sub-groups (males/females, urban/rural areas). This cross-sectional study aimed to assess the prevalence of 3- to 4-year-old children across five Canadian provinces meeting the 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for the Early Years, while examining associations with sex, age, and urban/rural location. Sleep and PA data were collected for 7 continuous days using waist-worn ActiGraph wGT3X+ accelerometers. Sleep duration was also gathered from parent reports, as were sedentary behaviour measures (screen and restrained time). Children were classified as meeting guidelines if they accumulated 10-13 h/day of sleep, ≥ 180 min/day of total PA (TPA), including ≥ 60 min/day of moderate-to-vigorous-intensity PA (MVPA), ≤ 1 h/day of screen time, and ≤ 1 h of restrained sedentary bouts. Within the final sample (n = 631), 29.0% met overall movement guidelines when prioritizing accelerometer-estimated measures. Between 74.6% and 92.0% met the sleep recommendation (accelerometer-estimated versus parent-reported), while 92.4% met PA recommendations (TPA: 100%, MVPA: 92.4%). The proportion meeting sedentary behaviour recommendations was lower (40.7%), with 57.1 and 71.8% meeting recommendations for screen time and restrained time, respectively. Females were significantly less likely to meet the MVPA recommendation (aOR = 0.37, 95% CI [0.19, 0.68]) than males. Urban children were more likely to meet recommendations for sedentary time than their rural counterparts (aOR = 1.51, 95% CI [1.09, 2.09]). Older children were less likely to meet overall guidelines (aOR = 0.49, 95% CI [0.31, 0.77]) and sleep recommendations (aOR = 0.96, 95% CI [0.93, 0.98]), but more likely to meet the MVPA recommendation (aOR = 1.08, 95% CI [1.03, 1.14]). While most children in this sample met sleep and PA recommendations, fewer met sedentary time recommendations. A focus should be placed on public health policies to limit sedentary time in all children, while continuing to encourage healthy sleep and PA. Specific strategies should also be developed to support young females' PA participation.
papers.journal: Journal of activity, sedentary and sleep behaviors

papers.title: Compositional data analysis of the associations among 24-hour movement behaviours and cognitive development of preschoolers across Canada: a SUNRISE study.
papers.abstract: Children experience rapid cognitive development throughout the preschool years. Movement behaviours (sleep, sedentary behaviour, physical activity) may be associated with cognitive development during this critical period. When assessed using compositional data analysis, findings are inconsistent and differences between demographic subgroups (3- versus 4-year-olds, males/females, urban/rural) are largely ignored. This cross-sectional study examined the associations among compositional movement behaviours and cognitive development in preschoolers across Canada, including potential differences by age, sex, and urbanicity. Movement behaviours were measured over 7 days with waist-worn ActiGraph wGT3X+ accelerometers. Children's inhibition and working memory were assessed with validated Early Years Toolbox iPad assessments. Compositional substitution and Goldilocks analyses were conducted. Based on data from 654 preschoolers from across Canada (Mage = 47.4 ± 6.7 months; 53% male), the movement behaviour composition was significantly associated with inhibition (R2 = 0.03, p < 0.001) and working memory (R2 = 0.02, p = 0.001) in unadjusted models but was no longer significant after adjusting for covariates. Replacing light physical activity (LPA) with sedentary time was associated with better inhibition. No significant reallocations arose in subgroups. Goldilocks analysis revealed the following optimal days for inhibition and working memory, respectively (minutes/day): moderate-to-vigorous physical activity ([MVPA], 118; 164), sleep (726; 664), LPA (258; 323), and sedentary time (337; 288). In both cases, sleep values fell within the 24-hour movement guidelines, while optimal values for LPA and MVPA were 1-2 hours higher than current recommendations. Movement behaviours may play a role in preschool cognitive development, though the magnitude of this effect is likely small. Based on our findings, meeting sleep recommendations, engaging in more than twice the recommended amount of MVPA, and maintaining modest sedentary time was associated with optimal inhibition and working memory in this age group. This information serves as a useful point of comparison for researchers in this area; however, more work is needed to establish the utility of movement behaviours in terms of their relationship with preschooler cognitive development.
papers.journal: Journal of activity, sedentary and sleep behaviors

papers.title: Sleep disruption exacerbates allergic airway inflammation through sympathetic-mediated activation of the mtDNA-cGAS-STING pathway in pulmonary macrophages.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption (SD) is increasingly recognized as a systemic stressor that worsens inflammatory disease, yet how it reshapes lung immunity remains poorly defined. To address this, we combined an ovalbumin (OVA)-induced allergic airway inflammation model with sleep disruption paradigms, together with transcriptomic profiling, in vivo pharmacological interventions, and in vitro RAW264.7 macrophage-like cells. In an OVA-induced allergic airway inflammation model, SD markedly increased methacholine responsiveness, aggravated peribronchial inflammation and mucus metaplasia, and promoted a more severe inflammatory airway phenotype. These changes were accompanied by enhanced pulmonary catecholaminergic signaling, reflected by increased tyrosine hydroxylase immunoreactivity and elevated norepinephrine levels. Mechanistically, SD induced mitochondrial dysfunction in the lung, characterized by ultrastructural injury, increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and accumulation of cytosolic mtDNA, together with activation of the cGAS-STING pathway. Cell-type localization analysis showed that activated STING signaling was predominantly associated with F4/80-positive pulmonary macrophages, whereas overlap with Ly6G-positive neutrophils was limited. In vivo, chemical sympathectomy with 6-hydroxydopamine attenuated airway hyperresponsiveness and reduced pulmonary STING pathway activation. In RAW 264.7 cells, norepinephrine (NE) amplified lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammatory responses, promoted mitochondrial oxidative stress, increased cytosolic mtDNA accumulation, and enhanced IRF3 activation, effects that were attenuated by adrenergic blockade and STING inhibition. Together, these findings support a model in which sleep disruption increases catecholaminergic exposure in allergic lungs, thereby driving macrophage mitochondrial stress and mtDNA-cGAS-STING dependent inflammatory amplification. This work identifies a brain-to-lung neuroimmune mechanism linking sleep loss to worsened airway disease and highlights sympathetic-macrophage signaling as a potential mechanism-informed therapeutic target.

papers.title: Chronic pain in Italy: exploring patient perspectives on care gaps and opportunities.
papers.abstract: Chronic pain represents a significant public health burden, yet comprehensive data on patient perspectives in Italy remain limited. Despite Law 38/2010 guaranteeing access to pain therapy, gaps persist in understanding how patients experience care, navigate the healthcare system, and access treatment. This study explored patient perspectives on chronic pain management in Italy, examining therapeutic pathways, barriers to care, legal awareness, and unmet needs. A nationwide cross-sectional survey was conducted between 31 October and 11 November 2025, using Computer-Assisted Web Interviewing (CAWI). Eligible participants were adults (≥ 18 years) with chronic pain lasting ≥ 3 months, reporting pain intensity > 3 on a Numerical Rating Scale (NRS 0-10) in the preceding week or receiving specific pain therapy. Of 2,989 individuals invited, 492 met the inclusion criteria and completed the survey. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, with results presented as frequencies and percentages. Participants (53% female, mean age 62 years) reported moderate-to-severe pain intensity (mean NRS 6.2 ± 1.8), with 52% experiencing severe pain (NRS 7-10). Despite this burden, 28% received no specific pain therapy. Among those treated, initial prescribers were disease specialists (44.1%), general practitioners (42.9%), or pain specialists (13%). Only 22% of patients initially seen by pain specialists continued under their care. Chronic pain significantly impacted daily functioning: sleep (74.8%), work/study (75.5%), and caregiving (64.1%). Barriers to care were prevalent: 71.7% experienced difficulty finding competent specialists, 54% encountered medication access problems, and 65.4% lacked clear treatment information. Only 7.5% had good knowledge of Law 38/2010, and 47.6% could not distinguish palliative care from pain therapy. Access to opioid/cannabinoid therapies was considered difficult by 58.8%, attributed to restrictive regulations (58%) and physician reluctance (54.9%). Most participants (74.5%) perceived chronic pain as inadequately addressed in public discourse, and 67.2% felt unsupported by the National Health Service. This study reveals substantial gaps in chronic pain management in Italy, characterized by high rates of untreated pain, limited specialist involvement, poor care continuity, inadequate legal awareness, and perceived institutional neglect. These findings highlight urgent needs for enhanced access to specialized care, improved primary care training in pain management, regulatory reform to facilitate appropriate opioid/cannabinoid prescribing, public awareness campaigns, and patient-centered care pathways.

papers.title: Inheritance-dependent genotype-phenotype architecture in DEAF1-associated neurodevelopmental disorders: five unrelated patients with de novo DEAF1 variants and an updated synthesis of 67 individuals.
papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants in DEAF1 cause DEAF1-associated neurodevelopmental disorders (DAND) with autosomal-dominant (typically de novo) and autosomal-recessive (biallelic) presentations. We sought to characterize five unrelated children with de novo DEAF1 variants, define epilepsy phenotypes, and refine inheritance-specific genotype-phenotype architecture with developmental context. Trio-based whole-exome sequencing with Sanger confirmation was performed in five unrelated children. Missense variants were evaluated using structural modeling and in silico stability/physicochemical assessments. DEAF1 expression was examined using GTEx, the Human Protein Atlas, BrainSpan, Evo-devo mammalian organ transcriptomes, and single-cell brain organoid datasets. A systematic literature review (inception-March 2026) curated eligible cases for intersection-based UpSet analyses and system-level stacked summaries. Five unrelated children carried heterozygous de novo DEAF1 missense variants; four mapped to the SAND domain (p.Leu203Pro, p.Gly212Ser, p.Ile228Met, p.Leu272Ser) and one was N-terminal (p.Ala29Pro). p.Ala29Pro and p.Ile228Met were not recorded in ClinVar, HGMD Professional, or the reviewed literature. All five patients had intellectual disability/developmental delay with prominent expressive language impairment and motor delay/hypotonia. Epilepsy was observed in all patients, with onset ranging from 7 months to 2 years 8 months, and focal impaired consciousness seizures (FIC) predominated. EEG abnormalities were observed in 4 of the 5 patients, and all five were seizure-free on anti-seizure medications at the last follow-up. Structural modeling suggested variant-dependent perturbations, particularly among SAND-domain substitutions, but these findings remain computational predictions. Expression analyses supported brain-enriched, developmentally regulated DEAF1 expression and broad neuronal/progenitor expression in human brain organoids. A literature review identified 62 individuals from 15 studies; combined with our cohort, 67 individuals were analyzed (de novo n = 52; biallelic n = 15). De novo variants clustered within/around the SAND domain, whereas biallelic variants were more broadly distributed. UpSet and stacked-bar analyses revealed a shared neurodevelopmental core but distinct co-occurrence patterns, with autism/epilepsy shaping dominant intersections in de novo cases and microcephaly/MRI abnormalities contributing more prominently in biallelic disease. Our study refines the de novo clinical and allelic spectrum of DAND and delineates inheritance-specific genotype-phenotype architecture with developmental and cellular context.

papers.title: tACS and nervonic acid inhibit microglial overactivation via the Rap1 signaling pathway and ameliorate sleep deprivation-induced cognitive impairment.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) has become a critical global health concern, with consequences including cognitive decline. Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) holds significant potential for improving cognitive impairment. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of tACS on SD-associated cognitive deficits. Male C57BL/6 mice were subjected to SD using the horizontal platform method. Cognitive function was assessed via multiple behavioral tests, and local field potential (LFP) signals were recorded. Untargeted metabolomics was employed to identify key metabolites and regulatory pathways in mouse brain tissue. Mouse models and co-culture systems were combined to investigate the regulatory relationships among microglia, synapses, and neurons. tACS significantly improved memory and cognitive function in SD-induced model mice, accompanied by inhibited microglial phagocytosis, increased synaptic density, and reduced neuronal apoptosis. Untargeted metabolomics revealed that tACS may regulate nervonic acid (NA) abundance and the Rap1 signaling pathway during SD. Further studies demonstrated that NA suppresses lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced microglial overactivation and synaptic loss via the Rap1 signaling pathway, thereby blocking neuronal apoptosis. Additionally, similar to the therapeutic effects of tACS, NA administration markedly alleviated cognitive impairment and neural damage in SD mice. These data support the regulatory roles of tACS and NA in neuronal activity and synaptic plasticity and propose novel therapeutic targets for SD-related cognitive deficits.

papers.title: Impact of a national educational intervention on academic burden and health-related behaviours among children and adolescents in China: a repeated cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Excessive academic burden adversely affects health-related behaviours and mental health among children and adolescents. In July 2021, China implemented the "Double Reduction" policy to reduce homework and extracurricular tutoring. However, robust evidence on its impact on academic burden and health behaviours is lacking. We aimed to evaluate the changes in academic burden and related health behaviours among school-aged children in Guangzhou before and after the policy. We conducted a repeated cross-sectional study using data from the Guangzhou Student Common Diseases and Health Influencing Factors Surveillance Program (2019-2025). Students in Year 4 - Year 12 from 66 schools were included. Academic burden (daily homework and weekly tutoring time) and health-related behaviours (sedentary time, moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), and sleep duration) were assessed via self-report. Mixed-effects models were used to examine the overall and stratified trends by educational stage, sex and location. Daily homework time decreased significantly from 2019 to 2022 (β = -0.10, 95% CI: -0.11 to -0.09), followed by a rebound from 2022 to 2025 (β = 0.05, 95% CI: 0.04 to 0.06). Weekly tutoring time showed a similar pattern (2019-2022: β = -0.19, 95% CI: -0.20 to -0.18; 2022-2025: β = 0.06, 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.07). The rebound was most pronounced among primary school and suburban students. Urban students showed a rebound primarily in tutoring time, whereas suburban students exhibited a clearer rebound in homework time. Sedentary time followed a comparable U-shaped trajectory. Sleep duration increased initially but declined after 2022. In contrast, compliance with MVPA guidelines improved steadily throughout the study period (2019-2025). The "Double Reduction" policy achieved initial reductions in academic burden and short-term improvements in some health behaviours, but these effects were not sustained. Achieving sustainable improvement requires systemic educational reforms beyond mere workload reduction, addressing the fundamental tension between well-being-oriented policies and the enduring examination-centric ecosystem.

papers.title: Neural dynamics of resting-state EEG microstates in youth major depressive disorder with suicidal ideation.
papers.abstract: Youth major depressive disorder (MDD) is a debilitating condition associated with high rates of suicidal behavior. Although abnormal neuroimaging alterations have been reported in MDD patients with suicidal ideation (SI), little is known about the mechanisms of brain dynamics at high temporal resolution. This cross-sectional study included 177 participants aged 15-30 years: 95 with drug-naïve MDD (53 with SI, 42 without SI) and 82 healthy controls. All participants underwent a standardized 5-minute resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) acquisition. Comprehensive clinical assessments were administered, including the collection of psychosocial data and evaluation of suicide risk using the Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation (BSI-C). Group differences in microstate parameters were analyzed, and correlations between these parameters and clinical variables were examined. Resting-state EEG microstate analysis indicated that the SI group, relative to the NSI group, exhibited higher occurrence, coverage, and duration of microstate A, along with decreased indices for microstate B and reduced occurrence (but not coverage or duration) of microstate D. Alterations in transition probabilities were most prominent in microstates A and B, highlighting specific network-level differences associated with SI. In the SI group, BSI-C scores were positively correlated with the transition probability from C to B. Our findings suggest that young individuals with MDD and SI show specific changes in microstates, especially A and B. These findings reveal altered EEG microstate dynamics associated with SI in young MDD patients and may inform future research on neurophysiological correlates of suicidal ideation.

papers.title: Patterns of sleep duration, quality, and midpoint across pregnancy in a longitudinal cohort study.
papers.abstract: Sleep health is a critical component of maternal well-being, and poor sleep during pregnancy is associated with adverse maternal-fetal and cardiometabolic outcomes. Although sleep across pregnancy has been examined in several longitudinal studies, fewer studies have included frequent repeated assessments in racially and ethnically diverse populations with a high representation of lower socioeconomic status. We aimed to characterize longitudinal patterns of sleep duration, sleep quality, and sleep midpoint across pregnancy; identify groups with similar sleep profiles; and examine maternal and pregnancy characteristics associated with sleep health. This secondary analysis included individuals enrolled in the Human Placenta and Phthalates Study in Norfolk, Virginia and Galveston, Texas (2016-2020). Self-reported sleep duration and quality were collected at up to eight visits (13-36 gestational weeks). Sleep midpoint was calculated from reported bedtime and wake time. Generalized estimating equations evaluated associations between participant characteristics and repeated sleep measures. Group-based trajectory modeling identified joint trajectories of reported bed and wake times for perceived overnight sleep duration and perceived sleep quality; sleep midpoint was excluded because models incorporating it did not converge. Among 303 individuals, 43% were non-Hispanic Black (NHB), 39% non-Hispanic White (NHW), 16% Hispanic/Latina, and 72% had government-assisted health insurance. Across pregnancy, the proportion of individuals reporting short sleep increased modestly, perceived sleep quality worsened, and sleep midpoint remained relatively stable, with no differences in overall patterns by race and ethnicity. On average, NHB individuals were 8% more likely to report short sleep (< 7 h), and Hispanic/Latina individuals reported better sleep quality than NHW individuals. Higher BMI, lower educational attainment, parity, and government insurance were associated with worse sleep across domains. Three joint trajectory groups were identified: "Worst Sleepers" (short duration/poor quality; 60.7%), "Restless Sleepers" (7-9 h/lower quality; 25.4%), and "Best Sleepers" (adequate duration/high quality; 13.9%); 64% of NHB and 53% of nulliparous individuals were classified as "Worst Sleepers." Adverse sleep patterns were common across pregnancy. The findings support evaluating both sleep quantity and perceived quality during prenatal care and investigating modifiable clinical, social, and environmental contributors to persistent sleep difficulties, particularly among groups disproportionately represented in unfavorable sleep profiles.

papers.title: Burnout syndrome, sleep quality and the effect of the practice of physical activities among community pharmacists in Douala, Cameroon: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Burnout is a human psychological response to work stress, increasingly prevalent among healthcare professionals and associated with multiple contributing factors. The present study aimed to determine burnout prevalence and its associations with physical activity (PAc) and poor sleep quality (PSQ) in community pharmacists. A cross-sectional study was conducted among community pharmacists in Douala, Cameroon. Burnout was assessed using the Maslach Burnout Inventory Human Services Survey (MBI-HSS). PSQ and PAc were assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ short form), respectively. Associations were tested using chi-squared tests and bivariate analysis, with statistical significance set at P < 0.05. A total of 136 pharmacists (mean age 32 ± 7 years) with female dominance (n = 72%, 52.9%) were included. The overall prevalence of burnout was 65.4% (n = 89/136), with low severity in 82.0% (n = 73/89), moderate in 7.9% (n = 7/89) and severe in 10.1% (n = 9/89). High emotional exhaustion (EE), high depersonalization and low personal accomplishment were found in 20.6% (n = 28), 14.0% (n = 19) and 51.5% (n = 70) of participants, respectively. Burnout was more (P > 0.05), in males (n = 45, 50.6%), in pharmacists under 30 years old (n = 41, 46.1%) and in those who found work exhausting (n = 29, 32.6%). Likewise, most of the assistants' pharmacists were suffering from burnout (n = 77, 86.5%), more than half of participants with PSQ (n=,62, 69.7%) and moderate PAc (n = 61, 68.5%) were affected by burnout. Ppresence of burnout was significantly associated with taking annual holidays (OR: 0.34; 95% CI. 0.13-0.89; P = 0.02). Pharmacists with other activities were associated with low burnout (OR: 2.29; 95% CI. 1.10-4.77; P = 0.02). Depending on the dimension, pharmacists with PSQ were associated with high or moderate EE (OR: 2.26; 95% CI. 1.10-4.78; P = 0.03). Furthermore, moderate PAc was associated with higher odds of high/moderate depersonalization compared with low PAc (OR: 5.10; 95% CI. 1.41-18.40; P = 0.01) No statistically significant association was found between overall burnout and PAc or PSQ. This study revealed a high prevalence of burnout among community pharmacists, predominantly of low severity. PSQ was associated with high or moderate EE. Even moderate PAc was associated with higher odds of depersonalization.

papers.title: "I'll be alarmed and I'll want to take action": experiences responding to high blood pressures among pregnant women engaged in home blood pressure monitoring.
papers.abstract: Home blood pressure (BP) monitoring is an emerging strategy to increase BP monitoring in pregnancy. Effective programs require women to recognize elevated readings, understand when urgent action is needed, and receive clear, consistent advice after contacting healthcare providers. Challenges in low-resource settings include lower health literacy and limited engagement in health monitoring and antenatal care. This qualitative study explored how women measured and responded to elevated BP readings during a home monitoring intervention at a tertiary hospital in Ghana. We purposively sampled 20 postpartum women who had recorded at least five elevated home BP readings during pregnancy. Semi-structured interviews were conducted from November to December 2024 and examined participants' understanding of high BP, confidence in interpreting readings, responses to elevated values, and experiences communicating with the midwife phoneline. Interviews were coded and analyzed thematically. The Health Belief Model was applied after inductive analysis to organize and interpret the themes. Participants' mean age was 32.6 years. Thirteen were married and four had chronic hypertension.
